name: A/B Testing AI Changes
definition: A/B testing AI changes means comparing a metric across randomized conditions to measure whether a change to an AI system improves outcomes. Hypotheses come from error analysis rather than speculation, and tests may run on a small randomized carve-out cohort or in several parallel improvement tracks before the change reaches everyone.
explanation: The core method is an A/B test: a systematic measurement of quality with a metric, compared across conditions. Shreya frames A/B tests as another form of eval, and Hamel adds that the evals vs. A/B debate is just data science thinking, since the same analytics apply to AI products. Her caution is that people run A/B tests prematurely on hypothetical requirements, while actual errors (such as handoff or text-message issues) differ from what you imagined. So hypotheses should come from error analysis of real failures. Two variants show how to structure the testing. Sharma describes a post-training loop: design a rewards model aimed at an outcome such as price, performance or quality, roll it out, A/B test it rigorously, and tie it to the job to be done or use case where it makes the most sense. The interaction data it generates feeds further learning. She has never seen a single loop for a product; multiple tracks run in parallel, like assembly lines. Tomer Cohen contributed the randomized carve-out cohort. When large-scale experiments on LinkedIn's whole feed caused metric swings and escalations, he carved out a randomized cohort of two million members, a small share of the total, and gave them a substantially different AI-driven experience. Over months they showed dramatic behavior change, strong evidence that the approach could grow the pie rather than just reslot it between teams. That evidence was used to bring the experience to the main product. The cohort stayed in overall metrics because it was small. He also mentions negative tests purely for learning and ad tests on the separated experience.
when_to_use: After error analysis surfaces real problems and you want to test fixes
When tuning or post-training a model toward outcomes such as price, performance or quality
When you want to learn from the interaction data a deployed model generates
Turning around an established product where entrenched flows and metrics resist large-scale experiments
When a big change to an AI algorithm or objective would swing company-wide metrics and trigger escalations
When you need strong evidence from an isolated population before rolling out an AI-driven change broadly
when_not_to_use: As a replacement for error analysis, or with hypotheses invented without looking at data
When leadership explicitly accepts short-term metric hits and you can ship broadly, since carving out is the workaround when that cover does not exist
metric_or_method: Randomized A/B test of an AI change on a product metric, with hypotheses derived from error analysis. Run it on a small randomized carve-out cohort observed over months, or per use case in parallel rewards-design loops, then extend to everyone.
common_pitfalls: Testing hypothetical improvements without looking at data; real errors differ from what you imagined
Treating evals and A/B testing as opposites rather than the same data science thinking
Relying on a single improvement loop for a product; multiple parallel tracks are described instead
Not tying the tuned model to a specific job to be done or use case
Running mass-scale experiments on the whole user base, causing metric swings, team panic and escalations
Expecting quick results; the carve-out cohort's behavior change took months, not a week
Using top-level metrics that every shift moves, instead of metrics specific to the carved-out experience
source_excerpt: I think a lot of people prematurely do A-B tests, because they've never done any error analysis in the first place.
one_liner: Test fixes from error analysis on a randomized carve-out cohort before shipping your AI change to everyone.
codex_prompt_template: I am running an A/B test on an AI change for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. The hypothesis comes from error analysis of real failures: [FAILURE_MODE]. The proposed change is [CHANGE_DESCRIPTION]. The primary metric is [PRIMARY_METRIC], and guardrail metrics are [GUARDRAIL_METRICS]. My data is in [DATA_SOURCE] with columns [USER_ID_COLUMN], [VARIANT_COLUMN], and [OUTCOME_COLUMNS]. Write Python that does the following: (1) Assigns users to control and treatment deterministically by hashing the user ID. Use a randomized carve-out cohort of [COHORT_SIZE_PERCENT]% of users, and keep the cohort stable across the test. (2) Runs a power analysis to estimate the sample size and test duration needed to detect a minimum effect of [MIN_DETECTABLE_EFFECT]. (3) Checks for sample ratio mismatch and covariate balance. (4) Computes the lift in the primary metric with confidence intervals and a significance test, and reports the guardrail metrics. (5) Tracks the metric over [TEST_DURATION] to catch novelty effects and long-term behavior change. (6) Tags failure-mode examples from [FAILURE_MODE] in each arm to confirm the change fixed the real error rather than a hypothetical one. Output a short decision summary: ship, iterate, or stop, with the evidence behind it.

name: Adversarial Red-Team Datasets and Defense Testing
definition: A method for building a dataset of real adversarial prompts, typically crowdsourced through a red-teaming competition, and using it to benchmark AI defenses (prompt instructions, guardrails, safety-tuning, fine-tuning) against motivated attackers, while reading attack-success and detection rates skeptically because any residual success rate is exploitable.
explanation: The core method has three linked steps. (1) Collect attacks: run a public red-teaming competition with prizes and a game format that draws a large global crowd to make models do or say bad things. Schulhoff's first competition gathered 600,000 prompt injection techniques. Crowdsourcing is argued to beat hourly contracted red teams because competitors are strongly incentivized, and rewarding ever-shorter solutions keeps driving improvement after the problem is solved. Tracks can target high-severity harms such as CBRN uplift, and indirect challenges are used for content that cannot be possessed or studied directly. (2) Test defenses empirically: run candidate defenses against the corpus, including obfuscated variants (typos, Base64 or ROT13, story framings), and measure how many attacks still succeed. Schulhoff reports that major AI companies have used the HackAPrompt dataset to benchmark and improve their models. Prompt-based defenses (e.g. 'do not follow malicious instructions', separators, randomized tokens) did not work in HackAPrompt 1.0 in May 2023 and still do not. Guardrails have limited effect against motivated attackers because of the intelligence gap between the guardrail and the main model, for example Base64 input the guardrail cannot understand. Word blocklists built from attack datasets are called insane. Safety-tuning and fine-tuning are described as more effective, especially for narrow harm sets. (3) Interpret scores skeptically: Willison argues that detection or effectiveness rates such as 70% to 85% (Claude system cards) or 97% give a false sense of security, since 97% still means three in a hundred attacks succeed. Filters cannot cover all phrasings, such as the same instruction in Spanish or novel character sequences. Even 100% would not suffice without proof that the attacks are no longer a problem, so design for limited blast radius rather than relying on detection rates. Across all three steps the conclusion is that prompt injection is mitigatable, not solvable.
when_to_use: You want to discover novel jailbreak and prompt injection strategies against a model or agent
You are assessing high-severity harms (e.g. CBRN uplift) where adversarial creativity matters
You are preparing agentic deployments and need adversarial test cases
Choosing between candidate defenses (prompt instructions, guardrails, safety-tuning, fine-tuning) for a deployed model or agent
Verifying that a claimed protection holds against obfuscation attacks such as typos, Base64 or ROT13 encodings, and story framings
Interpreting vendor-reported prompt injection scores
Deciding whether a guardrail is sufficient to protect sensitive actions
when_not_to_use: As a claim or proof that the problem is solved or secure: prompt injection is only mitigatable, and passing a test set cannot guarantee that a new attack will not succeed later
When harmful content is so dangerous (e.g. child sexual abuse material) that it cannot be possessed or studied directly; use indirect challenges instead
Low-stakes applications where leaks cause no real harm and heavy red-teaming is not warranted
metric_or_method: Collect successful adversarial prompts through a prize-driven public competition (rewarding shorter solutions), then run candidate defenses against this corpus, including obfuscated variants, and measure the attack success rate. Treat any detection rate below 100% as insufficient on its own and pair it with architectural limits on blast radius.
common_pitfalls: Relying on contracted red teams paid by the hour who are not strongly incentivized
Assuming patched attacks stay patched: you can patch a bug but not a brain
Treating media reports of prompt injection as evidence of AI-specific vulnerabilities when many are really classical cybersecurity failures
Assuming a defense works because it is published by a large company or is widely proposed
Using a guardrail model less capable than the main model, which can be exploited via encoding and other obfuscation
Blocking attacks by matching common words from prompt injection datasets, or assuming deny-list filters cover all phrasings and languages
Treating a high but sub-100% detection rate as safe, since attackers only need the leftover cases
Normalization of deviance: lack of past incidents increases institutional confidence
source_excerpt: And I went ahead and got a bunch of sponsors together and we ran this event and collected 600,000 prompt injection techniques. And this was the first data set and certainly the largest around that time that had been published. [...] Because if you look at contracted AI red teams, maybe they get paid by the hour, not super incentivized to do a great job. But in this competition setting, people are massively incentivized. And even when they have solved the problem, we've set it up so you're incentivized to find shorter and shorter solutions.
one_liner: Crowdsource attacks in a red-team contest, test your defenses against them, and never trust a 97% block rate.
codex_prompt_template: I have a [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] built on [MODEL_NAME] with these defenses: [DEFENSES_IN_PLACE, e.g. system prompt instructions, input guardrail, safety-tuned model]. I have an adversarial prompt dataset at [ADVERSARIAL_DATASET_PATH] (format: [FORMAT, e.g. JSONL with prompt, attack_category, goal]). Write an eval harness in [LANGUAGE, e.g. Python] that: (1) expands each attack into obfuscated variants (typos, Base64, ROT13, story framing, translation into [LANGUAGES]); (2) runs every original and variant against each defense configuration separately (baseline, prompt-based defense, guardrail, fine-tuned/safety-tuned); (3) uses [JUDGE_METHOD, e.g. string match or LLM judge] to decide if the attack succeeded at achieving [HARMFUL_GOAL]; (4) reports attack success rate and guardrail detection rate per defense, per attack category, and per obfuscation type, with confidence intervals; (5) lists the successful attacks, sorted by shortest prompt first, as regression tests. Also output a summary that flags any defense with a non-zero residual success rate and lists which sensitive actions ([SENSITIVE_ACTIONS]) need architectural blast-radius limits (least privilege, human confirmation) instead of relying on detection.

name: Agentic QA Testing
definition: An automated QA method in which an AI agent acts as a tester. It uses the product end to end (running fixed workflows, sample questions, or simulated end-user requests), records what happens, and the results are checked against past test history or a rubric to flag regressions, breakages, and off-spec responses.
explanation: The core method is to have an agent exercise the product the way a human QA tester or obsessive power-user would, capture the outcome, and assess it. Three variants contributed different pieces. (1) Release-over-release regression testing: a QA tester bot is given a fixed list of about ten key workflows for each bug report or new desktop build. It writes results to a shared Notion document holding past tests and compares them across client versions. It can also try to reproduce incoming bugs and feedback. (2) Rubric-based QA of AI responses: an internal tool has an agent run through many sample questions and follow-ups, record and screenshot the experience, and a model scores it against a comprehensive rubric. The rubric covers rendering correctness (for example LaTeX math without weird characters) and expected response format (for example a visual treatment for a visual query rather than text only). Agents that detect broken output increasingly fix it themselves, creating a feedback loop. (3) Simulated QA swarm with simulated dependencies: for software nobody reads, a swarm of agent testers acts as simulated employees making requests (such as Jira access in a simulated Slack channel) around the clock. Because real services have rate limits, coding agents built clones of Slack, Jira, Okta and others from public API docs and open source client libraries. This ran at about $10,000 a day in tokens, and a passing virtual QA team does not prove the software is secure. Common sub-steps are: define the tests (workflows, questions, or simulated user requests), let the agent drive the product, record results (logs, screenshots), compare to history or a rubric, and feed failures into triage or fixes.
when_to_use: Checking that key workflows improve or hold steady across product releases
Triaging bug reports and feedback by trying to reproduce them
Scaling up the obsessive product use a QA team or power-user PMs would do manually
Responses have format-specific expectations, such as correct math rendering or a visual response for visual queries
Detecting broken or off-spec experiences and feeding them into an automated fix loop
Code is not reviewed by humans and you need alternative evidence of quality
Testing against real third-party systems is blocked by rate limits
Continuous, round-the-clock end-user-style testing is needed
when_not_to_use: You need statistically rigorous or ground-truth-labelled evaluation of model quality (not covered by these sources)
As a replacement for judging whether the product emotionally delights users; feel, motion and haptics are human craft
Budget cannot absorb large token costs (about $10,000/day in the swarm case)
You rely on it alone for security assurance
metric_or_method: Define a fixed set of workflows, sample questions, or simulated user requests. Have QA agents run them against each new build (using simulated dependencies where real services are rate-limited), record results and screenshots, then compare to prior version history and/or score with a comprehensive rubric covering rendering and response format.
common_pitfalls: Not keeping a persistent record of past tests, which removes the basis for release-over-release comparison
Rubric not comprehensive enough to catch rendering issues such as weird characters in math output
Checking only text correctness and missing whether the response format matches the query type, such as visual versus text-only
Assuming a passing virtual QA team means the software is secure; other characteristics need separate checks
Very high token cost for large always-on swarms
Testing against real services hits rate limits; simulated dependencies are needed
Simulated clones are built from public API docs and client libraries, so they may not fully match the real systems
source_excerpt: Use the product as an agent. So, like literally like go to Google, type in a question, go to the AI, ask a follow-up, and then record that experience, screenshot it, and then evaluate what you see based on a really comprehensive rubric. And what we found out was that the model actually was incredibly capable to look at things like, hey, there's a math question, or this is like a school homework thing. Is it doing a great job rendering math and latte? Or is it, you know, emitting weird uh characters? Or if you ask about bioluminescence, is it adding a visual tray, which is what the response should have if you're asking about something visual or is it just text?
one_liner: Deploy AI agents as tireless QA testers that use your product, screenshot results, and flag regressions against…
codex_prompt_template: Build an agentic QA testing harness for [PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION]. Requirements: (1) Define a fixed test suite of [NUM_WORKFLOWS] key workflows / sample questions with follow-ups: [WORKFLOW_LIST]. (2) Write an agent runner using [AGENT_FRAMEWORK_OR_BROWSER_TOOL, e.g. Playwright] that drives the product end to end for each build or release, and records logs, outputs, and screenshots for every step. (3) Implement an LLM-judge scorer that grades each run against this rubric: [RUBRIC_CRITERIA, e.g. LaTeX renders correctly, visual query gets a visual response, expected format present]. Output a score and a short rationale per criterion. (4) Store results in [RESULTS_STORE, e.g. JSON files, Notion, SQLite] keyed by build version, and compare each run to the previous version's results to flag regressions, breakages, and off-spec responses. (5) If [THIRD_PARTY_DEPENDENCIES] are rate-limited, create simple mock/simulated services based on their public API docs. (6) Produce a summary report listing failures with screenshots and repro steps, ready to feed into triage or an automated fix loop. Include a README with how to run it in CI on every new build.

name: AI Reviewer Agents (Cross-Model Critique)
definition: A verification method in which one AI generates output (typically code) and a different model or agent instance reviews, critiques, or debugs it to find errors. Humans stay in the loop by triaging findings, running acceptance tests, or defining the specs the reviewer checks against.
explanation: Core method: a generator model produces output and a separate reviewer model or instance critiques it. The idea is that a second agent finding errors in the first agent's misses may be tractable, trading compute for human cognitive capacity. Taylor's argument (AI Supervising AI) is that a 90%-accurate generator plus a 90%-accurate error-finder gives roughly 99% accuracy, though this assumes the reviewer's errors are independent of the generator's and is given only for argument's sake. Variants and sub-steps: (1) Cross-Model Critique / LLM Council (Andreessen, Rachitsky): one AI writes, another debunks, and the two argue; it is anecdotal, with no metrics or scoring rules. (2) Cross-Model Peer Review with Dev-Lead Rebuttal (Zevi): after manual QA, run /review in the authoring model and reviews in other models such as Codex or Composer on a branch; paste the findings into a /peer-review command that tells the authoring agent to act as dev lead and either fix each issue or explain why it is invalid, repeating until no issues remain, with a /learning opportunity command to understand findings. (3) External Code Review for Diagnosis (Lazar): when your own agent cannot fix a problem, export to GitHub or compress with Repomix, give an independent model (Codex, Claude, ChatGPT) the app description, problem, and console logs, and use it for diagnosis only, applying the fix in the original tool. (4) AI code review as a checklist with human triage: run a review skill over the whole codebase pre-ship and treat output as a checklist, accepting, rejecting, or fixing each item. (5) AI Review plus Human Acceptance Testing (Claude Code team, Krieger): when PRs outgrew line-by-line human review, a different Claude instance reviews them and humans do acceptance testing, with a flagged risk of an unmaintainable codebase. (6) Spec-Based Automated Code Review (Fiona, with a duplicate note on checked-in specs): specs, content design skills, and tests that define what good looks like are checked into the repo and kept current so Claude code review can validate changes against them, linked to test-driven development with the model writing the tests; experts still review areas needing deep subject matter expertise, and how far to push full automation is an open question.
when_to_use: AI-generated code or PR volume exceeds what humans can review line by line
You cannot reliably review AI output yourself (e.g. non-technical PM or builder) and want diverse error detection from other models
Before shipping an AI-built codebase, as a pre-launch pass for state issues, missing error handling, and subtle logic bugs
Your own agent cannot resolve a problem after console-log debugging and you want an independent diagnosis
A single agent's accuracy is not high enough for production and you want to scale oversight without reading every line
You can express what good looks like as a spec, skill, or test checked into the repo for the reviewer to validate against
Several disciplines (PMs, designers, engineers) are checking in code and you need higher confidence
when_not_to_use: When you need guarantees only deterministic verification gives; combine with formal verification and unit tests rather than relying on AI review alone
As a replacement for manual QA, user testing, or human judgment
Areas needing deep subject matter expertise (e.g. distributed systems), where humans should still review
Heavy database migrations or big projects, where non-technical builders should not ship without technical people
When simpler steps such as try-to-fix and console logs would solve the problem
When you cannot tolerate the risk of an unmaintainable or poorly understood codebase
When experience quality is hard to capture in a spec and cannot be verified by an automated reviewer
metric_or_method: Generator model produces output; one or more different models or instances review it (e.g. /review plus Codex or Composer on a branch, or checks against specs checked into the repo); findings go back to the authoring agent as a dev-lead rebuttal to fix or refute until no issues remain; humans triage the findings as a checklist and perform acceptance testing. Combined accuracy can be roughly estimated from the stage accuracies (90% x 90% gives about 99%) only if errors are independent.
common_pitfalls: Blindly accepting every reviewer suggestion or taking findings at face value instead of making the authoring agent fix or justify each one
Assuming the 99% combined accuracy holds when the reviewer's errors are correlated with the generator's
Relying on a single model's self-review, which misses issues other models catch
Letting an external reviewing tool edit code when you do not know how to steer its agent, or omitting the problem description and console logs
Specs drifting out of date with the code, or pushing fully automated review too far without experts in the loop
The codebase becoming unmaintainable or not understandable by the model, and review/merge queues becoming a bottleneck as volume grows
Reviewing the live codebase rather than a branch, and never learning why a finding matters
Having no scoring or reconciliation rule for critiques, since LLM-council accounts give none, and the reviewer's accuracy on experience quality beyond correctness is hard to verify
source_excerpt: they would do very line by line pull request reviews in the way that you would for any other project. And they've just realized Claude is generally right and it's producing pull requests that are probably larger than most people are going to be able to review. So can you use a different Claude to review it and then do the human almost acceptance testing more than trying to review line by line.
one_liner: Let a second AI critique the first one's code, then triage findings and accept or reject by test, not line-by-line…
codex_prompt_template:
You are an independent reviewer agent critiquing code written by a different model. Repository/branch: [BRANCH_OR_PR]. Feature description and intent: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Specs, tests, or acceptance criteria to check against: [SPEC_OR_TEST_PATHS]. Known risk areas: [RISK_AREAS].

Tasks:
1. Review the diff and flag bugs, missing error handling, state issues, subtle logic errors, and spec violations. For each finding give: file/line, severity (high/medium/low), evidence, and a suggested fix.
2. Output findings as a markdown checklist a human can accept, reject, or fix.
3. Write a script that runs the reviewer on [BRANCH_OR_PR], then feeds the findings back to the authoring agent with the instruction: 'Act as dev lead. For each finding, either fix it or explain why it is invalid.' Loop until the reviewer reports no valid issues or [MAX_ROUNDS] rounds are reached.
4. Log per-round counts of findings raised, fixed, and rejected as invalid, and flag any finding the human must triage.
5. Generate acceptance tests for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] that a human can run to confirm the final behavior without reading every line.

Use a different model for review than the one that wrote the code ([REVIEWER_MODEL] vs [AUTHOR_MODEL]) so errors are less correlated.

name: Autonomous Resolution Rate as Agent Outcome Metric
definition: A measure of the share of customer interactions an AI agent solves on its own, with the customer happy and no human involvement (also called call deflection or containment), tracked alongside satisfaction scores like CSAT.
explanation: Taylor describes resolution-based outcomes: the AI agent solves the customer's problem, the customer is happy, and nobody had to pick up the phone. He contrasts this with usage or token counts, which in AI may not correlate with value. A long call that doesn't solve the problem adds negative value. He cites automated resolution rates of 50-90% for Sierra customers and CSAT scores such as 4.6 and 4.7 out of 5. Teams improve the rate (e.g. 65% to 75%) in a virtuous cycle where AI tools identify improvement opportunities, figure out why people are frustrated, and suggest new agent capabilities.
when_to_use: Evaluating customer-facing agents for service or sales where the outcome is clearly measurable and the agent works autonomously
When you want a metric aligned with business value rather than usage
when_not_to_use: When the agent is not autonomous or the outcome can't be measured or attributed; Taylor notes this is not always possible
Don't substitute token or usage counts for outcome measurement
metric_or_method: Automated resolution rate (share of interactions solved without a human and with the customer satisfied), paired with CSAT. Iterate by using AI to surface conversations that failed and why.
common_pitfalls: Using usage or token consumption as a proxy for value; a long call can leave the problem unsolved and produce negative value
Counting an interaction as resolved when the customer left unhappy or had to call again
source_excerpt: So in our industry, basically we say, "Hey, if the AI agent solves the customer's problem, they're happy with it and you didn't have to pick up the phone," there's a pre-negotiated rate for that and we call it resolution based. [...] If you want to go from a 65% automated resolution rate to 75%, we have a billion tools to let AI help you do that, identify opportunities for improvement, figure out why people are frustrated, what new capabilities can we add to our agent to improve the resolution rate? And you let AI put the needles at the top of the haystack on your behalf and I think that's really the way to optimize these systems.
one_liner: Count only the chats your AI agent fully resolves, no human needed and customer happy, then pair that rate with CSAT.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build an eval for autonomous resolution rate for a customer-facing AI agent: [AGENT_DESCRIPTION].

Input: a dataset of conversation logs at [LOG_PATH_OR_SCHEMA]. Each record has the transcript, a human-handoff or escalation flag ([ESCALATION_FIELD]), the customer satisfaction signal ([CSAT_FIELD]), and any outcome or ticket-reopen data ([OUTCOME_FIELD]).

Tasks:
1. Write Python that defines a conversation as 'autonomously resolved' only if (a) no human handoff occurred, (b) the customer's issue was actually solved (use an LLM-as-judge with a clear rubric, and fall back to [RESOLUTION_SIGNAL] such as no reopen within [REOPEN_WINDOW_DAYS] days), and (c) satisfaction is at or above [CSAT_THRESHOLD].
2. Compute the overall resolution rate and CSAT, with 95% confidence intervals, segmented by [SEGMENT_DIMENSIONS] such as intent, channel, and customer tier.
3. Flag the failure cases (escalated, unresolved, or low CSAT). Cluster them by root cause, for example missing knowledge, missing tool or capability, policy ambiguity, or customer frustration. Output the top [N] clusters with example conversation IDs and a suggested new capability or fix for each.
4. Report conversation length versus resolution to show that long calls that do not resolve add negative value, and compare resolution rate against raw usage or token counts.
5. Produce a weekly trend report so I can track movement from [CURRENT_RATE]% toward [TARGET_RATE]%.

Return runnable code, a sample output table, and the judge prompt used for the resolution check.

name: Bad vs. Sad Severity Framework
definition: A high-level quality framework that sorts poor experiences into 'bad' (a very bad, irrecoverable error) and 'sad' (a recoverable pain point). Each team defines what counts as bad and sad for its own product surface or service, sets a goal against those definitions, and uses them alongside raw performance and reliability numbers to decide what to address first.
explanation: Raw performance or reliability dashboards are hard to interpret across many product surfaces, because it is unclear whether a given number is good or bad, and dashboards differ per surface, so it is hard to zoom out to an overall theme. The bad/sad framework adds a simple severity lens on top of those numbers. The method: (1) each team (surface or service owner) defines what is bad and what is sad for its area, (2) it sets its own goal against those definitions, (3) it focuses first on eliminating bad experiences, and (4) it tracks sads separately and watches how they stack up and trend over time, since stacked sads can turn into bad. Both members describe the same core idea and add complementary emphasis. One member stressed the sequencing of eliminating bad first and then monitoring sad trends, with the aim of proactive quality and earlier detection. The other stressed the shared vocabulary that lets teams own their thresholds while speaking a common language, and used the framework to decide what to address first. Example given for a CLI: a crash is bad because work is lost (crash rate as the bad metric), while flickering is sad because it is recoverable. The framework is motivated by high code and feature velocity, where manual review alone is not enough.
when_to_use: You have many product surfaces or services, each with its own dashboards, and it is hard to judge whether a number is good
You want proactive, earlier detection of quality problems and trends over time
Code and feature velocity or shipping velocity is too high to rely on manual review alone
You want teams to own their quality thresholds while sharing a common vocabulary
You need to prioritize which experiences to fix first
when_not_to_use: You would rely only on raw performance or reliability numbers with no notion of what a bad experience is
metric_or_method: Per-team definitions of 'bad' (irrecoverable errors, e.g. CLI crash rate) and 'sad' (recoverable pain points, e.g. flickering), tracked on dashboards as trends over time against a goal set by each team.
common_pitfalls: Relying only on raw numbers such as time to load or reliability, without a framework for what counts as a bad experience
Ignoring sads: many individual sad experiences can stack up and add up to something bad, so they still need monitoring
Dashboards that differ per surface area make it hard to zoom out to an overall theme of the experience
Not having each team define its own bad and sad for its surface and set a goal, leaving thresholds ambiguous

name: Benchmark Contamination and Gaming Defense
definition: A benchmark hygiene practice that keeps models from learning the correct answers of a public benchmark. It withholds answer keys and labels from public posts, publishes only aggregated results, and keeps secret alternate prompts in reserve to check whether labs trained specifically for the public prompt.
explanation: The method combines prevention and detection. Prevention (from the data contamination note): posts that document LLM failures and reveal the answers can end up in future models' training data and contaminate the benchmark. The authors would avoid this by not revealing which solution was AI (or human) and only tallying aggregated results. The trade-off is lower accessibility, because people cannot rerun the evaluation without the answer key, and the authors hope researchers have better suggestions. Detection (from the pelican SVG note): Willison's pelican-riding-a-bicycle SVG prompt is a qualitative benchmark. Drawings are compared by eye across models or thinking levels, and it exercises text models' code generation and spatial reasoning. He observed a correlation between pelican quality and general model quality, though he cannot explain why. To detect gaming he holds secret alternates, such as an ocelot on a moped. Good pelicans with bad ocelots would suggest cheating. In practice, Gemini 3.1 also handled other animal and vehicle combinations, so the check was not conclusive. Together: keep answers private, publish aggregates, and maintain held-out variants of the public prompt, while accepting reduced reproducibility and imperfect proof of gaming.
when_to_use: Publishing or maintaining a public benchmark that future models may be trained on
You suspect labs are tuning to a public benchmark and want a way to detect it
You want a quick, qualitative sanity check of relative model capability that is easy to eyeball
Comparing the same model at different thinking or reasoning levels
when_not_to_use: Internal one-off evaluations where the content won't be published or scraped
You need a rigorous, quantitative measure for a specific product requirement
You need a validated predictor of performance on your own task, since the correlation is unexplained
Full public reproducibility is required, since withholding answer keys prevents others from running the evaluation themselves
metric_or_method: Withhold answer keys and AI/human labels from public posts, publish only aggregated results, and compare outputs on the public prompt against held-out secret alternate prompts (e.g. ocelot on a moped) to detect overfitting.
common_pitfalls: Revealing correct answers or documented failures online, which future models can learn from
Reduced accessibility and reproducibility when answer keys are withheld
Labs may cover the alternate combinations too, making cheating hard to prove
Once a benchmark becomes a meme, labs are aware of it and may optimise for it
The correlation with general capability is unexplained and may not hold
Judging by eye is subjective
source_excerpt: One big problem is [data contamination](https://ehudreiter.com/2024/03/12/data-contamination-worries/), where the LLMs learn which answers are “correct” when they are trained on fresh data from the internet, which includes posts like this one that document common LLM failures and reveal what the correct answers are. With an updated post, we would avoid data contamination of the evaluation benchmark by not revealing which solution was AI and just tallying the aggregated results.
one_liner: Keep answer keys private, publish only aggregates, and test secret prompt variants to catch benchmark gaming.
codex_prompt_template:
I maintain a public benchmark for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] and want to defend it against training-data contamination and benchmark gaming. Write code and a short plan that does the following:
1. Takes my benchmark items in [BENCHMARK_DATA_FORMAT] and splits them into a public prompt set and a private held-out set of [NUM_SECRET_VARIANTS] secret alternate prompts. Each alternate should test the same underlying skill as a public prompt but differ in surface details (for example, an ocelot on a moped instead of a pelican on a bicycle).
2. Strips answer keys and labels (such as which output was AI vs human) from anything intended for public release, and outputs only aggregated scores per model (mean, confidence interval, N) in [OUTPUT_FORMAT].
3. Runs each model in [MODEL_LIST] on both the public prompts and the secret variants, scores the outputs with [SCORING_METHOD], and computes the gap between public-prompt and secret-variant performance per model.
4. Flags models whose public score is much higher than their secret-variant score, using a threshold of [GAP_THRESHOLD] and a bootstrap or permutation test, and reports the result as suggestive evidence of overfitting, not proof.
5. Documents the trade-off that withholding keys reduces reproducibility, and suggests how trusted researchers could get controlled access to the answer key.
Return the code, a sample report, and a list of limitations, including cases where a model generalizes well to the variants so the check is inconclusive.

name: Blind Pairwise Human Preference Evaluation
definition: A head-to-head human evaluation in which raters see two (or more) responses to the same prompt or task, with the source hidden, and choose which is better. Votes are aggregated into a win rate or vote share per answer or model, optionally paired with a guess-the-AI question, explicit tie handling, and private voting.
explanation:
Core method: show an AI response and a human response (or outputs from different model versions) side by side without saying which is which, and have raters vote for the better one. The winner is determined by vote share, and comments explaining the vote add qualitative insight. The authors used the Coke vs. Pepsi analogy for blinding: strong attitudes toward AI, positive or negative, can skew results if the source is revealed. In their polls the AI won 2 of 3 tasks (55%, 68%, and 42% for the third).

Variants and sub-steps: (1) Guess-the-AI detection rate: each rater also guesses which answer was AI. In the polls 77%, 70% and 65% correctly identified the AI in Tasks 1-3, yet many still preferred the AI answer. The guess data and comments revealed tells (comprehensiveness, verbosity, lack of grammatical errors or niche references), which were used to adjust the prompt. (2) Counting ties as AI wins: equal-quality outcomes are credited to the AI because a human worker is far more expensive. AI win rate = (AI votes + tied votes) / total votes, reported alongside the strict win rate (Task 2: 68%, or 86% with ties credited). (3) Private blind voting: public feeds led to groupthink, guessing how others would vote, and many 'neither was good' answers. The authors recommend private votes (inspired by LMSYS Chatbot Arena), repeated periodically as attitudes toward AI change. (4) Human win-rate evals against previous models (Nguyen): trainers or internal raters see a prompt with several model completions and pick the best, for example the best comment or edit. Aggregated choices give a continuous win rate, and each new model should win over previous ones. This is the more prevalent human eval type, and what you measure determines which eval type to use.
when_to_use: Output quality is subjective and there is no ground-truth label
You want to know whether AI output can match or beat a human baseline on a real job task
People's attitudes toward AI could bias ratings if the source were revealed
You want to know whether AI is preferred even when raters can tell it is AI, or to find stylistic tells to remove via prompt changes
Judging whether AI is good enough to substitute for human work where cost and speed matter (with ties credited and disclosed)
Comparing a new model version against previous versions during iterative training
Tracking changing attitudes toward AI over time with periodic private tests
when_not_to_use: You need a rigorous, scientific measurement (the authors say their small poll was not intended as scientific)
Tasks have objective correct answers that can be checked automatically or with deterministic pass/fail evals
Quality parity isn't sufficient and the AI must clearly beat the human, or cost advantages don't apply (tie-as-win scoring)
Source guessing is irrelevant to the decision being made (skip the detection question)
Public discussion is itself the goal (private voting not needed)
metric_or_method: Vote share or win rate per answer/model in a blind pairwise (or multi-way) human preference poll, with ties tallied separately. Optionally report AI win rate with ties credited alongside the strict rate, the percent of raters correctly identifying the AI versus the percent preferring it, and qualitative comments. Collect votes privately and repeat on a schedule or across model versions.
common_pitfalls: Revealing which answer is AI skews votes
Public voting invites groupthink, signaling, and 'neither was good' posturing; use private voting
Counting ties as AI wins inflates results if undisclosed; ties can mean both were bad, so report the strict win rate too
Some raters only vote preference and others only guess the source, so totals don't reconcile
Changing prompts between platforms makes results not directly comparable (X 38% vs. LinkedIn 59% for AI after prompt changes)
Manual tallying of social comments is slow and open to interpretation, and a sample of three tasks is not comprehensive
A new model that wins on one behavior may regress elsewhere, so also watch other intelligence evals
Raters may lack domain expertise to judge outputs outside their field
source_excerpt: This adds another interesting dimension to evaluations where the responses are public: there’s a risk of groupthink once the vote sways in one direction, and bias if our mental models of what other people think about AI are out of date. [...] It’s best to run private blind tests periodically to see what people really think about AI results.
one_liner: Hide which answer is AI, let raters pick the winner, and count ties as AI wins to see if AI beats humans.
codex_prompt_template: Build a blind pairwise human preference evaluation for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Inputs: a CSV of [DATASET_SIZE] prompts, each with response A and response B from [SOURCE_A] and [SOURCE_B] (e.g., AI vs. human, or new vs. previous model version). Write Python that: (1) randomizes left/right position and strips source labels to create a blinded rating sheet; (2) generates a private-voting form or CSV template with fields for preferred answer (A/B/tie/neither good), a guess-which-is-AI question, and a free-text comment; (3) ingests the completed votes and computes per-source strict win rate, tie rate, and win rate with ties credited to [CREDITED_SOURCE], with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals; (4) reports the AI-detection accuracy versus the preference rate, and the share of raters who preferred the AI answer even though they identified it as AI; (5) clusters the comments to surface stylistic tells (verbosity, comprehensiveness, lack of typos) for prompt adjustments; (6) checks inter-rater agreement and position bias. Output a summary table and a short markdown report with recommendations on whether [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] is good enough to ship or substitute for human work.

name: Capability Backlog Re-Testing on New Models
definition: A process of keeping failed or not-yet-reliable tasks, prototypes and personal probes in a backlog and re-running them each time a new model is released, so you can tell when a missing capability has arrived instead of assuming past limits still hold.
explanation: The core method is to stop treating a failure on today's model as final. Capture the task (a prototype, a hard task, or a reference artifact) in a reusable form, then re-run it on every new model release and compare the result to the earlier baseline. Willison supplied the backlog idea: he constantly throws tasks at models that he expects to fail, learns the current limits, and keeps the failures so he can spot the first model that succeeds. Shipper supplied the 'turn the rock over' habit: he re-runs a personally important hard task, and his senior engineer benchmark moved from about 30 to about 60 out of 100 on a new model. Rauch supplied a personal regression benchmark: he rebuilds his own website with v0 after each model generation. It took 10 to 15 prompts on the previous model and two on the latest, and he also compared the quality of the output (accessibility) to his own code. Kalinowski supplied the daily-use version: use AI on real work to find boundaries (e.g. surfaces or point clouds but not solid CAD, or physical reasoning like folding paper), then re-test every release. Cat Wu supplied the prototype swap-in variant: build products that don't work yet so you know what is missing, then swap the new model into the prototype. Code review became reliable enough to rely on before merging PRs only with Opus 4.5/4.6 and Sonnet 4.6. The Anthropic computer-use story supplied the harness version: park the failed project, run it in an eval harness on each new model, and read transcripts to confirm it now succeeds more often than not. The failed project is externalized as an eval and shared with research. The failure mode is being 'capability blind': trying once, never retrying, and concluding models will never do it. Rauch's adversarial fitness function adds a way to fill the backlog: push the product with wild ideas to find what it can't build, and check that successes hold up on quality and performance. Most variants are informal and anecdotal. A harness with transcript review adds rigor, but none of the notes claim statistical robustness.
when_to_use: A prototype or feature fails or is not reliable enough to launch because current model capability or accuracy is insufficient
A new model is released and you want to quickly detect step-change improvements (e.g. agentic or computer use, code review reliability)
You want to calibrate your sense of what AI can and can't do on real work, since past estimates are outdated
You have a stable, personally relevant task or reference artifact with a known baseline that works as a capability probe
You want to hand the research team a concrete, reusable eval of what models can't yet do
You want the team to stress-test beyond happy-path demos to discover boundaries
when_not_to_use: You need rigorous, controlled, statistically robust comparisons between models; informal probes are single anecdotal tasks
The project fails for reasons unrelated to model capability, such as unsolved user problems or lack of product-market fit
Features already work reliably with the current model
The team has no conviction in the idea; a team assigned an area it isn't excited about produces a poor product
As a replacement for systematic, repeatable test sets
metric_or_method: Maintain a backlog of previously failed tasks, prototypes or reference artifacts with recorded baselines. Re-run each on every new model release, via manual probes or an eval harness. Compare against the prior result (e.g. score, prompt count, or whether success beats failure), read transcripts to confirm the improvement, and judge against the launch bar. No formal metric is specified.
common_pitfalls: Becoming capability blind: trying something once, never retrying or building an eval, and concluding models will never do it
Relying on stale intuition or judging from an older model instead of the latest one, or assuming past failures or boundaries still hold
Not recording the baseline, so comparisons stay anecdotal; relying on a single task that may not generalize
Waiting to build until the model is good enough, so you don't know what is missing, or launching before accuracy is high enough
Only testing easy prompts, or accepting output that looks right but isn't performant or real (e.g. surfaces versus solid CAD)
Throwing a project away too early, or building too far ahead of what the models can do
Not reading transcripts, which makes it hard to confirm an apparent improvement is real
Ignoring new models because trying them feels scary, or company restrictions delaying access to the latest models
source_excerpt: One fitness function that I'm keeping in my head is I really want to find the thing that it cannot build with v0. [...] I'm part of the team that is really trying to break this and say, "Can it not build something?" And even when it does build it, we're very obsessed with quality and performance. It has to be real. That's our commitment to our users.
one_liner: Keep failed AI tasks in a backlog and re-run them on every new model to catch the moment a capability arrives.
codex_prompt_template: Build a capability backlog re-testing harness in [LANGUAGE, e.g. Python]. Requirements: 1) Store each backlog item as a JSON/YAML file with fields: id, description, input prompt or prototype entry point, success criteria (programmatic check or LLM-judge rubric), launch bar, baseline model, baseline result (score, number of prompts needed, or pass/fail), date added, and notes on the failure mode. Seed it with these items: [LIST_OF_FAILED_TASKS_OR_PROTOTYPES]. 2) Write a runner that takes a list of models [NEW_MODEL_NAMES], runs every backlog item [N_RUNS_PER_ITEM] times per model through [MODEL_API_OR_AGENT_HARNESS], and saves full transcripts and outputs per run. 3) Score each run against the success criteria and compute the pass rate per item and model. 4) Generate a report comparing each new model to the stored baseline. It should flag items that crossed the launch bar of [PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD], items that improved without crossing it, and regressions. For flagged items, include the transcript paths so a human can confirm the success is real and not a fluke. 5) Add a command to append new items, including adversarial 'wild idea' probes of [PRODUCT_AREA], and to export unresolved items as a standalone eval set to share with the model research team. Include a README with usage and a sample run.

definition: A framework for acting on eval insights through three levers: model learning (post-training, updating weights), context learning (what information the agent sees), and harness learning (system prompt, tool schemas, control flow, routing, retries).

name: Code-Based Evaluators
definition: Automated evaluators written as code, such as unit-test-style assertions, string tests, exact-match or schema checks, and comparisons against ground-truth labels, that detect an objective, rule-based failure mode in an output or trace without calling an LLM and return pass/fail.
explanation: The core method is to write a Python function or assertion that checks an output or trace against a clear rule and returns pass or fail. These checks are fast, cheap, and deterministic, so they can run on thousands of traces or in CI, and they are often quicker on a first pass than an LLM judge, which needs inference and calibration. Typical checks include valid JSON, markdown, or short length, a required keyword or user ID present, generated code that is valid and runs without error, and API calls that are well formed. Several members add variants. Agent assertions work like unit tests: they check whether the agent granted a required concession and compare its tool calls with the expected outcome to measure instruction-following accuracy. Tool-call checks go further: if tool calls are persisted as JSON in an array, exact match looks for a specific tool call with specific arguments, and schema validation checks JSON blobs and message envelopes against expected structure, all free to run. A ground-truth-label variant uses hand-labeled examples, such as conversations that should or should not trigger a feature like Canvas, or checks that an extracted time like 7:00 PM matches what the user said, scored as pass/fail accuracy. A related programmatic-accuracy variant scores prompts or techniques on verifiable datasets such as math or reasoning questions, where the answer can be compared automatically. That variant also shows a bias: evidence skews toward verifiable tasks, while valuable open-ended tasks, like writing interview questions, are hard to score automatically. Code-based evals are a weak signal for subjective qualities such as tone, relevance, or reasoning quality, where an LLM judge or human review fits better. Not every failure needs an eval either; some are simple engineering errors fixed by editing the prompt.
when_to_use: The failure mode is objective and rule-based, such as format, length, a required phrase or user ID, or valid JSON
Checking tool calls, arguments, or message envelopes for an agent against expected outcomes
Verifying generated code is valid and runs, or that API calls are correct
Scoring decision behaviors or structured extraction where hand-labeled ground truth exists
Comparing prompt variants on datasets with known answers, such as math or reasoning
Running fast, cheap, deterministic checks on many traces or in CI
As a quick first-pass eval before investing in LLM judges
when_not_to_use: Subjective or open-ended qualities such as tone, relevance, reasoning quality, or which edit is better
Complex judgment calls, such as deciding whether to hand off to a human
Free-form text answers where exact or substring matching would be unreliable
Open-ended generative tasks where success is hard to score automatically
Failures that a simple prompt edit trivially fixes and that do not need an eval
metric_or_method: Programmatic pass/fail assertions on outputs or traces (valid JSON, required keyword, tool-call exact match, schema validation, runs without error), aggregated as accuracy against expected results or ground-truth labels.
common_pitfalls: Using an LLM judge for something a simple rule can check, adding cost and calibration work
Applying exact or substring matching to free-text LLM answers, which gives false passes
Relying on code checks for subjective or open-ended quality, where they give a weak signal
Labeling only positive cases and forgetting conversations where a feature should not trigger
Over-generalizing from math or reasoning benchmark results to subjective or expressive tasks
Neglecting valuable tasks simply because they are hard to automate
Writing evals for errors that are fixed trivially by prompt changes

name: Confidence Intervals and Significance Testing on Eval Results
definition: A statistical-rigor practice for eval results: attach confidence intervals and proper sampling to reported rates, and accept that one variant beats another only if the difference is statistically significant, practically meaningful, and holds on fresh data and newer models.
explanation: The core method is to stop reporting bare point estimates. Add confidence intervals, calibration, and proper sampling so the same numbers become more meaningful, and test whether differences between variants are statistically significant and practically meaningful. The first member (Confidence Intervals on Eval Scores) contributed the sample-size and cost side. If two evaluators score 84% and 88% on 50 traces, a 4-point gain is small and 50 examples are not enough to know whether it is real. Bigger gains and paired designs need far fewer samples, and expensive rigor should be reserved for numbers that gate a shipping decision or go to company leaders. The second member (Statistical Significance Check for Prompt Technique Claims) contributed the skeptical-claims variant, applied to prompt techniques such as role prompting, threats, or tips. Schulhoff describes studies testing about a thousand roles where accuracy differed by about 0.01, which was not significant. Re-running the analyses on new datasets found no predictable effect of roles. For threats and promises there are only small Twitter experiments, no large-scale studies. Lenny adds that even a significant 0.1 gain may not matter in practice. Schulhoff concludes roles help for expressive tasks (style) but not accuracy-based tasks. Sub-steps: compare variants on a sizable dataset, compute intervals or run significance tests, check practical significance, use paired designs and larger samples for small gains, and re-run on new datasets and model versions.
when_to_use: When a number gates a shipping decision
When reporting numbers to company leaders
When comparing two evaluators or versions with small differences
Deciding whether a viral prompting tip (roles, tipping, threats) is worth adopting in a product prompt
Comparing prompt variants on accuracy-based tasks where differences are small
Re-validating a prompting technique when moving to a new model generation
when_not_to_use: For low-stakes numbers, where expensive rigor should be skipped
Expressive or style-driven tasks (writing, summarizing), where roles are useful and accuracy-style significance testing is not the right yardstick
metric_or_method: Confidence intervals on reported rates, calibration, proper sampling, and paired designs; significance tests plus practical-significance checks on accuracy differences between variants, with larger samples for small gains and re-runs on new datasets and model versions.
common_pitfalls: Reporting bare point estimates
Concluding an improvement is real from 50 samples and a 4-point gain
Reading meaning into tiny accuracy gaps (e.g. 0.01) as if they were real effects
Drawing conclusions from small, informal tests (e.g. Twitter experiments)
Assuming a technique that worked on older models (GPT-3 era) still works on modern ones
Judging a technique as effective without a practical-significance check
Applying expensive rigor everywhere instead of where it matters

name: Continuous Calibration / Eval Improvement Flywheel
definition: A continuous loop, modeled on CI/CD, for building and sustaining evals on non-deterministic AI features. Teams scope capability, curate a dataset, design evals and deploy with low agency. They then run evals on live traffic, manually review failures, fix the product and the evals, and add each discovered failure to the golden dataset. The cycle repeats while agency rises as behavior becomes predictable.
explanation:
The core method is Continuous Calibration/Continuous Development (CC/CD), described in two overlapping members. Continuous Development scopes capability, curates a dataset of expected inputs and outputs, sets up the application, designs evals, and deploys. Continuous Calibration runs evals on live data, analyzes behavior and error patterns, and applies fixes, including new metrics for emerging patterns. The speakers built it after end-to-end agents with large workflows became undebuggable and one customer support product was shut down because of constant hot fixes. Teams start with low-agency, high-control features and let the system earn more agency each cycle. The starting dataset is deliberately not comprehensive, because users behave in unpredicted ways and existing metrics only catch known errors. Not every error needs a new metric: one-off errors, such as a poorly defined tool, can simply be fixed.

The Iterative Four-Phase Eval Workflow gives the build-from-scratch sequence. Phase 1 collects real interactions, documents edge cases and builds a human-labeled dataset. Phase 2 runs first-pass eval prompts against it, aiming for at least 90% accuracy versus human labels, and looks for failure patterns. Phase 3 refines eval prompts, expands the dataset and iterates on the agent prompt. Phase 4 monitors production continuously, compares to real user outcomes and builds dashboards.

Living Dataset via Production Traffic Skimming is the data-maintenance step. After launch, real inputs and outputs are sampled, an internal team scores them manually, the judge is run on them, and agreement is checked. This keeps the golden dataset current and the judge calibrated, since production data goes stale. It treats an eval as a dataset, not a one-time thing.

The Eval Improvement Flywheel closes the loop. CI evals prevent regressions, and monitoring finds new or drifting failures, for example a spike in location ambiguity such as confusing West Berkeley with a non-existent Berkeley West. Manual review of flagged traces identifies the cause. The team improves the product, for example by refining a prompt, and adds the example to the CI golden dataset, so every discovered failure makes the system permanently more robust.

Eval Redesign Against Real Behavior is a sub-step of applying fixes. Evals are usually designed from a reference dataset that reflects expected behavior. If live review shows evals missed issues or gave high scores to flawed outputs, rebuild them. Multiple rounds are normal, and fixes can be re-evaluated on data you already have without redeploying each time.
when_to_use: Shipping an AI feature whose behavior is non-deterministic and cannot be fully predicted upfront
Building toward an agentic or autonomous system where error risk grows with agency
After deployment, when policies, user behavior, or failure modes may change over time
Moving from ad hoc checks to continuous improvement and operationalizing an eval suite
When live manual review shows high eval scores on flawed outputs or real behavior diverges from the reference dataset
When PMs, engineers and subject matter experts need to align on expected product behavior
when_not_to_use: Deterministic software where inputs and outputs are fixed and correctness is binary
One-off sanity checks or a one-time launch checklist with no plan to iterate
Before launch when no user traffic exists; use synthetic evals until real data is available
As the only way to constrain autonomy; the speakers say there are many ways to do it
metric_or_method: Loop: scope capability and curate data, set up application, design evals, deploy to a small cohort, run evals on live traffic, sample and human-score outputs, check judge agreement against human labels (target at least 90%), analyze error patterns, fix product and evals, add failures to the golden dataset, repeat while gradually raising agency.
common_pitfalls: Jumping to a fully autonomous end-to-end agent before testing what happens when it gets things wrong, leading to endless hot fixes
Assuming the initial dataset is comprehensive, or letting it go stale
Treating deployment as a finish line, or the eval system as a static dashboard
Fixing the product without adding the failure to the CI golden dataset
Treating the initial eval design as final, over-optimizing on the reference dataset, or trusting high scores without manual spot-checks
Letting model changes (e.g., 4o deprecated in favor of 5), policy changes, or user behavior shifts invalidate calibration or judge agreement unnoticed
Making evals too complex too quickly, building metrics for every one-off error, or overengineering before there is data
Not testing edge cases or not validating eval results against real user feedback
source_excerpt: As you go through steps 4 and 5 again, you may find consistent places where the evals missed issues or gave high scores to flawed outputs. So step 6 may also involve revisiting and rebuilding your evals—and that’s completely normal.
one_liner: Ship low-agency, eval live traffic, review failures, feed them to the golden set, then raise agency each loop.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build a Continuous Calibration / Eval Improvement Flywheel for an AI feature.

Feature description: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]
Current agency level (e.g. suggest-only, human-approved, autonomous): [AGENCY_LEVEL]
Production trace source and format: [TRACE_SOURCE_AND_FORMAT]
Existing golden dataset path (JSONL, may be empty): [GOLDEN_DATASET_PATH]
Known failure modes so far: [KNOWN_FAILURE_MODES]
LLM judge model: [JUDGE_MODEL]

Write a Python project that implements the loop:
1. Sampler: pull a random sample of [SAMPLE_SIZE] production traces per [SAMPLING_WINDOW], plus all traces flagged by simple signals (errors, thumbs-down, retries, escalations).
2. Judge runner: score each trace with an LLM-as-judge prompt for each metric in [EVAL_METRICS]. Output a pass/fail label and a short rationale.
3. Human review queue: export a CSV or JSONL with trace, judge verdict and an empty column for the human label and failure-category note.
4. Calibration check: after labels are filled, compute judge-vs-human agreement per metric (accuracy, precision, recall, Cohen's kappa) and flag any metric below [AGREEMENT_TARGET, e.g. 0.90]. Print the disagreement examples where the judge gave high scores to flawed outputs.
5. Failure clustering: group human-labeled failures by category and show the counts, with a flag for new categories not in [KNOWN_FAILURE_MODES]. Separate recurring patterns that need a new metric from one-off bugs that need only a fix.
6. Flywheel update: append each confirmed failure to the golden dataset with fields {input, bad_output, expected_behavior, failure_category, date_added}. Dedupe against existing rows.
7. Regression gate: a CI-style script that runs the full golden dataset against the current product and judge, and fails if the pass rate drops below [REGRESSION_THRESHOLD].
8. Agency gate: a report that recommends whether to raise, hold or lower agency, based on the pass rate over the last [N_CYCLES] cycles and the severity of the failures.

Use clear modules, type hints and a config file. Include a small synthetic example run and a README that explains how to run one calibration cycle.

name: Conversation and Query-Stream Classification
definition: Analyze real user conversations and query logs, using classifiers and targeted log review, to learn what people use an AI product for, which use cases are growing, and where the experience is failing them, while complementing the aggregate view with hands-on qualitative review and interviews.
explanation: The core method is to look at what users actually do instead of guessing. Run classifiers over user conversations to tag them and measure use-case distribution and growth, without anyone having to read every conversation. Nick Turley's contribution: he built the data science team before the product team because interviews alone could not keep up. Interviews of 15 minutes each all week kept surfacing new things, and classifiers revealed use cases and trends at scale. He still invests heavily in qualitative review for empathy, reads external sources like TikTok threads, and stops interviewing once he can predict what the next person will say. Stein's contribution is a query-stream variant focused on failure discovery. Reviewing real queries in AI Overviews showed people asking harder questions the product could not answer, queries where AI Overviews did not appear, and users appending the word AI to queries to force AI behavior. The team read these as signs they were failing users daily, which motivated building AI Mode. Later, real query data from the Labs release was used to see what people used it for and to tune it. Together: use classifiers for breadth and growth of use cases, mine the query stream for unanswered, untriggered, and workaround queries, and keep qualitative review and interviews in the loop for empathy and emergent behavior.
when_to_use: For general-purpose AI products with open-ended, emergent usage
To decide which use cases to improve systematically
To complement qualitative learning when interview volume cannot cover the breadth of usage
Finding coverage gaps in an AI feature that triggers on only some queries
Deciding whether a new AI capability or mode is needed, based on observed user behavior
when_not_to_use: As the only input; qualitative review is still important for empathy
When no real usage logs exist yet; use testers or qualitative methods instead
metric_or_method: Classifier-based tagging of conversations to measure use-case distribution and growth, plus review of the real query stream for unanswered or harder questions, queries where the AI feature does not appear, and workaround behaviors such as appending 'AI', complemented by interviews (continued until the next answer is predictable) and qualitative review.
common_pitfalls: Relying only on interviews and missing breadth
Relying only on aggregate classifications and losing qualitative empathy
Assuming you know the use cases in advance, when many are emergent
Dismissing hard queries as not the most addressable next thing instead of treating them as failures
Noticing the behavior but not building a solution for the underlying user problem

name: Converting User Feedback and Failures into Eval Sets
definition: A method for turning user feedback and real-world failures into eval sets. You dig into what the feedback actually means, require a reproducible example (shared chat or exact prompts), collect a small set of failing examples with a golden or ideal answer, and standardize them so researchers and ML teams can consume them as eval or training data.
explanation: The core method: take user feedback, work out what users specifically mean, confirm the failure is reproducible and consistent, decide whether it is a big enough issue, then collect a small set of failing examples (prompt plus golden answer) and standardize them into the eval repository. If the eval consistently catches the failure, it is doing its job. Building an Eval Set from User Feedback contributed this core flow. Penn's example: early Claude 2 feedback said it was 'not good at following instructions'; asking users for exact situations, prompts and responses showed about 80% of complaints were really about not writing the right JSON. The team generated 30 to 40 failing examples with golden answers and made them the eval. Structured output was fundamental to making Claude a good agent. Reproducible Failure Examples (Shared Chats) contributed the intake step: Logan Kilpatrick says OpenAI needs shared chats or tangible, reproducible examples including the actual prompts, and cites the 'model laziness' reports as the cautionary case where vague complaints gave the team nothing to investigate. A concrete example someone else can rerun turns an impression into a debuggable case. PM-Authored Behavior Spreadsheet (Current vs Ideal) contributed an authoring variant: PMs or model designers fill a spreadsheet with tabs, one row per example, with columns for current behavior, ideal behavior and why, and notes. It serves as eval data and sometimes training data, and lets non-research PMs and designers contribute. Real-World Failure Cases Over Saturated Benchmarks contributed the strategic rationale: Nick Turley argues academic benchmarks are increasingly saturated, so the source of improvement targets is shipping and getting use-case distribution back. Failures become a concrete message to ML teams ('people are trying to do X and the model is failing in these ways'), and some risks, like sycophancy, would not have been found in a lab without real users and experts.
when_to_use: When you receive vague feedback like 'bad at following instructions' or 'the model's lazier' and need to pin down the specific failure
When you want a quick, small eval to hand to researchers
When standard benchmarks no longer differentiate model quality
When you need concrete, prioritized improvement targets for ML teams
When non-research PMs and designers should contribute eval cases or capture gaps between current and ideal behavior
When a perceived regression is hard to diagnose because the triggering prompts are unknown
When a capability (e.g. structured output) underpins downstream agent behavior
when_not_to_use: When the failure can't be reproduced or isn't consistent
When the issue isn't big enough to justify an eval
When you need scalable automated measurement; a hand-built spreadsheet or small set should not be the only eval
For frontier-model safety releases, where a separate rigorous process (red teaming, system card, external input) applies rather than fast shipping
metric_or_method: Dig into feedback to find the exact failure, require a reproducible example (shared chat or exact prompts), collect roughly 30-40 failing examples as prompt plus golden/ideal answer (optionally with rationale and notes in a spreadsheet), verify the eval consistently catches the failure, then add it to the eval repository.
common_pitfalls: Taking feedback at face value without learning what users specifically mean
Accepting vague impressions or reports without the prompts, examples or shared chat that triggered the problem
Not checking that the failure is reproducible and consistent before building the eval
Not standardizing the examples into a form researchers can consume
Recording ideal behavior without the 'why', which gives less usable signal
Relying on saturated academic benchmarks to judge real quality
Polishing the wrong things before you know what people actually do
Using 'ship to learn' as an excuse never to follow through and polish once use cases are known

Include a short README describing how ML teams can consume the file as eval or training data.

name: Cross-Model Comparison
definition: Running identical analysis inputs and prompts through multiple LLMs, then comparing the themes, evidence quality and confidence scores each produces to expose model-specific weaknesses.
explanation: The author ran the same analysis process across Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini over 100 times. Without extra instruction, the models show meaningful differences. ChatGPT missed the user's value/price sensitivity reaction. All three gave different confidence scores and quotes, some verbatim and some summarized. ChatGPT summarizes and mashes together verbatim quotes, Claude is more conservative with confidence scores, and Gemini often chooses too-short snippets. Claude gives breadth and depth but does not filter validated patterns from half-formed hypotheses. Gemini gives fewer, better-evidenced themes and can analyze video. ChatGPT is best for final framing and stakeholder communication but least reliable for real evidence. Teams with a single enterprise LLM account rarely see their model's shortcomings.
when_to_use: When choosing which LLM to use for a qualitative analysis workflow
When you suspect your single model's output is missing themes or inflating confidence
When testing whether prompt fixes work across models
when_not_to_use: When the model is fixed by constraint and the findings are low-stakes
metric_or_method: Side-by-side comparison of themes, quote fidelity (verbatim vs. summarized), and confidence scores from the same prompt and data across models.
common_pitfalls: Relying on a single LLM and never seeing its shortcomings
Assuming a model's 'verbatim' quotes are exact (ChatGPT often combines quotes)
Assuming Claude's breadth means every theme is validated; its themes still need verification
Expecting Gemini's output to be complete without multiple prompts and requests for longer quotes
source_excerpt: Unless I give these models more instruction, there are meaningful differences in output. There’s theme overlap, but ChatGPT misses the user’s value/price sensitivity reaction, and all three models give different confidence scores and quotes—some verbatim, some summarized.
one_liner: Run the same prompt through Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini to expose each model's blind spots in themes, quotes and…
codex_prompt_template: Write a Python script that runs the same qualitative analysis prompt and dataset through multiple LLMs and compares their outputs side by side. Inputs: PROMPT = [ANALYSIS_PROMPT], DATA = [INPUT_DATA_PATH], MODELS = [MODEL_LIST e.g. claude, gpt, gemini]. For each model, require structured JSON output with: themes (name, description, confidence 0-1, supporting quotes). Then: (1) compute theme overlap across models using embedding similarity and list themes found by only one model; (2) check quote fidelity by verifying each quote is a verbatim substring of the source data, and flag paraphrased or fabricated quotes; (3) report average quote length and the confidence score distribution per model to detect over- or under-confidence; (4) flag themes in [KNOWN_KEY_THEMES] that any model missed. Run each model [N_RUNS] times to measure variance. Output a markdown comparison table and a summary of model-specific weaknesses.
