name: Custom Private Benchmarks on Your Own Use Case
definition: Build and maintain a private, use-case-specific benchmark from your own real tasks, usage, or non-public data. Run it against each new model, with the best-effort prompting, and measure results against a human or task-specific baseline instead of relying on public benchmarks, leaderboards, or generic model evals.
explanation:
The core method is to collect hard, real tasks or private data from your own product, job role, or value chain. Then run the best current models on them with a controlled, well-engineered prompt, score the outputs against a human or expert baseline, and re-run on every new model release. This surfaces step changes and real gaps that public benchmarks hide.

Why not public benchmarks: Chen's benchmark skepticism notes that public benchmarks are often wrong or messy, are easy to hill-climb because answers are objective, and can be gamed through leakage, system-prompt tweaks, or number of runs. The leaderboard critique adds that crowd-voted arenas reward emojis, markdown, and length over accuracy. Aishwarya's model-vs-product-evals distinction says checking LM Arena or Artificial Analysis is model selection, not product evaluation on your own dataset and feedback loop. Mike Krieger's Cursor-bench idea says the useful benchmark lives in your own usage and hard problems. Asking the model a really hard problem repeatedly is how you notice a step change in a new release. Weil's custom evals for fine-tuned models extend this to proprietary data. Teams build task-specific evals from problems with good answers, use them to gather data and fine-tune, and measure the specialized model against them.

Sourcing and structuring tasks: The hard-task job-skills benchmark crowdsources tasks practitioners failed to get AI to do. It selects high-impact ones, maps them to a skills framework (Shape, Ship, Sync), runs several questions per category across models, and reports win rate per category to estimate how much of a role is automatable. The enterprise value-chain eval applies this to a company. Identify what you produce for your end customer and design a systematic test of how well AI does it, before applying AI across the business. Some enterprises avoid this because it may show their value chain can be automated.

Private-data and expert-baseline variants: Dan Shipper's CEO benchmark tests whether frontier models can predict what he will say next in his private meeting transcripts, which are not on the internet. He built it over a weekend. Models did badly, which he attributes to the context problem rather than low intelligence. His senior engineer benchmark gives each model a minimal prompt to rewrite a messy vibe-coded app from first principles. Output is scored out of 100 against two independent human senior engineers (high 80s to low 90s). Models scored about 30 until GPT 5.5 reached about 62. The prompt is tuned so it does not give away the answer, and the benchmark can be re-zeroed once models saturate it.

Prompting fairly: The best-model, prompt-engineered principle says to measure the upper bound. Use the best current model, control the system prompt, and apply role, a 'Thinking' section, and a worked example. Iterate on the prompt after seeing tells, then keep it fixed between runs.

Keeping it honest over time: Benchmark saturation awareness says new benchmarks saturate within about 6 to 12 months, and a flat score may reflect the ceiling instead of a plateau, so build harder tasks with headroom. The saturation caveat says benchmarks only score problems humans have already framed. A model that scores well may still not decide on its own to reframe the problem, and benchmark names can suggest more than they measure.
when_to_use: Choosing or upgrading models for a specific product use case where public benchmark scores don't reflect your real tasks
Estimating how much of a job role or enterprise value chain AI can take on
Testing on private or proprietary data absent from public training sets, including verifying a fine-tuned model improved on your task
Detecting step-change improvements across successive model releases using hard problems
Replacing or extending an eval suite that models already score near 100% on
Interpreting launch claims or leaderboard rankings that diverge from real-world experience
when_not_to_use: A public benchmark already measures what you care about, or general benchmarks adequately reflect the use case
You lack a private, representative dataset or real tasks
Your use case is too easy to stress the model, so you won't feel capability differences
You need a statistically robust, generalizable benchmark (a single-codebase personal benchmark is not that)
You want to measure the out-of-the-box experience of average users with naive prompts
metric_or_method: Collect hard tasks or private data from real usage; use the best current model with a controlled, engineered prompt (role, 'Thinking' section, an example); score against a human or expert baseline (score out of 100, win rate per skill category, or prediction quality); re-run on each new model and re-zero or harden the benchmark when it saturates.
common_pitfalls: Treating public benchmarks or leaderboards (SWE-bench, LM Arena, Artificial Analysis) as proof your product works; they can be wrong, leaked, hill-climbed, or won with emojis, markdown, and length
Using old models or trivial prompts, or changing the prompt between runs, which breaks comparability; too many examples can also constrain creativity
Prompts that mirror the original task or give away the answer, causing models to patch instead of reframing or inflating scores
Blaming poor results on model intelligence when the real issue is missing context, which a large context window alone does not solve
Too few tasks (for example three) to be a comprehensive evaluation, and subjectivity across audiences
Reading a benchmark's name literally (for example 'senior engineer') or assuming saturation means role replacement, since framing and reframing aren't captured
Concluding progress has stalled when a benchmark is simply saturated
Avoiding evaluation out of fear it will show your value chain can be automated
source_excerpt: Thus, to realistically measure how close AI models are to replacing the work of a human—in our case, a product manager—we need to collect real-world examples of difficult PM tasks that AI tools seem to struggle with, use the best current model, and apply *prompt engineering* principles to give the models the best chance possible.
one_liner: Build a private benchmark from your hardest real tasks and rerun it on every new model release.
codex_prompt_template: Build a private, use-case-specific benchmark harness for [USE_CASE_DESCRIPTION] in [LANGUAGE_OR_FRAMEWORK]. Inputs: a folder of task files at [TASKS_PATH]. Each task has an id, a category from [SKILL_CATEGORIES], the input or private context, and a reference answer or rubric from [HUMAN_BASELINE_SOURCE]. Requirements: 1) Load the tasks and validate the schema. 2) Run each task against a configurable list of models [MODEL_LIST] using one fixed, engineered system prompt kept in a versioned file. The prompt should include a role, a 'Thinking' section, and one worked example that does not leak any benchmark answer. 3) Run [RUNS_PER_TASK] runs per task and record the model, prompt version, date, output, latency and cost. 4) Score each output on a 0-100 scale using [SCORING_METHOD], for example an LLM judge with a rubric, exact match, or expert comparison. Report the human baseline score next to each model score. 5) Produce a report with the overall score, win rate per category, the gap versus the human baseline, and the delta versus the previous model run. 6) Flag saturation when a model scores above [SATURATION_THRESHOLD] on a category, and list the tasks where every model fails as candidates for a harder v2. 7) Store results as JSON or CSV so each new model release can be re-run with one command, and include a README on how to add tasks and re-zero the benchmark. Add unit tests for the loader and scorer.

name: Custom Trace Review and Annotation Tooling
definition: A process in which a domain expert or PM owns error analysis, supported by tracing and simple review tooling (a custom or vibe-coded trace viewer with notes and axial-code counts, annotation queues, and an editable prompt view) so that traces can be reviewed, labeled and turned into ground-truth data without reading raw JSON.
explanation: The core method is to capture full traces and put them in front of the domain expert through an interface that makes review easy. Hamel's most repeated advice is to look at your data, so reduce friction as much as possible. Domain-expert ownership (member 1): error analysis should be done by the domain expert, usually the PM, rather than outsourced to engineers, because it is where you build your product and your moat. Roles can collapse on small teams (the Nurture Boss CEO acts as PM and AI engineer), and pairing with engineers may help at first, but one person should own the analysis. Custom trace viewers (members 1 and 4): Nurture Boss vibe-coded an app in a few hours that shows channels (voice, email, text, chatbot) and threads, hides the system prompt by default, supports open and axial coding with notes, and displays axial-code error counts in red. AI makes it cheap to build simple web apps that show data and write to a database. Prompt admin view (member 1): expose the prompt in an in-app admin view so non-technical people can edit it, because prompt playgrounds often lack access to tool calls and RAG. Tracing and annotation queues (member 2): tools such as LangSmith or Langfuse capture which nodes ran, what the LLM saw, tool calls, token usage and per-call latency, with optional metadata. Annotation queues give domain experts an easy UI to label or give feedback. Labeled traces feed offline datasets or are used to compute judge precision and recall, which grounds evaluator validation in ground-truth labels. Observability platform for prompt debugging (member 3): on the Confluence AI features, PMs began using Arize to find prompt issues and hand them to engineers faster. The source gives no further detail on that workflow. Off-the-shelf tools are a fine starting point if you cannot yet commit time to building a custom one.
when_to_use: Setting up roles and tooling for ongoing error analysis
When domain expertise is not coding, as in most non-coding apps
When you need human labels from domain experts at scale
When doing error analysis on multi-step agent flows
When generic observability tools make trace review painful for recurring, domain-specific review
When PMs want to diagnose prompt problems themselves and speed up the PM-to-engineer feedback loop
when_not_to_use: For coding apps, where the domain expert may be the developer
When you cannot yet commit time to build a custom tool; off-the-shelf tools are fine to start
metric_or_method: Assign one domain expert or PM to own error analysis; log full traces (e.g. LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize); build a simple custom trace viewer with notes, axial-code counts and an in-app prompt admin view; use annotation queue labels as ground truth for datasets and judge precision/recall.
common_pitfalls: Outsourcing error analysis to engineers or other humans, losing the personal touch and the moat
Tolerating a painful review workflow so that reviewers stop looking at data
Making domain experts read raw trace JSON instead of providing an annotation UI
Skipping tracing, on which the rest of the eval process depends
Separating the prompt from the product manager when it is written in English
Relying on prompt playgrounds that lack access to tool calls and RAG
Assuming a platform alone suffices; the Arize PM debugging example gives no detail on specific traces, metrics or review steps

name: Error Analysis on Traces (Open and Axial Coding)
definition: A data-analysis process in which a domain expert samples logged traces of an AI application, writes free-form notes on what went wrong (open coding), groups the notes into specific named failure-mode categories (axial coding), and counts them to get a prioritized list of what to fix or build evals for.
explanation: Evals should start with looking at the data, not with writing tests or adopting off-the-shelf metrics such as helpfulness, hallucination or toxicity, which produce scores that don't track real user problems. The method is classic error analysis for stochastic systems. Step 1, capture traces (in an observability tool, or in CSV, JSON or text files). Step 2, open coding: a domain expert reads each sampled trace, usually in about 30 seconds, and writes an informal but detailed note about the first or most upstream problem, then moves on. Variants add a pass/fail judgment with a critique. For a pass, say why the primary need was met. For a fail, name the critical elements. Critiques should be detailed enough for a new employee to understand, or to seed a few-shot prompt for an LLM judge. Notes must not be vague ('janky'); something like 'Did not confirm call transfer with user' is better. Don't hunt for every error, diagnose root causes, or build a taxonomy at this stage. In the Nurture Boss example, notes caught a missed human handoff, a hallucinated virtual tour, markdown in a text message, a promise to check something that was never done, and double-booking a tour instead of rescheduling. Sampling is random at first. Later you can target traces with negative feedback, unusual length, many tools or high latency. Step 3, axial coding: export the notes, have an LLM propose 5-6 candidate categories using the terms open codes and axial codes, then refine them by hand into specific, actionable categories that someone else could use for labeling, for example 'date formatting error' rather than 'temporal issues'. Aim for under 10 primary failure modes. Label each note with a category, including a 'none of the above' option so missing categories surface. Then count with a pivot table, drill into the underlying traces, and optionally add subcategories. Counting resolves paralysis about what to fix, but frequency is not the only signal: a rarer but catastrophic error such as a human handoff failure may warrant a fix regardless. Sample size: about 100 traces is a starting suggestion to unblock people. The real stopping rule is theoretical saturation, meaning you stop when new traces stop yielding new kinds of notes. With practice some people need only 15, 40 or 60. Who reviews: a single principal domain expert (a 'benevolent dictator', often the PM) does the labeling, which avoids committee paralysis and conflicting annotations in small and medium companies. Larger or multi-domain organizations may need several annotators and inter-annotator agreement. Engineers and LLMs tend to lack product context. An LLM will often say a trace looks fine because it doesn't know, for example, that the virtual tour feature doesn't exist. Related variants: (a) after running evals, start manual review from the weakest metrics, pulling 20 to 50 low-scoring examples per segment, looking at the user input, the system action and the outcome, and recording recurring error patterns in a simple table; (b) for vague user feedback such as 'Claude hallucinated', read consented transcripts and examine the failed trajectory to decide the failure theme, such as tool use, search/synthesis, alignment, hallucination or overconfidence, and to judge whether it is big enough to turn into a new eval; (c) for agents that start well but get stuck, identify the most important stuck points (for example login, data persistence, payments), tune the system quantitatively with a fast feedback loop, and note the work is ongoing. Finally, run this as a continuous loop on a weekly or bi-weekly cadence, not a one-off audit. Dive into raw traces, pinpoint failure modes, keep only metrics that change a decision, form a fresh premise, and repeat. Without looking at data you can't create meaningful criteria or labels, and without labels you can't validate judges.
when_to_use: At the start of building evals for any AI feature that has real or realistic traces and you don't know what is failing
Before choosing metrics or writing LLM judges, and when dashboards exist but are ignored
When user feedback is vague and needs to be traced to a specific failure theme in the trajectory
After running evals, to review the weakest segments and scope the next version
On a weekly or bi-weekly cadence for production agents, especially when a new or drifting failure mode appears
After open coding, to decide which failure modes to fix or build evals for first and to justify priorities
When critiques are needed later to seed an LLM judge's few-shot prompt
When an agent performs well initially but gets stuck partway, to find which flows to harden first
when_not_to_use: When there are no traces and no way to generate any; dog-food or create synthetic inputs first
As a one-off audit or a substitute for ongoing automated evals; it is a discovery step that should recur
When a failure is already a well-defined, objective rule that code can check, or is known and easy to fix
Before open-coded notes exist, or without enough detailed human notes, when axial coding is the step in question
When no one with relevant domain expertise is available to review the traces
For large or multi-domain products with a single annotator; these need multiple annotators and agreement measurement
When there is no way yet to observe where tasks fail or get stuck, or no evals or data to direct the review
metric_or_method: Sample traces (about 100 or until theoretical saturation, random at first); a single domain expert writes a free-form note on the first/most upstream failure in each (optionally with pass/fail and critique); an LLM proposes 5-6 categories that a human refines into specific ones; label each note including 'none of the above'; pivot-table the counts and weigh severity to produce a prioritized failure-mode list of under 10 categories; repeat on a regular cadence.
common_pitfalls: Skipping error analysis and jumping to off-the-shelf metrics (helpfulness, hallucination, toxicity) or straight to writing tests
Delegating the free-form review to an LLM or to engineers without product context; it misses issues like markdown in SMS or a hallucinated feature
Vague or terse notes ('janky') that can't be categorized later, or trying to catalogue every error, diagnose root causes or build the taxonomy while open coding
Accepting generic LLM categories ('quality', 'capability limitations', 'temporal issues') as-is, omitting a 'none of the above' option, or creating too many categories instead of under 10
Prioritizing by count alone and ignoring severity, or over-automating with an LLM without human validation
Committee consensus or too many annotators causing conflicts and paralysis, or letting the process become endlessly expensive
Treating 100 traces as a magic number, or stopping before the intuition for saturation has developed
Keeping noisy metrics that don't change decisions, ignoring data due to lack of time, or lumping distinct failure themes together; also skipping consent when reading user transcripts

name: Eval-Driven Synthetic Data Training for Product Behaviors
definition: A rapid model-iteration process for product features: identify the core behaviors the feature needs, synthetically generate training data with a model such as o1, and use evals to measure progress. Then shift the synthetic sets using real user feedback after launch.
explanation: For Canvas, Nguyen says it came down to three behaviors: when to trigger Canvas, how to update the document (targeted edit vs full rewrite), and how to make comments. For comments, o1 simulated user conversations and produced documents, a critique prompt was injected, and the model was taught to comment. She says it all came down to measuring progress via very robust evals. She prefers synthetic data over human data because it is cheaper and more scalable, and says the synthetic sets shift as beta users reveal real behavior, as with Canvas going from beta to GA. Human data is still needed for hard expert knowledge.
when_to_use: Shipping new ChatGPT-style product features that need rapid model iteration
When you can name a small set of core behaviors the model must learn
When you want to refine behaviors based on beta feedback
when_not_to_use: Tasks that need expert knowledge, such as chemistry or biology, where she says human expert data is still needed
metric_or_method: Per-behavior robust evals (deterministic and human win-rate) used to measure progress on synthetic-data-trained behaviors, with the synthetic distribution updated using user feedback from beta to GA.
common_pitfalls: Synthetic data lacking diversity, which she calls one of the hardest and most important questions
Not shifting the synthetic distribution to match real user behavior after launch
Over-relying on synthetic data for tasks that only experts know
source_excerpt: And so the way you synthetically train the model is physically figuring out what are the most core behaviors that you wanted the product feature to do. And for Canvas, for example, it came down to three main behaviors. [...] And it all came down to measuring progress via very robust evals. But, yeah, this is how you used o1 and a synthetic data generation for the training.
one_liner: Name 3 core behaviors, synthesize training data with o1, gate on evals, then reshape data with beta feedback.
codex_prompt_template:
I'm building an eval-driven synthetic data pipeline for the product feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION].

Core behaviors the model must learn: [CORE_BEHAVIORS] (e.g., when to trigger the feature, targeted edit vs full rewrite, how to comment).

Write Python code that:
1. For each behavior, uses a strong teacher model ([TEACHER_MODEL]) to simulate user conversations and artifacts, then generates target outputs (inject a critique/rubric prompt where useful). Produce [DATASET_SIZE] examples per behavior in JSONL with fields: behavior, input, expected_output, metadata.
2. Builds a per-behavior eval suite: deterministic checks (e.g., correct trigger decision, edit-vs-rewrite classification, output format) and an LLM-judge or human win-rate comparison against [BASELINE_MODEL].
3. Reports pass rate and win rate per behavior, so I can track progress after each training iteration.
4. Includes a function that ingests real user feedback logs from [FEEDBACK_SOURCE] (thumbs, edits, failures), clusters failures by behavior, and re-weights or regenerates the synthetic dataset to match the real-user distribution.
5. Flags behaviors that need human-labeled expert data because synthetic data quality is low.

Include a README-style docstring explaining how to run one iteration loop (generate -> train -> eval -> update from feedback).

name: Eval Type Selection and Prioritization
definition: A decision framework for deciding whether to write an eval at all, which type to write (fix directly, code-based check, LLM judge, or rely on user signals), and how many to build. It weighs failure persistence, business risk, cost, and expected return, and it starts small with the cheapest check that works.
explanation:
Start after error analysis, with a list of failure modes. For each one, decide whether to just fix it (Prioritizing Which Evals to Write; Code-Based vs LLM-as-Judge). Dumb engineering errors, such as a missing formatting instruction in the prompt, can simply be fixed, perhaps with a cheap code test added. Write evals for pesky failures where the ideal behavior is already in the prompt but still fails, and for failures that are risky for the business. One member ends up with four to seven judges; the point is to improve the application, not to build a beautiful eval suite.

Next, choose the eval type (Code-Based vs LLM-as-Judge; Cost Ladder). Objective issues, like markdown in a text message, get a code-based assertion. Subjective ones, like whether the assistant should have handed off to a human, may need an LLM judge. The cost ladder says to use the cheapest check that works: unit tests, then regex or pattern matching, then trace validation (message envelopes, inputs, outputs, tool calls, call counts and durations), and only then a judge on the cheapest adequate model. In the demo the speaker used GPT-3.5 Turbo, then GPT-4o mini, which he called practically free for such use cases. A typical end-state suite has several code-based evals in CI, maybe one or two LLM evals in CI, and LLM evaluators run periodically on sampled production traces for monitoring.

Then decide whether to formalize evals at all (Eval ROI Triage). Compare the effort (for example, two engineers for a move from 80% to 85%) with alternative uses such as a new feature. Vibe checks can be enough for non-core features. Evals matter most at scale, where failures can be catastrophic, or where the feature is a competitive advantage. Without any metrics you risk the product doing something very dumb.

In complex, open-ended use cases (Context-Dependent Choice), new failure patterns keep emerging and narrow judges (for example, for verbosity) can't keep up, leaving you with too many evals. There it can make sense to look at user signals, fix issues, check for regressions and move on. The right approach depends on the application, but this is not an excuse to skip evals.

On quantity, the members disagree with fixed counts and with building hundreds. Build Roughly 10 Great Evals suggests about 5 to 10 high-quality evals per feature that quantify the goal, show progress, and show what is missing, with a record of which pass or fail, how to run them, and the prompt that raised the success rate. It is especially useful for features like memory, and not every feature needs evals. Goal-Driven Coverage says to scale the number to the coverage and confidence needed, segment results to find weak spots (for example, a poor user segment that turned out to be a messaging problem), and focus on the core, most common path. A broad, general product may justify hundreds of metrics.

For teams new to evals (Start Small), pick one critical feature, such as hallucination detection for a context-dependent chatbot or agent. Write a simple eval, run it on 5 to 10 representative examples, then review results and iterate on the eval prompt. Evaluate a well-defined component before deep internal logic, and add sophistication later to avoid noisy signals and lost trust.
when_to_use: After error analysis, when deciding per failure mode whether to fix, write a code check, or build an LLM judge
Budgeting an eval pipeline and choosing between deterministic checks and an LLM judge
Teams new to evals who need a first eval on one critical feature
Deciding how many evals a feature or product needs, or whether formal evals beat vibe checks
Operating at scale, with catastrophic failure risk, or on a competitive-advantage feature
Ambiguous features that need product definition, or features like memory hard to judge by feel
when_not_to_use: For trivial failures that are easy to fix directly in the prompt or code
Before error analysis has shown which failures matter
For low-key, non-core features where vibe checks are good enough
When the expected gain is incremental and engineers could build a higher-impact feature
Where regex is demonstrably misleading on subjective quality or policy questions
As an excuse to skip evals entirely, or to build hundreds of metrics for a narrow product
metric_or_method: For each failure mode from error analysis: fix directly, write a code-based check, or build an LLM judge, prioritized by persistence and business risk. Choose the cheapest check that works (unit test, regex, trace validation, then cheapest adequate judge). Weigh effort against expected gain and failure severity. Scale to roughly 5-10 evals per feature, or whatever coverage and confidence require, starting with one critical feature on 5-10 examples. Run code evals in CI and sample production traces for LLM monitoring.
common_pitfalls: Writing evals for everything or for show instead of for failures you want to iterate against
Using an LLM judge when a cheap code assertion would do, or starting with the most expensive judge model
Fuzzy regex on free-form LLM answers, causing false greens
Making evals too complex too quickly, creating noisy signals and eroding team trust
Picking an arbitrary fixed number of evals, or spreading effort over areas already doing well
Building a proliferating set of narrow judges in complex use cases where new patterns keep emerging
Skipping evals with no metrics at all, leaving no visibility when the app does something very dumb
Treating good-enough as permanent, or treating evals as someone else's job rather than the PM's

name: Evals as Product Requirements
definition: A product-management method in which the PM expresses user needs, real use cases and ideal behavior as evals, which serve as the product requirements for an AI model or agent. Researchers and engineers iterate against these evals (experiments, RL, post-training) and measure progress across versions. This is described as test-driven development for PMs.
explanation: The core method: understand the user pain point or goal, state success clearly as an eval, hand it to research or engineering, and measure improvement against it. Dianne Penn frames evals as the 'personification of that user need', shortening the distance to actionability, and compares this to test-driven development. Foody's variant treats the eval set as the PRD itself: once it exists, researchers run many experiments and reinforcement learning can climb it quickly (as with Olympiad Math and SWE-bench). The main barrier to automating workflows with agents is therefore measuring success, so PMs must write evals for everything agents should do. Nick Turley contributes the beginner entry point: write down ideal behavior per use case, even in a spreadsheet, as the AI-era version of articulating success first. This is the lingua franca for telling researchers what the product should do, and it differs from generic research benchmarks. Sub-steps and variants: (1) Use-case-driven evals for research collaboration: collect concrete use cases, review sample sessions to see why the model failed, write evals from them, and if a prompt and skills already achieve the outcome, take that to research as a case for post-training. Trust with research builds as you consistently bring specific user data. (2) Evals as living PRDs: a judge prompt encoding expected behavior is effectively a running PRD, but it should be derived from data via open and axial coding, because analysis surfaces expectations you could not have imagined. The traditional PRD is still written up front, then improved from error analysis, possibly with LLMs helping from open codes. (3) Division of labor: Tamar Yehoshua describes PMs who traditionally wrote evals working with engineers on Confluence Slides so engineers understood how PMs wanted the product evaluated, with a reported 2x eval throughput. Eval ownership varies by team. PRDs are not dead: they still align large groups (engineering, legal, safety) around a source of truth and suit ambiguous problems with no defined user pain points yet.
when_to_use: When there is a well-defined user problem that can be captured as a measurable failure
When you need to make user feedback actionable for researchers or engineers
When a model fails real user goals and you need to communicate this to research and set up an iteration loop
When you want a capability moved from prompt/skills workarounds into the model via post-training
When you want an agent to automate a specific workflow and need an unambiguous target to improve against
When starting a new AI feature with no success definition, or making evals approachable for non-technical PMs
When updating requirements and judge prompts based on error analysis
When evals are critical to get right and PMs hold the product judgment while engineers run or scale them
when_not_to_use: For very ambiguous problems with no defined user pain points yet, where a PRD's product vision is more valuable
When aligning a large cross-functional group (engineering, legal, safety) around a shared source of truth; a PRD fits better
When you have no concrete use cases or session data yet
When there is no way to define or measure what success looks like for the task
As a substitute for learning from real users after launch, or for skipping traditional PRDs and one-pagers before building
For purely UI/UX changes that do not depend on model behavior
metric_or_method: Convert user feedback, session reviews and ideal-behavior descriptions into an eval set (and judge prompts) that encodes the desired capabilities, hand it to researchers or engineers, run repeated experiments, RL or post-training against it, and track score improvements across versions while refining the requirements from error analysis.
common_pitfalls: Treating evals as a total replacement for PRDs, or treating the PRD as fixed
Passing vague feedback such as 'Claude hallucinated' to researchers instead of specific, actionable cases
Writing evals or judge criteria only from pre-data hypotheses rather than real user pain points and discovered expectations
Optimizing against generic academic benchmarks rather than the capabilities your product needs
Coming to research without specific use cases or clear user goals, or without building trust through quality user data
Treating evals as arcane technical work only researchers can do, or ignoring that working with research differs from working with engineering
Having no systematic way to measure success, which blocks applying agents to a workflow
Poorly defined rewards that invite reward hacking (mentioned only in passing)
source_excerpt: It's derived from our own data, so of course, it's a product manager's expectations. What I find that a lot of people miss is they just put in what their expectations are before looking at their data, but as we look at our data, we uncover more expectations that we couldn't have dreamed up in the first place, and that ends up going into this prompt.
one_liner: Turn user needs into evals that act as your PRD, then hand researchers a score to climb. Test-driven dev for PMs.
codex_prompt_template: You are helping a product manager use evals as product requirements for an AI feature. Feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Target users and their pain points: [USER_PAIN_POINTS]. name: Execution-Based Verification of AI-Generated Code
definition: Judging AI-generated code by mechanically checking it, mainly by executing it and applying tests and other automated checks, so each attempt gets an unambiguous pass/fail verdict without relying on line-by-line human review. The verdict can also drive agent iteration or reinforcement learning.
explanation: The core method is to run the generated code or app and treat success versus failure as a binary signal, ideally across many cases or permutations. Simons contributed the rationale: software is deterministic (it runs or it doesn't), unlike domains such as case law where outcomes depend on society, politics and juries. That is why reliable data can be generated at scale and why models should improve faster at code. Scott Wu contributed the feedback-loop variant: in the RL paradigm the agent does work, is judged correct or incorrect, for example by running code against test cases, and uses that result to decide what to do next and to learn. Cognition chose code for this reason, and early on applied it to contest programming problems with an agentic loop evaluated on test cases. Willison contributed a practical workflow, red/green TDD: the agent writes tests first, confirms they fail (red), implements the code, then confirms they pass (green). Watching a test fail first shows the test is meaningful. The tests confirm the agent actually ran the code and accumulate in the repo as regression protection. The short prompt 'use red/green TDD' triggers this. Taylor contributed the layered view: stack several mechanical verification layers, such as compile-time guarantees (e.g. Rust memory safety), formal verification, unit tests, AI code review, self-reflection and supervisor models, so correctness is checked automatically. He frames this as a 'programming system' built so that people can produce complex software quickly and know it works. Together: run the code for a binary verdict, use test-first discipline to make the check meaningful and durable, and layer further automated checks where run/not-run is not enough.
when_to_use: AI generates more code than humans can realistically read line by line.
Evaluating or improving code-generation and app-building agents whose output can be executed.
The task has a checkable outcome, such as code that can be run or test cases that pass or fail.
You want an agent to iterate and self-correct from automated feedback, or you are tuning coding agents with RL-style feedback.
Generating large volumes of training or evaluation data automatically because correctness can be checked by running the result.
Working with coding agents on code others will use, and you want new features not to break old ones.
Judging whether a model is reliable enough to build a product on by checking whether the apps it produces actually run.
Designing tooling, languages or pipelines around code-generating agents.
when_not_to_use: The output has no automatically checkable correctness signal, or the domain is non-deterministic (e.g. legal case-law reasoning).
As the only check on subjective qualities such as whether an app looks good, which run/not-run does not capture.
Tasks bigger and more ambiguous than test execution can verify, where human steering and review are still needed.
Throwaway personal vibe-coded prototypes where only you are affected, or quick prototypes where robustness is not the concern.
metric_or_method: Execute the generated code or app (e.g. against test cases) and record a binary run/pass versus fail signal. Write failing tests first, confirm red, implement, confirm green, and keep the accumulating suite as regression protection. Layer extra automated checks (compile-time guarantees, formal verification, AI review, supervisor models) and feed the verdict back into agent iteration or RL.
common_pitfalls: Reading every line of AI-generated code (becomes the bottleneck) or reading none and shipping unverified code.
Treating 'it runs' as sufficient: earlier models' failures included apps that looked ugly as well as broken ones.
Assuming a deterministic domain makes the model perfect; it is not, and Devin still makes mistakes, so human review is still needed.
Not confirming a test fails first, so it may not test anything.
Tests only protect what they cover; large suites that test nothing interesting are costly, though agents reduce maintenance burden.
Dropping tests in exchange for development speed, which Willison calls a huge mistake.
Building eval or training data in non-deterministic domains by inventing expected outcomes.
Optimizing generated code for human ergonomics instead of verifiability.
source_excerpt: What we care about is when this machine generates code, do we know that it did what we wanted it to do? [...] I think we need more things like that because if an AI is generating this code, by definition, if you have to read every line that is going to be the limiting factor for producing the code or worse, you're just not going to read every line and you're going to emit a bunch of unsafe unverified code into the wild. [...] you could probably layer on some techniques that are out of fashion, like formal verification, unit testing, other things.
one_liner: Run the code, don't read it: red/green TDD and layered automated checks give AI-written code a pass/fail verdict.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build an execution-based verification harness for AI-generated code in [PROJECT_NAME] (language: [LANGUAGE], test framework: [TEST_FRAMEWORK]).

Feature the AI agent must implement: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]

Follow red/green TDD:
1. Write tests first for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION], covering normal cases, edge cases, and [KNOWN_FAILURE_MODES].
2. Run the tests and show the output confirming they FAIL (red). If any test passes before implementation, flag it as not meaningful and fix it.
3. Implement the feature.
4. Run the tests again and show the output confirming they PASS (green).
5. Run the existing suite [EXISTING_TEST_COMMAND] to confirm nothing regressed.

Then build a verification script that, for each of [NUM_GENERATED_SAMPLES] AI-generated code samples in [SAMPLES_DIRECTORY]:
- Runs layered checks in order: compile/type-check ([TYPECHECK_COMMAND]), linter, unit tests, and any extra checks [OPTIONAL_EXTRA_CHECKS].
- Executes the code in a sandbox with a timeout of [TIMEOUT_SECONDS] seconds.
- Records a binary pass/fail verdict per sample, plus the failing layer and error message.
- Outputs a JSON report with pass rate overall and per layer, and a list of failures.

Finally, add a loop option that feeds failure messages back to the agent for up to [MAX_ITERATIONS] retries and reports pass rate by iteration.

name: Expert-Authored Failure Cases with Ground Truth and Step-Level Reasoning
definition: A GPQA-style approach in which an expert breaks the model, provides the right answer, writes out the reasoning steps, and checks reliability across repeated attempts. This pinpoints where reasoning fails.
explanation: Lord cites the public GPQA paper as the example. An expert produces a question the model gets wrong, supplies the ground truth and the step-by-step reasoning. Because models are non-deterministic, a model may get an answer right once but fail three out of five times, so failure has to be demonstrated. The focus is on the steps: the model may know the question and reach the answer while its steps are wrong. For example, in a 10-step math problem, steps 6 through 10 might be wrong. Lord says the average person cannot break the models, which is why PhD-level experts are needed in advanced domains.
when_to_use: Evaluating or probing reasoning models in advanced domains such as physics, math or chemistry
When you need to find weaknesses in reasoning steps, not just final answers
When non-determinism means a single correct answer does not prove reliability
when_not_to_use: Tasks where average users can easily surface errors and expert review is unnecessary (the text says it is hard for the average person to break the model)
metric_or_method: Expert-written hard questions with ground-truth answers and step-by-step reasoning, with failures verified across repeated attempts (for example, right once but not 3 of 5 times) and the failing step identified
common_pitfalls: Judging only the final answer: the model may get the right answer while its reasoning steps are wrong
Relying on a single attempt: models are non-deterministic and may pass once but fail three out of five times
source_excerpt: A great example is a public paper called GPQA. So, for the engineers out there that want to read about it, essentially the crux of the paper is you break the model, you provide a ground truth, the right answer to the question, you provide the step-by-step a reasoning steps. So, you might imagine because models are non-deterministic, the model can get the answer right once, but it might not get the answer right three out of five times. So, you actually prove where the model's failing. You actually break down into where is it failing?
one_liner: Have experts break the model, supply ground truth and steps, and re-run to expose exactly where reasoning fails.
codex_prompt_template: Build an eval harness for expert-authored failure cases in [DOMAIN, e.g. physics/math/chemistry]. Input: a JSONL file at [DATASET_PATH] where each record has: question, ground_truth_answer, and reasoning_steps (ordered list of expert-written steps). For each record: (1) call [MODEL_NAME] [N_ATTEMPTS, default 5] times at temperature [TEMPERATURE] and record each response; (2) grade the final answer against ground truth; (3) use an LLM judge, with the expert steps as reference, to label each model reasoning step as correct/incorrect and identify the first failing step index; (4) flag cases where the answer is right but the steps are wrong. Output per-question: pass rate across attempts (e.g. 2/5), reliability flag (unstable if 0<pass<N), first failing step distribution, and right-answer-wrong-reasoning rate. Then produce a summary report ranking questions and step types by failure frequency, and list the top [TOP_K] failing steps for expert review. Write it in Python with pytest-style tests and a CLI.

name: Expert-Authored Rubric Evaluation
definition: A domain expert (for example a lawyer, doctor, banker or rater-guideline author) defines what a high-quality output looks like for a specific task and context. They turn that into rubric criteria, a dataset, and rating guidelines, and graders then score model outputs against them.
explanation: The core method is that an expert writes the criteria a good deliverable must meet, much as a professor writes a grading rubric and a TA applies it. In the contract-redlining example, a lawyer lists the key points, and the model earns points per key point identified. The same rubric can measure progress on a capability and also serve as training data to reward the desired behavior. Task-specific eval design covers the whole build around that rubric. Someone with real domain understanding decides what makes the capability good, designs the dataset and criteria, writes guidelines, and trains raters to apply them consistently. This matters most for model developers improving a capability such as code writing, where no existing way to measure it exists. The "what good looks like" variant applies this to enterprise and government deployments. Experts such as doctors or bankers author and label a comprehensive eval set encoding the best recommendation or course of action for each case. It favors "good" over "correct" because these probabilistic systems make judgments on a person's behalf. It also stresses that good is company-specific, shaped by culture, objectives and incentives. The human-rater-guidelines variant is a ready-made set of expert criteria for informational responses. It asks whether the content satisfies user intent, cites sources, and is original rather than repeated. It matters because AI answers are built from searches and their paired content. It can be combined with search signals such as spam detection and authoritativeness.
when_to_use: Professional or open-ended deliverables (legal redlines, banking analysis) where correctness depends on expert judgment
Measuring progress on a capability and also rewarding it during post-training
Models make a handful of mistakes or miss key points that experts can enumerate
Improving a model or product on a specific domain capability, such as code writing, when no existing benchmark captures good
Enterprise or government deployments where the system makes judgment calls and company-specific judgment is needed beyond off-the-shelf models, RAG and fine-tuning
Assessing source content quality or defining rater criteria for informational, retrieval- or search-based AI answers
when_not_to_use: Success can be checked by an automatic verifier such as a unit test, where a rubric may be unnecessary
A simple good/bad check on a basic chatbot suffices and bespoke eval design isn't warranted
Non-informational uses such as creativity or productivity tasks, where the information-quality criteria fit poorly
metric_or_method: Expert-authored rubric with per-criterion points (e.g., points per key issue identified), plus a dataset and rating guidelines, applied by trained graders to each output to produce a score.
common_pitfalls: Rubrics written by non-experts miss what professionals care about, so expert quality drives eval quality
Defining the rubric loosely so the model can exploit it (reward hacking risk)
Skipping rating guidelines and rater training, so criteria are applied inconsistently
Treating judgment as universal when what is good varies by company, bank or health system
Framing evals as a single correct answer rather than the best recommendation for a probabilistic system
Assuming large volumes of enterprise data are the right data when most of it is not useful
Treating rater guidelines as only an SEO checklist rather than a statement of what makes information good
Ignoring what people actually use AI for (advice, how-to, complex needs) when judging whether content meets the need
source_excerpt: Say you have a model that you want to write a red line for a contract in the way that a lawyer would, and it makes a handful of mistakes, misses a bunch of key points in doing so. What you could do is have a lawyer create a rubric similar to how a professor might create a rubric to create a deliverable for what are the things we want the model to be able to do?
one_liner: Have a domain expert write the grading rubric, then score model outputs point by point against it.
codex_prompt_template: Build an expert-authored rubric evaluation for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] in the domain of [DOMAIN, e.g. contract redlining, banking analysis, code writing]. Inputs: a domain expert's list of what a high-quality output must contain [EXPERT_CRITERIA], and a dataset of [DATASET_SIZE] test cases in [DATASET_PATH]. Tasks: 1) Convert the expert criteria into a structured rubric (JSON or YAML) where each criterion has an id, description, point value, and clear pass/fail anchor examples. 2) Write rating guidelines that cover edge cases and company-specific definitions of 'good', so human raters or an LLM grader can apply them consistently. 3) Implement a grader that scores each model output per criterion and sums to a total score, using [GRADER_TYPE: human, LLM judge] and returning a short rationale per criterion. 4) Add an inter-rater agreement check (e.g. Cohen's kappa) between [NUM_RATERS] raters, or between the LLM judge and expert labels on a calibration subset, and flag criteria with low agreement. 5) Output a report with the overall score, per-criterion pass rates, and the top missed criteria so the results can guide product fixes or serve as a reward signal for post-training. Provide runnable Python code and a sample rubric file.

name: Expert Human Evaluations for Measuring Model Progress
definition: Human annotators who are experts at the top of their fields hold realistic conversations with a model on tasks from their own work. They evaluate the outputs in depth, for example by checking code and physics equations, and judge dimensions such as accuracy and instruction following.
explanation: Edwin Chen says Surge measures model progress this way instead of relying on benchmarks. Experts such as a physicist, a teacher or a coder converse with the model on their real problems. They work through the responses themselves, so they catch errors that casual users who just pick the flashiest answer miss. He contrasts this with popup A/B comparisons and says it is a much better approach than benchmarks or random online A/B tests.
when_to_use: When you need to measure real-world model progress rather than benchmark performance
When evaluating chat models across specialized domains such as physics, teaching and coding
When benchmark scores may be gamed, leaked or saturated
when_not_to_use: When you cannot access qualified domain experts (the transcript does not discuss alternatives)
metric_or_method: Expert annotators converse with the model on realistic domain tasks and evaluate responses deeply across dimensions such as accuracy and instruction following.
common_pitfalls: Casual users skim and pick whatever looks flashiest rather than evaluating deeply
Evaluators who do not verify content (code, equations) miss hallucinations and errors
source_excerpt: So for example, what we do is, yeah, we will take Gore human annotators, and we'll ask them, "Okay, go have a conversational model." [...] they're going to evaluate the code that it write. They're going to double check the physics equations that it writes. They're going to evaluate the models in a very deep way, so they're going to pay attention to accuracy and instruction following, all these things that casual users don't
one_liner: Skip benchmarks: let domain experts grill your model with real work tasks and check its code and equations.
codex_prompt_template: Build an expert human evaluation pipeline for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Domains to cover: [EXPERT_DOMAINS, e.g. physics, teaching, coding]. Deliver: (1) an annotator brief telling each expert to hold a realistic multi-turn conversation using a task from their own work and to verify outputs in depth (run the code, re-derive equations, check facts) rather than pick the flashiest answer; (2) a scoring rubric with 1-5 scales and written justifications for dimensions [EVAL_DIMENSIONS, e.g. accuracy, instruction following, completeness]; (3) a JSON schema for storing conversation transcripts, expert ID, domain, per-dimension scores, and the specific errors found; (4) Python code to aggregate scores per domain and per model version, compute inter-annotator agreement on overlapping samples of size [OVERLAP_SAMPLE_SIZE], and report progress between [MODEL_VERSION_A] and [MODEL_VERSION_B] with confidence intervals; (5) a comparison of expert verdicts against the benchmark scores [BENCHMARK_RESULTS] to flag where benchmarks and experts disagree.

name: Failure-Mode Probing Rituals
definition: A repeatable practice in which a PM runs a few short probes (obviously wrong, ambiguous, unexpectedly difficult tasks, and wrong-vs-ideal comparisons) on an AI workflow to map its failure signature, find its first point of failure, and define the guardrails and failure responses the product should have.
explanation: Every AI feature has a failure signature, the pattern of breakdowns it falls into when inputs get messy. The core method is to run short probes on the workflow you are building, under 15 minutes in total on a weekly cadence (Weekly Failure-Mode Mapping Rituals). Four rituals of about 2-3 minutes each: ask the model to do something obviously wrong, something ambiguous, something unexpectedly difficult, and add explicit failure responses. Capture the gaps as product requirements. This surfaces issues that would otherwise appear weeks later in production and helps separate product problems from model limitations. Sub-steps and variants: (1) Wrong-vs-Ideal Output Comparison is a two-pass test. Feed messy context (Slack threads, meeting notes, Jira comments) and ask for something like strategic decisions; models tend to confidently invent structure. Re-run the identical input with a line describing expected behavior (only include items explicitly mentioned; say 'Not enough information' if missing). Compare what changed, which guardrail fixed it, whether the good version feels shippable or brittle, and what the user would experience in each. (2) Ambiguous Prompt Testing gives the model an ambiguous request, e.g. uploading a PRD to NotebookLM and asking it to summarize for execs and list top risks and open questions. Check for over-summarizing, latching onto an irrelevant detail, ignoring caveats, or assuming the wrong audience. The failures show where the product should ask the user to choose a goal, give more context, or constrain the action. The aim is to understand where communication breaks, not to trick the model. (3) First-Point-of-Failure Stress Test picks one task that feels simple to a human PM but stresses reasoning, context, or judgment (e.g. 'Group these 40 bugs into themes and propose a roadmap'). Observe where output first degrades; that marks where to add guardrails, narrow inputs, or split the task into smaller steps. The finding is the intended behavior, not a final solution. (4) Failure-Response Guardrail Patterns is the follow-through. Guardrails don't make the model smarter; they protect users by deciding how the system slows down, asks for help, narrows scope, or says 'I don't know'. Four patterns: when the model seems unsure, ask a clarifying question instead of guessing; when context is too long, give the user a choice rather than silently dropping information; when the model invents structure, say so (e.g. 'I didn't see any decisions here—would you like themes instead?'); when outputs bounce around, add light structure (what was discussed, decided, needs follow-up). In one example, a Slack-summarization feature wrongly assigned owners, and a single system-prompt rule (only assign an owner if someone explicitly volunteers or is confirmed) removed the biggest trust issue, showing the fix was a guardrail and not a different model. Re-test against the same failure case after adding the response.
when_to_use: While building any AI workflow, on a recurring (e.g. weekly) cadence
Before launch, to catch issues that would otherwise appear in production
To separate product problems from model limitations
Probing how a model handles messy, underspecified, or low-signal input
Testing summarization or assistant features that take open-ended requests and deciding where clarifying questions or scoped actions are needed
Early in design to locate where a task needs decomposition or guardrails
After failure modes are identified and a quality bar is defined, to decide failure responses
when_not_to_use: As a substitute for exhaustive testing or comprehensive evaluation of model capability; the goal is early signal, not full coverage
When you need statistically robust quality measurement; this is a qualitative sense-building exercise
When the goal is to trick the model rather than understand where communication breaks
When the underlying model is truly inadequate and a guardrail cannot compensate
metric_or_method: Weekly, run four short rituals (about 2-3 min each): ask for something obviously wrong, something ambiguous, something unexpectedly difficult, and add explicit failure responses. Use wrong-vs-ideal two-pass comparison on identical input, note the first point of failure, then add a guardrail (ask, give user a choice, be transparent, or add light structure), capture gaps as product requirements, and re-test the same failure case.
common_pitfalls: Treating a demo or controlled flow as proof the feature works, or waiting for real users to reveal failure modes
Trying to test exhaustively rather than finding where it breaks first
Changing the input between the failure run and the ideal run, which makes the comparison meaningless
Being fooled by output that looks authoritative, clean, and structured but is wrong
Treating the finding as the final solution instead of turning it into a product rule or requirement
Not translating findings into design work (clarification prompts, added context, constrained actions)
Asking to 'fix the model' instead of deciding what the product does when the model hits its limits
Letting the model silently drop information from long context or hiding uncertainty rather than surfacing it
source_excerpt: Now that you have the obviously wrong results, you’ll need to generate the “ideal” response and compare the two responses to understand what signals the model needs to behave correctly.
one_liner: Probe your AI weekly with wrong, vague, and hard inputs to find where it breaks first, then add guardrails.
codex_prompt_template: Build a failure-mode probing harness for my AI feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. The model is called via [MODEL_OR_API_CALL] and the sample messy input is in [INPUT_SOURCE_E.G._SLACK_THREAD_OR_PRD]. Write a script that runs four probes and saves results to a markdown report. (1) Obviously-wrong probe: ask for something the input cannot support, such as [UNSUPPORTED_REQUEST]. (2) Ambiguous probe: send an underspecified request such as [AMBIGUOUS_REQUEST], and flag over-summarizing, latching onto irrelevant details, ignored caveats, or a wrong assumed audience. (3) First-point-of-failure stress test: run a task that looks simple to a human but stresses reasoning or context, such as [HARD_TASK], at increasing input sizes of [INPUT_SIZES], and record where output quality first degrades. (4) Wrong-vs-ideal two-pass: run the identical input once with the baseline prompt and once with a guardrail line, [GUARDRAIL_INSTRUCTION, e.g. only include items explicitly mentioned; say 'Not enough information' if missing]. Output a side-by-side diff of the two responses. Add simple automated checks for [FAILURE_SIGNALS, e.g. invented owners, fabricated decisions, no 'I don't know'] and a pass/fail summary. At the end, generate a table of failure signature, first point of failure, proposed guardrail (clarifying question, user choice, transparency message, or light structure), and a product requirement. Make the script rerunnable so I can re-test the same failure cases weekly after each change, and log results with a date to track regressions.

name: Faithfulness and Hallucination Evaluation
definition: An evaluation that checks whether an LLM output is faithful to the context it was given (accurately using provided content rather than making things up), and, for RAG generators, whether the answer is also relevant to the user's original question.
explanation: The core method is a judge LLM that labels whether an output is grounded in the provided context or hallucinated, with the judge's accuracy validated against human labels. The Hallucination Detection Eval member contributes the beginner-friendly, first-eval version. It suits chatbots or agents that reason over supplied documents such as PDFs. Write a simple eval checking whether the output correctly references provided content or invents information, run it on 5 to 10 representative examples, and iterate on the eval until accuracy improves. The RAG generator member contributes the two-part framing and the sequencing. Faithfulness asks whether the answer sticks to the facts in the retrieved context. Answer relevance asks whether the answer directly addresses the user's question. These are separate, because an answer can be perfectly faithful to the source documents and still miss the user's intent. This member also says to evaluate the generator only after the retriever performs well on a diverse set of queries, so the right information is consistently fed to it. Otherwise generator failures cannot be told apart from retrieval failures.
when_to_use: Chatbots or agents that answer using documents or context you provide
As the first eval to build for a product
RAG systems after the retriever performs well on diverse queries
Diagnosing hallucination in RAG answers
Checking that answers address the user's original question, not just the source
when_not_to_use: Products with no provided context to ground against (not stated explicitly in the source)
Before the retriever is fixed and reliably returning the right documents
metric_or_method: A judge LLM labels whether each output is grounded in the provided or retrieved context or hallucinated (faithfulness), and for RAG also judges whether the answer addresses the user query (answer relevance); judge accuracy is validated against human labels on 5 to 10 representative examples, then iterated.
common_pitfalls: Starting with deeply internal logic rather than a well-defined component
Not iterating on the eval prompt after reviewing results
Evaluating generation before the retriever is fixed
Assuming a faithful answer is also relevant to the question
Not validating the judge LLM's labels against human labels
source_excerpt: First is **faithfulness**: does the generated answer stick to the facts provided in the retrieved context, or is it hallucinating? Second is **answer relevance**: does the answer directly address the user’s original question? An answer can be perfectly faithful to the source documents but still fail to be relevant to the user’s intent.
one_liner: Have a judge LLM flag answers that invent facts beyond the context, then check they actually answer the question.
codex_prompt_template: Build a faithfulness and hallucination eval for my [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] (a [CHATBOT_OR_RAG_OR_AGENT] that answers using [CONTEXT_SOURCE, e.g. retrieved chunks or uploaded PDFs]). Input: a JSONL file at [DATASET_PATH] with fields: question, context, answer, and optional human_label (grounded or hallucinated). Do the following: 1) Write a judge LLM prompt for [JUDGE_MODEL] that labels each answer as grounded or hallucinated relative to ONLY the provided context, lists the unsupported claims, and gives a short rationale. Return structured JSON. 2) Write a second judge prompt for answer relevance that scores whether the answer directly addresses the user's question, separately from faithfulness. 3) Write a Python script that runs both judges over the dataset and reports faithfulness rate, answer relevance rate, and a 2x2 breakdown (faithful and relevant, faithful but irrelevant, unfaithful but relevant, neither). 4) Validate the judge against the human labels on [NUM_LABELED_EXAMPLES, start with 5-10] examples: report accuracy, precision and recall on the hallucinated class, and print every disagreement so I can iterate on the judge prompt. 5) If this is RAG, add an optional check that flags rows where the retriever did not return the needed information, so generator failures are separated from retrieval failures. Output runnable code with clear comments and a sample dataset of 5 rows.

name: False Positive / False Negative Rate Monitoring for Proactive AI Assistants
definition: For an AI that proactively monitors data and surfaces items of concern, track over time whether it is flagging things that don't matter (false positives) or missing things that do (false negatives), and use declining rates to justify relying on it.
explanation: Amol uses Cowork on a schedule to look at 20 to 25 charts every morning and tell him what to pay attention to, what is concerning, and what is interesting. For the long and medium tail of metrics he can't check daily, he gains confidence as the false positive rate and false negative rate of what Claude brings to him fall. He also notes that quality on similar soft-coaching tasks is still hit or miss.
when_to_use: AI assistants that monitor dashboards, metrics, or Slack and surface alerts or insights
When the human can't manually verify everything the AI watches and needs a basis for trust
when_not_to_use: Tasks where the AI output is a single generated artifact rather than a detection or flagging task
metric_or_method: Track false positive rate (flagged items that weren't worth attention) and false negative rate (important things the AI failed to surface) over time. Rely more on the AI as both decline.
common_pitfalls: Only noticing false positives and never checking for misses (false negatives)
Over-trusting output that is still hit or miss. The speaker describes quality on related tasks as decent on some things and not on others.
Relying on a gut feeling of confidence without tracking the rates
source_excerpt: But then there's the long tail of things, and even the medium tail where it's like, you don't have time to look at it every day, that if Claude is proactively looking at it and you start to feel good over time of, okay, it's like the false positive rate is going down, the false negative rate is going down of the things that Claude brings to you, then you just get a little bit more confidence and peace of mind there.
one_liner: Track false positives and false negatives on your proactive AI's alerts until the rates fall enough to trust it.
codex_prompt_template:
I have a proactive AI assistant that monitors [DATA_SOURCE] (e.g., dashboards, metrics, Slack) on a [SCHEDULE] schedule and surfaces items of concern. Build a Python script that tracks its precision and recall over time.

Inputs:
- A log of AI-surfaced items at [ALERT_LOG_PATH] (fields: date, item_id, severity, summary)
- Human feedback labels at [LABELS_PATH] marking each surfaced item as useful or not useful (false positive)
- A list of missed items that humans later found important at [MISSED_ITEMS_PATH] (false negatives)

The script should:
1. Compute false positive rate (flagged items not worth attention / total flagged) per [TIME_WINDOW] (e.g., week).
2. Compute false negative rate (missed important items / (caught important + missed important)) per [TIME_WINDOW].
3. Break down both rates by [SEGMENT] (e.g., metric category, head vs. long-tail metrics).
4. Plot both rates over time with a trend line and a rolling average.
5. Output a trust-readiness verdict: flag when both rates are below [FP_THRESHOLD] and [FN_THRESHOLD] for [N_CONSECUTIVE_WINDOWS] consecutive windows.
6. Include a lightweight way to seed false negatives, such as periodically injecting known anomalies into [DATA_SOURCE] and checking whether the AI surfaces them.

Include unit tests with synthetic data and a README explaining how to collect human labels with minimal effort.

name: Golden Dataset Regression Evals in CI
definition: Treat evals as fuzzy unit tests: run the system against a curated golden dataset of test cases with expected behavior, score each output with a judge or code-based checks, aggregate into a pass score, and compare to the previous baseline on every prompt, code, or model change, blocking the change when checks fail.
explanation:
The core method is a golden dataset (curated stress test, not a random production sample) holding core features, edge cases found in error analysis, and a regression case for every significant bug fixed. On each code, prompt, or model change, the system is rerun on this dataset in CI. Fast deterministic code-based evaluators check the outputs and the build breaks on any failure. A pass signals that known failures have not returned, not overall production quality.

Several members shape the sub-steps. The unit-test framing (Evals as Fuzzy Unit Tests, plus the two 'unit tests for AI/models' notes) explains why this is needed: outputs are non-deterministic, so a test case needs an input, expected behavior (a direction rather than an exact string), a judge, and aggregation into a probability-like score. Evals define what good looks like (correctness, safety, helpfulness, tone), and model accuracy varies by task and changes over time, so it must be measured for your use case. The eval-driven regression note adds the benchmark step: when swapping a model (e.g., GPT-4o to Claude 3.7 Sonnet) or changing a prompt, rerun the dataset through the updated agent and compare scores to the baseline to measure the impact of that one change. The model-versions note adds a shared eval repository built from past pain points, rerun on each new model release to confirm solved areas stay solved (e.g., 100% or 99.9%) and to see whether other areas are improving.

The config-driven harness note covers operationalizing this: a standardized, parallelized scaffold with primitives (task, datasets, personas, LLM adapter, evaluator) and YAML configs that analysts can edit, defined once and run locally, in pre-commit hooks, and in CI/CD as a regression and acceptance suite. The eval-suite note covers suite shape and monitoring: once an LLM judge aligns with human labels, use it to iterate on prompts and recompute error rates on curated cases. Run the full suite to check that fixing one problem did not break another. Typical shape is several code-based evals in CI, perhaps one or two LLM-based evals in CI, and LLM-powered evals roughly weekly on sampled production traces to spot new data distributions or user cohorts.
when_to_use: Preventing old bugs and fixed failures from reappearing
Gating every code, prompt, or model change before it ships
Swapping or upgrading models and needing a baseline comparison on the same dataset
Checking that previously solved pain points stay solved across new model versions
Any system with non-deterministic outputs where you need ahead-of-time confidence in policy-following, tool use, and resolution
When eval scripts are scattered and many contributors, including analysts, need to add or run evals
After an LLM judge has acceptable alignment with human labels, to iterate quickly on a known failure mode
Periodically monitoring sampled production traces for drift or new user cohorts
when_not_to_use: As evidence of overall production quality or for discovering new failure modes; use error analysis and production monitoring for that
With an unvalidated LLM judge
For deterministic code or skills where ordinary unit tests suffice
As the only evaluation method for tasks with unclear success criteria, since exact-match checks do not work on non-deterministic outputs
For failures you can trivially fix without needing ongoing measurement
metric_or_method: Run the system on the golden dataset in CI, score each case against expected behavior with fast code-based evaluators (and a validated judge where needed), aggregate into a pass rate or error rate, compare to the previous baseline on the same dataset, and block the change on failure.
common_pitfalls: Treating a passing CI build as proof of production quality; green does not mean working, and evals themselves can lie
Building the golden dataset from a random sample of production data instead of core features, edge cases, and a regression case per fixed bug
Not expanding the dataset with new examples and edge cases, so evals fail to generalize
Using exact-match, substring, or regex checks on LLM outputs (e.g., a check for 'cannot' passed on 'you cannot pay for the shipping')
Treating a one-shot judge example as an eval instead of building a dataset
Letting solved evals go stale and unrun, or assuming model performance is static
Scattering eval scripts across notebooks and repos, running slow serial suites, or limiting contributions to engineers
Building hundreds of evals when a few suffice, or ignoring new data distributions and cohorts that change failure patterns
source_excerpt: our eval harness is config driven and these are typically stored as YAML file that's easily editable uh by different contributor and not just by engineers. [...] Uh these are high level things like task, data sets, personas, LM adapter and an evaluator. [...] We can run these at pre-commit hook uh to make sure that our performance doesn't degrade before we push a change uh to uh our agent service. Uh another area that we are looking at is also at CI/CD and how we can use our eval harness to uh build our regression test suite
one_liner: Turn every fixed bug into a golden test case, rerun in CI, and block any prompt or model change that regresses.
codex_prompt_template: Build a golden-dataset regression eval suite that runs in CI for my [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] (stack: [LANGUAGE_AND_FRAMEWORK], CI system: [CI_PROVIDER]). Requirements: 1) Dataset: create a versioned file [DATASET_PATH] (JSONL or YAML) where each case has id, input, expected_behavior (a description of the required behavior, not an exact string), tags (core, edge_case, or regression), and source (e.g. the bug or error-analysis finding it came from). Seed it with [NUM_SEED_CASES] cases covering core features, edge cases from [KNOWN_FAILURE_MODES], and one regression case per fixed bug. 2) Evaluators: implement fast deterministic code-based checks first (e.g. [CODE_CHECKS] such as schema validity, required tool calls, forbidden phrases, policy rules). Add an optional LLM-judge evaluator for [JUDGE_CRITERIA] with a rubric and a pass/fail output, and flag that it must first be validated against human labels. 3) Harness: a config-driven runner (YAML config with task, dataset, persona, model adapter, evaluator) that runs cases in parallel and writes per-case results and an aggregate pass rate to [RESULTS_PATH]. 4) Baseline: store the previous baseline scores and compare the current run against them. Report newly failing cases, newly passing cases, and the pass-rate delta by tag. 5) Gating: exit non-zero if any regression-tagged case fails or if the overall pass rate drops more than [MAX_DROP_THRESHOLD] below baseline. Provide a pre-commit hook and a CI workflow file that triggers on changes to prompts, code, or the model config. 6) Include a README section on how to add a new regression case after a bug fix, how to update the baseline, and a note that a pass means known failures have not returned, not overall production quality. Also suggest a weekly job that runs the LLM judge on sampled production traces to detect drift.

sources.title: An AI glossary
sources.excerpt:
Evals (short for “evaluations”) are structured ways to measure how well an AI system performs on specific tasks, such as correctness, safety, helpfulness, or tone. They define what “good” looks like for your AI system and help you answer the question: Is this model doing what I want it to do?

Evals are basically unit tests or benchmarks for your AI product. They run your model through predefined inputs and compare its responses against expected outputs. This helps you quantify progress, catch regressions, and guide you toward improvements.
