name: Ground-Truth Reference Dataset Curation
definition: Curate a structured reference dataset of expected behavior, with inputs, expected outputs or human-labeled ground truth, and decision metadata. Seed it with roughly 10 to 100 examples from real interactions, past logs, or synthetic generation. Cover key topics, edge cases, must-not-fail cases, and both failing and should-not-fail situations. Extend it as monitoring reveals new failure modes.
explanation: The core method is to collect a concrete reference to evaluate against, because user behavior is non-deterministic. Gather examples from direct feedback, analytics, manual inspection, or past logs. If feedback is lacking, sample data and have subject-matter experts or PMs label it. Generate examples from expected product behavior if no traffic exists yet. Balance the set across topics (for a trip agent: hotel booking, flight booking, support, trip planning advice) and include edge cases. Start in a spreadsheet and later move to open-source tooling such as Phoenix for logging and managing data. Each member contributed a variant or sub-step. The Ground Truth Dataset from Real Interactions note supplies the sourcing, labeling and balancing steps, with a rule of thumb of 10 to 100 labeled examples to use before writing a first LLM judge. The Reference Dataset note covers the cold-start, pre-deployment use: examples with query, expected output and routing metadata (product type, user tier, channel) used to evaluate performance, validate eval design and show what context the assistant needs. It advises 20 to 100 examples, broad coverage and no over-optimization, since production behavior will differ. The Failure-Mode-Driven note frames the dataset as product thinking encoded in data. It starts with about 10 questions that must never go wrong and adds datasets for failure modes found in monitoring, such as an agent offering refunds it was configured not to. Run it on every prompt, tool or model change. Building it with PMs and SMEs also exposes team misalignment on expected behavior. The On-Distribution Coverage note adds a quality check on each new eval built from failed trajectories. Confirm it includes both the situations where the model fails and those where it should not fail, and that it reflects the real user distribution. This catches over-correction before the eval is handed to researchers to measure improvement.
when_to_use: Cold start, before any live traffic exists or before deploying an AI feature
Before writing your first LLM judge, or when validating that an automated eval matches human judgment
After production monitoring reveals a critical failure mode that must not recur
When creating a new eval from observed failures and handing it to researchers to measure improvement
Validating eval design and making early tweaks to the application setup
When the team needs to align on expected product behavior
when_not_to_use: As the only source of truth, since real user behavior will differ from expectations
Expecting a fixed dataset to cover all customer interactions in highly customizable products like coding agents
metric_or_method: Collect about 10 to 100 examples (query, expected output or human label, decision metadata) from real interactions, logs or synthetic generation. Have PMs or SMEs label them, balance across topics, and include edge cases, must-not-fail cases, and both failing and should-not-fail situations. Run on every change to prompts, tools or models, and add cases for newly observed critical failures.
common_pitfalls: Datasets that are unrepresentative of real-world usage or unbalanced across topics
Omitting edge cases
Building an eval only from failing examples, so it cannot catch over-correction
Over-optimizing evals on the reference dataset instead of aiming for broad coverage
Believing the dataset is comprehensive and assuming it mirrors real user behavior
Not involving PMs and subject matter experts, leaving the team misaligned on expected behavior
Skipping scoping and curation and jumping straight to setup, or only testing by vibes
source_excerpt: Collect these interactions into a structured dataset, ideally annotated with “ground truth” (human labels) for accuracy. I’d recommend having between 10 and 100 examples with human labels to start with, as a rule of thumb, to use as ground truth for evaluation.
one_liner: Build a 10-100 example labeled gold set of must-not-fail and edge cases, then grow it from monitoring.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me curate a ground-truth reference dataset for an AI feature.

Tasks:
1. 2. Write a Python script that samples and de-duplicates examples from [DATA_SOURCES] (or generates synthetic examples via an LLM if no traffic exists) and stratifies them across [TOPICS].
3. Generate a labeling sheet for PM/SME review with clear labeling guidelines and a column for disagreement notes.

5. Add a function that appends new cases when a new failure mode is found, and a runner that evaluates the feature on the whole dataset on every prompt, tool, or model change and reports pass rate per slice.

name: Guardrail Evals (Runtime Blocking)
definition: A synchronous evaluator that runs in the request path (a just-in-time harness) for critical, high-impact failures and can block, redact, or regenerate a response before the user sees it. It works as the runtime layer alongside ahead-of-time evals run before deployment.
explanation: The core method is an inline guardrail check. Most guardrails are fast, deterministic checks such as regexes, keyword blocklists, or schema validators, because they must add minimal latency. They need a very low false-positive rate, since blocking a valid response is a production bug. An LLM-as-a-judge can serve as a guardrail only if the latency budget allows. In high-stakes domains like medical advice, a slower, more powerful inline judge may be justified, while in creative applications the cost of false positives may be too high. The second member frames this as a layered reliability strategy. Ahead-of-time evals, run in CI before release, provide reliability and mitigate exploits, much like TypeScript's compile-time checks. Just-in-time harnesses, the runtime guardrails, provide reliability while the user is running the system, like JavaScript's runtime resolution. Using both gives layered protection. The Instagram support chatbot incident illustrates this: an agent with elevated API access added an attacker's email to accounts, and either an eval or a harness could have caught it. The speaker also argues that a strong harness and eval set lets you go far with cheaper, less capable models.
when_to_use: Critical, high-impact failures that must be stopped before the user sees them
High-stakes domains where a false negative is very costly
Building or operating an agent with elevated permissions or account-mutating tools
When security and policy failures should be caught both before shipping and at runtime
when_not_to_use: When latency budgets are tight and only a slow LLM judge could do the check
Creative applications where blocking valid responses is too costly
When you are only a user of someone else's harness and the behavior is deterministic (the speaker does not eval skills he writes himself)
metric_or_method: Run evals in CI before release (ahead of time) and keep an inline runtime guardrail (just in time) using fast deterministic checks (regex, blocklists, schema validators), optionally an LLM judge if latency allows, with a very low false-positive rate.
common_pitfalls: High false-positive rates that block valid responses, which count as production bugs
Using slow LLM judges that exceed the latency budget
Moving too fast and skipping evals on agents with powerful tool access
Relying on only one layer, either eval or harness, when both are needed
source_excerpt: For critical, high-impact failures, you can use a special type of synchronous evaluator called a **guardrail**. These run in the request path and can block, redact, or regenerate a response before the user ever sees it.
one_liner: Block, redact, or regenerate bad outputs in the request path with fast regex and schema checks before users see them.
codex_prompt_template: Implement a runtime guardrail layer for my [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] that runs synchronously in the request path before the response is returned to the user. Critical failure modes to catch: [FAILURE_MODES] (e.g., PII leakage, policy violations, unauthorized account-mutating tool calls). name: Human Baseline Comparison
definition: Evaluate an AI system by comparing its outputs or outcomes with a reference baseline of real human performance (or the prior human-accessible state of the art) on the same task, so that quality, safety, or risk is judged relative to what people actually achieve.
explanation: The method is to pick a human-derived baseline for the task, make it fair, and compare the AI against it on a defined metric. Sourcing real human work: one member found the hardest part was locating real examples of humans doing the task. Advice posts did not work, so they used PM interview answers from Exponent's database as the baseline, edited one answer by adding numbers to keep the comparison fair, and compared through blind ratings. They also note that human performance is often under-measured and that people disagree about whether the human answer was good. Seniority-anchored metric: for an experimentation agent, the AI's experiment win rate is compared with what you would expect from a human PM at a given level. The CASH system is described as roughly a junior PM with two to three years of experience, not yet senior. This is a qualitative expectation, not a formal benchmark, but it makes progress easy to communicate. Human-with-AI baseline: for benchmark design, reference solutions can come from experts who used AI tools, so the comparison is one human using AI against another human using AI. This reflects real use, where a human steers and verifies the AI, and avoids racing an unaided human against a machine. Rate-based safety baseline: for safety-critical systems, the system's incident rate (for example collisions per 100,000 miles) is compared against a benchmark built from available human data. Waymo builds its own because no industry-wide standard exists, and aims to beat it. It pairs this with progress or assertiveness metrics because a system can be very safe by not moving. Uplift trial: for dangerous capabilities, the baseline is people using Google Search, the previous state of the art. Model-assisted performance is compared against it in an A/B uplift trial run with domain experts. This was used to evaluate biological uplift, found somewhat significant with ASL-3 models, and to give policymakers evidence.
when_to_use: You want to know whether AI can match or replace human work on a specific task and can obtain real human examples or data
Evaluating an AI agent whose actions have measurable outcomes (such as experiment win rate) and you want to communicate quality in human terms like junior vs. senior
Designing a human-vs-AI benchmark for tasks where professionals normally use AI tools
Evaluating safety-critical systems where a human performance baseline can be estimated from data, including when no industry standard exists
Assessing misuse risk in high-severity domains by comparing against the previous state of the art, such as Google Search
Providing policymakers or stakeholders with evidence of risk or capability
when_not_to_use: The task has no meaningful human equivalent or comparison, or no clear win/loss outcome
No meaningful human baseline data is accessible
You specifically need to measure fully autonomous operation with no human involvement
Everyday quality evaluation of non-hazardous product features (uplift trials are for high-severity risk)
Used as the only metric for safety; pair it with progress or assertiveness metrics
Large experiments needing cross-functional alignment, which win rate does not capture
metric_or_method: Pair each AI output or outcome with a vetted, comparably formatted human baseline (real human answers, human-with-AI expert solutions, human incident rates, or a prior-tool control group) and compare via blind ratings, win rate versus an expected human level, rate per exposure, or A/B uplift.
common_pitfalls: Using advice articles instead of real examples of the work, or a weak human answer (e.g., missing numbers) that makes the comparison unfair
Under-investing in measuring human performance and ignoring subjectivity about what a good human answer is
Using unaided human experts as the baseline, or reading results as more autonomy than exists while ignoring the human who steers and verifies
Treating a seniority comparison as a precise benchmark, or generalizing from small experiments (copy changes, minor UI tweaks) to larger ones
Judging on a snapshot when the system is improving rapidly with each model release
Oversimplifying benchmark and system calculations, or assuming a single standard human safety benchmark exists
Optimizing for safety alone, producing a system that barely moves
Running dangerous-capability uplift trials without domain experts, or dismissing a small current uplift because future models may be larger
source_excerpt: The hardest part of doing a blind evaluation was finding real examples and results from a human doing the task. [...] We used PM answers from Exponent as the human responses for all three selected tasks. I’ll add that there could certainly be better human answers, but thousands of PMs are using these answers in their interview prep monthly, so it’s a strong benchmark to use.
one_liner: Race your AI against real human baselines with blind ratings to prove it beats people, not just benchmarks.
codex_prompt_template: You are helping me build a human baseline comparison eval for an AI feature. Feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Task: [TASK_DEFINITION]. Human baseline source: [HUMAN_BASELINE_SOURCE] (e.g. expert answers, human-with-AI solutions, historical incident rates, or a prior-tool control group). Comparison metric: [METRIC] (e.g. blind pairwise preference, win rate vs expected human level, incidents per [EXPOSURE_UNIT], or A/B uplift). Sample size: [NUM_TASKS] tasks. Write Python code that: 1) loads AI outputs and human baseline outputs from [DATA_PATH] and aligns them by task ID; 2) normalizes format and length so the comparison is fair (strip style tells, match level of detail and numeric specificity, and log every edit made to a human answer); 3) randomizes and anonymizes A/B order for blind rating, and generates a rater sheet or LLM-judge prompt using this rubric: [RUBRIC_CRITERIA]; 4) aggregates ratings into win/tie/loss rates with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, and reports inter-rater agreement and the human-human disagreement rate, so noisy human baselines are visible; 5) for rate-based or uplift metrics, computes the rate per exposure unit or the treatment-vs-control difference with a significance test, and pairs it with a counter-metric [COUNTER_METRIC] (e.g. progress or task completion) so the system can't win by doing nothing; 6) outputs a summary table plus a plain-language verdict such as 'comparable to a junior human at [HUMAN_LEVEL]' with caveats about baseline quality. Include unit tests on the pairing and randomization logic.

name: Human End-to-End Output Review
definition: A manual quality pass in which a named human reviewer experiences AI-generated output the way a user would, inspecting it closely (item by item for batches, pixel by pixel for details) and judging whether it solves the problem, is coherent, and is faithful to its source. The reviewer then pushes unfinished work toward completion through iteration and, optionally, adversarial-agent critique.
explanation: The core method is a human review after the build. A designated editor walks the end-to-end user journey and asks: Does it solve the problem? Is it attuned to how the user thinks? Is it coherent and fully formed? Post-Build Editor Review contributed this framing. When AI makes building cheap, the upstream filters (staffing limits, long planning) disappear, so filtering must happen after the build, when it is harder to say no. Pieces that look good alone can feel disconnected in the full journey. The editor's job is not a yes/no ship verdict but deciding whether the work is fully formed and how to complete it, and the editor is accountable for every decision. Iterative Scrutiny and Adversarial Stress-Testing contributed the push-further loop. Examine details such as motion, color and lines, and regenerate repeatedly. In the event-animation example the first version looked cool but moved in a jilted way, and 56 iterations were needed to get realism and life. Improve inputs (specific prompts, your beliefs, source material), then stress outputs, using adversarial agents to critique and bang up the result while the human keeps pushing. This counters the burrito dilemma, where speed leads people to overlook serious flaws. Item-by-item review of batch outputs contributed the batch variant. After generating 250+ pixel-art avatars from podcast cover photos with a CLI tool, the author inspected every output against its source for consistent style and size and fidelity. This surfaced edge cases automation missed: a guest who really has rabbit ears in the cover photo (nearly deleted as an error), and covers with two people that needed a separate image per person. Together: review the whole experience, scrutinize each item against its source, and iterate until the output is actually good, not just done.
when_to_use: When AI lets a team produce many prototypes or features quickly and upstream filters are gone
When AI output looks polished but may not solve the user's problem or differentiate
When assembled pieces may look good in isolation but feel disconnected in the user journey
When AI output looks finished quickly but may be prematurely so
When subtle details such as motion, color and lines determine whether the work feels cared for
After a batch or bulk generation run where outputs must be consistent with each other
When each output has a ground-truth source (e.g., an input photo) to compare against
When the batch is small enough, or the stakes high enough, that reviewing every item is feasible
when_not_to_use: As a replacement for upfront alignment on a point of view and standards; it works on top of them
When volume is too large for manual review of every item to be practical (the source does not discuss alternatives)
When no accountable person is available to own the end-to-end judgment
metric_or_method: Qualitative review by a named person who walks the end-to-end user journey and inspects each output against its source and the style/size standard, asking: Does it solve the problem? Is it attuned to the user? Is it coherent and fully formed? Combine with repeated regeneration (56 iterations in the animation example) and adversarial-agent critique, while the human stays responsible for pushing for better.
common_pitfalls: Believing that built means done and done means good
Being misled by an apparently polished state, such as nice corners and drop shadows
Having no one who looks at the product end to end and confirms it is a whole
Reducing review to a yes/no on shipping instead of asking whether it is fully formed
Evaluating pieces in isolation instead of in the full user journey
The burrito dilemma: being enamored by speed and overlooking serious flaws, or delegating the push for better entirely to adversarial agents
Using generic prompts without brand beliefs or source material
Mistaking a faithful source detail for an AI error (rabbit ears), or missing multi-subject inputs that need separate outputs
source_excerpt: But the filtering that used to be throughout the process now needs to happen post build when it is a lot harder to say no. This is where the role of an editor comes in and it is ultra important in this day and age. Who is doing this in your organization? Who's looking at the end to end and understanding whether or not we're actually building a whole? [...] The most important thing I can say to anybody working on their editing skills is you have to experience it like a user would. Does it actually solve the problem? Is it actually attuned to the way the user thinks about things? Is it actually coherent?
one_liner: Walk the journey like a user, check every output against its source, and iterate until it's finished, not just done.
codex_prompt_template: Build a human end-to-end review harness for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Inputs: a folder of AI-generated outputs at [OUTPUT_DIR] and, where available, their source inputs at [SOURCE_DIR]. Standard to enforce: [STYLE_AND_SIZE_STANDARD]. Tasks: 1) Generate a static HTML review sheet that shows each output side by side with its source, with fields for the reviewer's name, a pass/fix/regenerate verdict, and notes. 2) Add automated pre-checks for [AUTOMATED_CHECKS, e.g. dimensions, file format, style consistency] and flag outliers. Do NOT auto-delete anything flagged. Surface the flags to the reviewer, because apparent errors can be faithful to the source. 3) Add an end-to-end journey checklist for [USER_JOURNEY_STEPS] with three questions per step: Does it solve the user's problem? Is it attuned to how the user thinks? Is it coherent and fully formed? 4) Add an optional adversarial critique step: call an LLM agent with the output, its source, and the standard, and ask it to list the top [N_CRITIQUES] flaws and edge cases such as multiple subjects, odd but real details, and inconsistencies across the batch. Show the critique next to the human verdict. 5) Log each regeneration iteration, with the prompt changes and the reviewer's reason, to a CSV. 6) Output a summary with the pass rate, the items sent back for iteration, the edge cases found, and the named reviewer accountable for the ship decision. Write the code in [LANGUAGE] with a README.

name: Implicit User Signals as Quality Metrics
definition: Infer AI output quality from what users do in production instead of explicit ratings or hand labels. Signals include regeneration, product switch-off, acceptance of suggestions or code changes, and expressed frustration such as swearing. Use them alongside explicit feedback to decide which traces to inspect and to evaluate changes.
explanation:
The method is to log behavioral signals, aggregate them over time, and use them to monitor quality and surface traces worth reviewing. They also feed A/B tests of model or RL changes. Explicit feedback is often sparse, because users may not thumbs-down a bad answer but simply regenerate it. For Codex code review, annoyed users may switch the product off. Users also keep or omit parts of a suggestion, and those choices are tracked as implicit signals too.

Variant 1, frustration-signal dashboard: the Claude Code team began tracking swear words in user messages after an engineer suggested it when they saw frustrations. The dashboard shows how often users are frustrated. It is a lightweight proxy tied to the point that evals are about a delightful, less frustrating user experience, not only accuracy. It captures just one kind of frustration and not overall experience quality.

Variant 2, acceptance as a retrieval-quality signal: Windsurf receives tens of millions of pieces of user feedback per hour, including preference data from autocomplete. For retrieval, they log whether the right data was retrieved and whether the user accepted the code change that followed. Acceptance after retrieval is treated as a positive signal and needs no hand labels. This feedback is also used to train and evaluate models, such as their in-house retrieval model, on realistic, incomplete code states that public data does not resemble.

These signals point to where to look. They do not replace deeper evaluation, and they help teams find scenarios instead of predicting all of them upfront.
when_to_use: Production monitoring where explicit feedback such as thumbs up/down is sparse
You need a lightweight behavioral proxy for user frustration in a chatbot or agent
Quality problems show up in user experience rather than in accuracy numbers
Evaluating model or RL changes via A/B tests on user reactions
Evaluating retrieval or context selection in a high-volume product with a clear accept or reject action
Building preference data from real usage to train or evaluate in-house models
when_not_to_use: As a sole quality measure, since signals only indicate where to look
Early-stage products without enough user volume to produce meaningful signals
Cases with no observable downstream user action to treat as acceptance or rejection
metric_or_method: Track implicit behaviors (regeneration, product switch-off, partial keep or omit of suggestions, swear-word rate, acceptance of changes after retrieval) over time alongside explicit thumbs up/down, then use them to select traces for review and to compare variants in A/B tests.
common_pitfalls: Relying only on explicit feedback, since users often don't give a thumbs down
Trying to predict every scenario upfront instead of using signals to discover them
Treating swear-word counts as overall experience quality, when they capture only one kind of frustration
Reading acceptance after retrieval as pure retrieval quality, when the planning or editing model also affects it (an inference, noisy proxy)
Using public data or benchmarks as a stand-in for in-the-moment, incomplete user code, which can mislead

So that is a clear indication that the initial answer that regenerator is not meeting the customer's expectation. So these are the kind of implicit signals you always need to think about.

You are helping me build an implicit-signal quality monitor for my AI feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION].

I have production logs in [LOG_SOURCE_AND_SCHEMA] with fields such as [AVAILABLE_EVENT_FIELDS] (e.g., session_id, trace_id, user_message, model_output, regenerate_click, suggestion_accepted, suggestion_partially_kept, feature_disabled).

name: In-Product Explicit Feedback Capture
definition: A continuous process of collecting explicit human feedback inside the product (thumbs up/down, inline feedback forms, comment boxes, bug reports), optionally supplemented by labels from human labelers such as subject-matter experts, and using it to improve the next iteration of the model, prompt, fine-tuning, examples and retrieval (RAG).
explanation: The method is to put feedback controls next to AI output, such as thumbs up/down, a comment box, an inline feedback form or a bug-report path, and to feed what comes back into prompt optimization, fine-tuning (including RLHF), examples and RAG. The first member, human evals, frames this as a human feedback loop tied directly to end users. It adds a second source: labels from subject-matter experts or other human labelers, which can serve as human-labeled ground truth for validating automated evals. It warns that user feedback is very sparse because most people do not click, that a thumbs up or down has an unclear meaning, and that hiring labelers is costly. The second member, the in-product user feedback loop, describes the practice as Rauch advises it: create many opportunities for feedback, taking inspiration from Stripe's inline feedback button with four emojis, which Vercel routed straight into Slack in its early days. With AI products the feedback becomes a constant stream, and bug reports let users point out where the AI went wrong. Exposing the model's thinking helps users pinpoint those failures. He notes that a strong correlation between user love and retention serves as v0's fitness function. He argues that non-AI products will struggle to compete with this tight loop. He also observed that some feedback just needed to be said to v0 as a prompt. Together: capture explicit feedback cheaply in-product, add expert labels where ground truth is needed, route it somewhere the team sees it, and close the loop into changes.
when_to_use: Early in an AI product's life, to build a steady stream of real user signal
You want a signal directly tied to end users
You want specific, actionable reports of where the AI went wrong
You need data to improve the model, prompt, fine-tuning examples or RAG
You need human-labeled ground truth from subject-matter experts to validate automated evals
Aligning the application with human preferences through prompt optimization or fine-tuning
when_not_to_use: As the only evaluation signal: it is reactive and depends on users choosing to give feedback
When you need dense, high-volume, low-cost signal on its own, since feedback is sparse and labelers are costly
metric_or_method: In-product thumbs up/down, comments, inline emoji feedback forms (e.g. routed to Slack) and bug reports, plus optional subject-matter-expert labels as ground truth, tracked alongside the correlation between user love and retention and fed into prompt, model, fine-tuning, examples and RAG changes.
common_pitfalls: Sparse feedback because most users do not click thumbs up/down
Treating a thumbs up or down as a strong signal when its meaning is ambiguous
Making feedback hard to give, so little arrives
Not closing the loop into model, prompt, fine-tuning, examples or RAG changes
Missing feedback that could be solved by telling the AI directly as a prompt
High cost if hiring human labelers or subject-matter experts
source_excerpt: These are human feedback loops you can design into your product (i.e. showing a thumbs-up/thumbs-down or a comment box next to an LLM response, for your user to provide feedback). You can also have human labelers (i.e. subject-matter experts) provide their labels and feedback, and use this for aligning the application with human preferences via prompt optimization or fine-tuning a model
one_liner: Put thumbs, comments and bug reports next to every AI output, route them to Slack, and close the loop.
codex_prompt_template: I am building an in-product explicit feedback capture loop for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION], built on [STACK_OR_FRAMEWORK]. Please do the following. 1) Design and implement feedback controls next to each AI response: thumbs up/down, an optional free-text comment, an inline emoji rating, and a 'report a problem' path. 2) Define a feedback event schema that stores the feedback type, rating, comment, response_id, trace_id, user_id (hashed), prompt, model and prompt version, retrieved context (if RAG), and timestamp. 3) Add a backend endpoint that validates and persists events to [STORAGE_BACKEND], and a webhook that routes new negative feedback and bug reports to [NOTIFICATION_CHANNEL, e.g. Slack]. 4) Write an analysis script that joins feedback to traces and reports feedback response rate, thumbs-down rate by [SEGMENT, e.g. prompt version, intent, model], the top clusters of failure comments, and the correlation between feedback and [RETENTION_OR_ENGAGEMENT_METRIC]. Account for sparsity and selection bias, since most users never click. 5) Add an export that turns thumbs-down traces and [SME_LABELS_SOURCE] expert labels into a labeled dataset of [DATASET_SIZE] examples for validating automated evals, prompt optimization, few-shot examples, RAG fixes and fine-tuning. Provide the code, the tests, and a short weekly review checklist for closing the loop.

name: Internal Dogfooding for Quality Vetting
definition: A qualitative quality-vetting process in which a team uses its own product firsthand and extensively, in real daily work over an extended period, to find problems, judge output quality, and decide whether to ship or expand rollout. It complements metrics and dashboards and is calibrated for the ways internal users differ from the broader market.
explanation: The core method is to ship the product internally and have people, including leaders and non-engineering teams, use it on real tasks, then judge whether it works, retains users, and delights. Variants and sub-steps from the members: (1) Internal quality bar: the questions are uptake, retention, delight or surprise, whether it unlocks a new model use case, whether it aims about 2-3 months ahead of the models, and whether it gets out of the model's way. There is no fixed numeric threshold. (2) Release gate: GitHub teams across engineering, product, finance, legal and HR use chat, search, recommendations and PR summaries for months and ask whether answers and summaries are right. Nothing ships before that. (3) Qualitative vetting alongside data: Fiona's examples are a scam vector found by selling an item on Marketplace, VR floor-height issues, and slow LTE loading found on a customer visit in Chile. Customer visits are the fallback when the product is hard to use directly, and anecdotes are balanced with data. Claude helps generate manual test plans. (4) Leadership hands-on use: Block's CEO, CTO and exec team used Goose daily on specific real tasks to learn strengths, weaknesses and ergonomics. About 60% of a 10-item wishlist succeeded, and the agent struggled on the rest. Block pairs this with metrics to validate productivity. (5) Staged internal trial: Stripe ran a fairly rigorous Copilot trial with internal engineers, assessing productivity, generated-code quality and engineer feedback, and expanded access only after positive results. Quantified gains were too early to tell. (6) Audience-bias calibration: OpenAI's Codex dogfooding signal differed from the market because staff are comfortable with parallel, async, prompt-up-front workflows. This led them to lead with an interactive IDE/CLI experience. (7) Regular forums: Vercel uses v0 to build v0, and holds weekly Demo Fridays to surface learnings. (8) Informal error analysis: dogfooding works as lightweight error analysis when builders are domain experts, as with coding agents. It is weaker where they are not, such as in medical advice, and many teams claim to dogfood without enough depth to close the feedback loop.
when_to_use: Before shipping a new AI product or feature externally, when your own team can plausibly use it
When builders are the domain experts and heavy users, as with coding agents
When leaders need to learn a tool's real strengths and limits before applying it to team workflows
Before expanding an AI coding assistant across an engineering org, via a staged internal trial
To keep a pulse on real experience beyond dashboards, using customer visits if you cannot use the product yourself
To get early qualitative signals on output relevance, summary quality and unexpected usage
when_not_to_use: As the only quality signal; it does not replace testing with real external users
When internal users are unrepresentative of the target market, such as doctors or other domains with no natural dogfooding
When you need precise quantified productivity gains right after rollout
As a substitute for systematic review or error analysis
metric_or_method: Qualitative internal use on real tasks over an extended period, judged on uptake, retention, delight, correctness of output, code quality and engineer feedback, with informal tracking such as share of tasks completed. Findings are cross-checked against external users and metrics, and surfaced in regular review sessions. There is no fixed numeric threshold.
common_pitfalls: Assuming internal power-user workflows (parallel, async, prompt-up-front) generalize to external users
Claiming to dogfood without using the product deeply or long enough to close the feedback loop
Getting lost in metrics and dashboards only, or blindly following a metric that no longer reflects the desired outcome
Anchoring too heavily on present model capabilities, or building so far into the future that the product is unusable
Treating the bar as a fixed number rather than a judgment on retention and delight
Declaring productivity gains too early, or ignoring the quality of generated code
Limiting dogfooding to engineers, or having no regular forum to surface learnings
Forming opinions from think pieces, over-constraining the agent, or expecting full autonomy
source_excerpt: Dogfooding is a dangerous one, only because a lot of people will say they're dogfooding. [...] A lot of people aren't really dogfooding it at that visceral level that you would need to close that feedback loop.
one_liner: Use your own AI product daily on real work to catch what dashboards miss before you ship.
codex_prompt_template: Build a lightweight dogfooding toolkit for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] that will be used internally by [INTERNAL_USER_GROUPS] for [TRIAL_DURATION]. 1) Create a feedback log schema (CSV or SQLite) capturing: user role, real task attempted, task completed (yes/no/partial), output correctness (1-5), delight or surprise note, failure category, severity, and whether the user would use it again. 2) Write a script that ingests the log from [FEEDBACK_LOG_PATH] and reports weekly: active users, retention week over week, share of tasks completed, top failure categories, and the most severe open issues. 3) Add an audience-bias check that compares internal usage patterns (task types, workflow style) with [EXTERNAL_USER_PROFILE] and flags where internal users likely differ from the market. 4) Generate a ship/expand-rollout readiness checklist with these questions: uptake, retention, delight, correctness on real tasks, and whether the model's capability is getting in the way. Set thresholds from [SHIP_CRITERIA]; if none are provided, state that none are set and leave judgment to a human. 5) Draft a manual test plan of [NUM_TEST_SCENARIOS] realistic scenarios, including adversarial or abuse cases relevant to [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION], and a template for a weekly review session. Output the code, the schema, and the templates.

name: Judge Bias Audit (Position, Sycophancy, Self-Preference, Verbosity)
definition: A checklist of four judge biases to test for and mitigate: position bias, sycophancy bias, self-preference bias, and verbosity bias.
explanation: Position bias is a preference for the first option, especially with cheaper models and fine-tunes; test it by swapping the option order. Sycophancy bias is choosing the nicest answer, such as saying a customer can return headphones outside a 14-day policy. Self-preference bias is choosing text from the same model family; use a judge from a different family than the generator. Verbosity bias is preferring answers padded with tokens. In the live demo, GPT-3.5 Turbo as judge chose a same-family answer that was wrong. Putting the actual policy in the prompt (RAG) mostly removed the problem.
when_to_use: Before trusting any LLM-as-judge in an eval pipeline
When the judge model is in the same family as the generator
When using cheaper models or fine-tunes as judges
when_not_to_use: For deterministic checks such as exact match or schema validation, where no judge is involved
metric_or_method: Swap the order of options and see whether the verdict follows position; use a different model family for judging; include policy context; include sycophancy-tempting cases (flattering or pleading customers) in the dataset
common_pitfalls: Assuming a green eval means the system works
Using the same model family for generation and judging
Ignoring that helpful-assistant system prompts push the judge toward 'yes'
source_excerpt: the way of checking for this bias is you swap the order of options. And if it's still the first one, though the first one is wrong, that's how you know this. [...] your judge needs to be a different model family from the rest of your corpus if you're generating text.
one_liner: Swap option order, switch model families, and bait the judge to expose four hidden LLM-judge biases.
codex_prompt_template:
I use an LLM-as-judge to evaluate [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. The judge model is [JUDGE_MODEL] and the generator model is [GENERATOR_MODEL]. My labeled dataset is at [DATASET_PATH] with [DATASET_SIZE] examples, each with a ground-truth label and, where relevant, a policy or reference document in [POLICY_CONTEXT_FIELD].

Write a Python judge bias audit harness that tests four biases:
1. Position bias: run every pairwise comparison twice with option order swapped. Report the percent of verdicts that follow position instead of content, and the flip rate. Break results down by judge model.
2. Sycophancy bias: build or filter a set of tempting cases, such as flattering or pleading users and requests that violate [POLICY_EXAMPLE]. Report how often the judge approves the answer that bends the policy.
3. Self-preference bias: compare the judge's win rate on outputs from its own model family versus other families, controlling for ground-truth correctness. Flag the judge if it prefers same-family outputs when they are wrong.
4. Verbosity bias: pad correct answers with filler tokens and compare against concise correct answers. Report the win-rate shift as a function of length.

Then rerun the audit with the policy or reference text injected into the judge prompt and with a judge from a different model family, [ALTERNATE_JUDGE_MODEL]. Output a table with bias rates before and after mitigation, the 95% confidence intervals, and a pass/fail against a threshold of [MAX_ACCEPTABLE_BIAS_RATE]. Include unit tests and a CLI entry point.

name: Known-Answer Probing Against the Source Corpus
definition: A manual evaluation loop in which you pick questions whose ground-truth answers are in the source content (for example a specific benchmark number or a named fact), run them through the model, and compare the output to the source. Failures are diagnosed, a fix is applied, and the same questions are re-asked to confirm the fix.
explanation: Dan Shipper probes the baseline GPT-3 bot with questions whose answers he can verify in Lenny's archive. The activation-rate benchmark answer was in the right ballpark but lower than Lenny's published figure. The question about Substack's first publisher got a confident but wrong answer (Andrew Sullivan instead of Bill Bishop). The question about whether consumer startup ideas should come from founders solving their own problem got a confident but wrong "Absolutely". He attributes the failures to two intertwined causes: hallucination, and the model lacking the right data (a knowledge cutoff, and paywalled content). He then re-asks the same failed question with the relevant article text stuffed into the prompt, and later with the retrieval-based setup, and checks that the answer now matches the source (less than a third of founders). He also asks "What is good retention for a consumer social product?" and checks the answer against the archive. The article treats this as manual probing, not an automated or quantified eval.
when_to_use: Early prototyping of a chatbot or Q&A bot built on a specific body of content
When you can identify questions with known, verifiable answers in the source material
When testing whether a fix (adding context or retrieval) actually corrects a previously observed failure
when_not_to_use: When you need statistically reliable quality measurement at scale; the article only shows hand-picked, manual checks
When no ground-truth source exists to check answers against
metric_or_method: Manual side-by-side comparison of the model's answer to the known answer in the source article (qualitative correct/incorrect judgement), followed by re-testing the same failed prompts after changing the setup.
common_pitfalls: Confident-sounding answers can be wrong, so tone is not a signal of correctness
Answers that are in the right ballpark but do not match the source's specific benchmark can slip through as good enough
Hallucination and missing or outdated data (knowledge cutoff, paywalled content) are intertwined causes that need separate diagnosis
A few hand-picked questions give anecdotal evidence only; the author concedes the bot is promising but not yet perfect
source_excerpt: This answer sounds confident, but it is incorrect. (The correct answer is [Bill Bishop](https://sinocism.com/).) [...] Last time, when we asked GPT-3 if it was best for consumer business founders to try to solve their own problem, it responded, “Absolutely!” Which, given what’s in Lenny’s article, is wrong. [...] Success! Now it tells us that less than a third of founders were trying to solve their own problem.
one_liner: Ask questions you can verify in your source, catch confident wrong answers, apply a fix, then re-ask the same ones.
codex_prompt_template: Build a known-answer probing harness for my [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] that answers questions from [SOURCE_CORPUS]. Steps: 1) Create a JSON/CSV file of [NUM_QUESTIONS] probe questions. Each row has: question, ground_truth_answer, source_passage_or_url, and category (e.g. numeric fact, named entity, opinion/stance). 2) Write a script that runs each question through [BASELINE_SETUP] (e.g. plain LLM) and [FIXED_SETUP] (e.g. context stuffing or retrieval) and saves the answers. 3) Show a side-by-side table: question, ground truth, baseline answer, fixed answer, and a manual verdict column (correct / partially correct / incorrect) plus a failure_cause column (hallucination, missing data, outdated knowledge, paywalled content, other). Optionally add an LLM-as-judge pre-fill that I can override. 4) Report which previously failing questions are fixed, which still fail, and any regressions on questions that previously passed. 5) Make the script re-runnable so I can re-ask the exact same questions after each change. Keep it simple and qualitative. Start with these seed questions: [SEED_QUESTIONS].

name: Lethal Trifecta Risk Check for Agents
definition: An agent has a 'lethal trifecta' whenever it has (1) access to private information, (2) exposure to malicious instructions, and (3) a mechanism to send data back to an attacker. The fix is to cut off at least one leg.
explanation: Willison introduced the term as a subset of prompt injection that is hard to misinterpret. His email assistant example shows how an attacker's email can instruct the agent to forward private data. Because filters can't block every phrasing, assume anyone who can talk to your agent can make it do anything it is allowed to do and limit the blast radius. The easiest leg to cut is usually exfiltration. He also mentions the CaMeL design (privileged agent plus quarantined agent, with taint tracking so human approval is only needed on high-risk actions).
when_to_use: Designing or reviewing any agent with access to email, files or other private data
Deciding which permissions or tools to restrict
when_not_to_use: Agents with no private data and no outbound channel
metric_or_method: Checklist audit of three legs (private data, malicious instruction exposure, exfiltration channel); mitigate by removing one leg and limiting blast radius.
common_pitfalls: Relying on prompt-based guardrails or filters to block attacks
Human-in-the-loop approvals requested too often lead to click-through
Assuming SQL-injection-style fixes work for prompt injection
source_excerpt: You have a lethal trifecta anytime your agent has three things. It's got access to private information. [...] It's exposed to malicious instructions. [...] And the third leg is exfiltration, or some mechanism the agent can send data back to that attacker, like forwarding an email. [...] The only way to fix it is to cut off one of those three legs.
one_liner: Private data + untrusted input + an exfiltration path = breach. Audit your agent and cut one leg.
codex_prompt_template: You are a security reviewer applying Simon Willison's 'lethal trifecta' to an AI agent. Agent description: [AGENT_DESCRIPTION]. Tools and permissions: [TOOL_LIST_WITH_PERMISSIONS]. Data sources it can read: [DATA_SOURCES]. Untrusted inputs it ingests (emails, web pages, tickets, uploaded files, etc.): [UNTRUSTED_INPUT_SOURCES]. Do the following. 1) Build a table that classifies every tool and data source into one or more of three legs: (a) access to private data, (b) exposure to untrusted or malicious instructions, (c) an exfiltration channel (sending email, HTTP requests, rendering markdown images or links, writing to shared or public locations, etc.). 2) Flag every agent, or sub-workflow, where all three legs are present at the same time, and explain a concrete attack path for each one, with an example malicious payload. 3) For each flagged case, propose the cheapest mitigation that removes at least one leg, with exfiltration removal as the default (allowlist domains, disable outbound links and images, drop send permissions, require human approval for high-risk actions). Also consider a CaMeL-style split between a privileged agent and a quarantined agent with taint tracking. 4) Write a pytest-style red-team test suite in [LANGUAGE_OR_FRAMEWORK] that plants injected instructions in [UNTRUSTED_INPUT_SOURCES] and asserts that no private data from [DATA_SOURCES] reaches any outbound channel. Output the table, the attack paths, the mitigations ranked by effort vs risk reduction, and the test code.

name: LLM-as-a-Judge
definition: LLM-as-a-Judge uses an LLM with an eval prompt and explicit criteria to grade the output of an AI system. The recommended practice is a binary pass/fail decision for one specific failure mode, grounded in your quality bar and validated against a human-labeled dataset. A Likert scale (for example 1-5) is the weaker alternative.
explanation: Method: the judge is a natural-language prompt, so PMs can write it directly. You send the eval prompt plus the output or trace (as a variable) to a judge LLM and get one label per row. The recommended form is one judge per specific, subjective failure mode found in error analysis, returning a binary pass/fail (true/false). Likert scales are weaker. The gap between a 3 and a 4 is subjective, nobody knows what 3.2 vs 3.7 means, LLMs handle numbered scales poorly, and alignment is harder to check. Binary verdicts force a clear quality bar and match yes/no product decisions. One member describes the generic form: rate outputs 1-5 against named criteria with a short explanation per score. It is useful when human feedback is too slow or expensive, but those judgments may not align with humans. Sub-steps and variants: (1) Ground truth. A domain expert labels each interaction pass/fail with a detailed critique, and the critiques are the key ingredient for a high-fidelity judge. (2) Prompt structure. The four-part formula is role, context, goal (what success and failure look like), and defined terminology/labels. For example, the leasing-assistant handoff judge lists seven failure conditions plus notes on what is not a failure. You can bootstrap the prompt with an LLM, but read and edit it. (3) Few-shot examples. Add one or two good and bad examples to cover edge cases and ground the judge. (4) Pointwise over pairwise. Judge a single answer pass/fail against a policy rather than choosing between two. Pairwise judges are biased toward the first option, the nicest, their own family's text, or the longest answer. One cited study found pairwise 39% more vulnerable to attack vectors. Lowercase the verdict so output compares cleanly. (5) Grounding. Put the relevant policy into the judge prompt, hardcoded or retrieved via RAG from the same living source the production agent uses. Disagreements are usually knowledge gaps. Add explicit rules for sycophancy-prone cases such as loyal-customer pleas. (6) Business tie-in. Lyft found generic prebuilt metrics (helpfulness, naturalness, toxicity and so on) not actionable, so use them only as baselines. Build pass/fail rubrics with domain experts, such as the education rubric, so each failure points to a fix. (7) Rubric-based auto-evaluation. In non-verifiable domains such as educational design or reading an MRI, expert-authored rubrics let a model score responses automatically. (8) Few-shot calibration scales. For decision-specific custom scales, give each level a definition, a real example and a 'why this is a N' rationale so the model does not invent its own interpretation. (9) Domain uses. Faire uses GPT to grade search relevance for reporting and for offline model evaluation before launch, which is cheaper than human labels. In agent loops, a judge can critique drafts before they are returned, but earlier models inflated scores across turns, so check for sycophantic drift. (10) Validation. Split labeled data into train/dev/test, refine the prompt on dev, and report TPR/TNR on a held-out test set. Trust comes from measuring the judge against human labels. Judgments are probabilistic, so you need enough volume. Production systems may add confidence scores or panels of judges. Expect roughly four to seven judges, since many failures are fixable in the agent prompt.
when_to_use: A failure mode is subjective, found in error analysis, and cannot be checked by a code assertion
You need to scale nuanced evaluation (tone, relevance, coherence, writing quality) beyond what humans can review
The failure persists after describing ideal behavior in the agent prompt
Correctness depends on policies that change over time, so the judge needs a shared living policy
Domains lack a guaranteed right answer and domain experts can write a rubric
You need automated relevance grading for search or ranking models before launch
Generic or noisy judge scores are being ignored and need tying to business outcomes
You want an agent to self-critique drafts before returning them, using a judge shown to score honestly
when_not_to_use: A simple code-based check (string present, code runs) can detect the failure
The failure can be fixed with a prompt edit and does not warrant an eval
You have no labeled examples to validate the judge against
Inline guardrails with tight latency budgets, unless the budget allows
You need a relative ranking, where pairwise is a technique but not reliable
Verifiable domains with a single objectively checkable answer
As a generic helpfulness or conciseness score replacing error analysis, or with generic prebuilt metrics as core metrics
You need judgments guaranteed to match human judgment, since AI judgments may not align perfectly
metric_or_method: Write one judge prompt per failure mode (role, context, goal, defined labels, optional few-shot examples, policy if needed) that returns only pass/fail. Run it over traces, then validate on a held-out test set with TPR/TNR against human pass/fail labels.
common_pitfalls: Using Likert scales (1-5, 1-7) and reporting averages like 4.2, which are tedious to align, hard to interpret, and handled poorly by LLMs
Shipping the judge prompt without validating it against human labels, or using the whole dataset to build and test it (overfitting)
Treating it as a clever-prompt exercise, or blindly accepting an LLM-written judge prompt without reading and editing it
Asking one judge to evaluate many failure modes at once, or making the eval too complex too quickly, which creates noisy signals
Vague goals, undefined terms, or overly strict definitions, plus no few-shot examples for edge cases
Pairwise judging with position, niceness, self-family and length biases, or unnormalized output (mixed casing, extra text)
Judge and production agent using different policy versions, or no explicit rules for sycophancy-prone cases
Sycophantic score drift, or using a weak fast model for the judge without checking it, and over-engineering scaffolding to compensate
source_excerpt: This technique utilizes an external LLM system (i.e. a “judge” LLM), with a prompt like the one above, to grade the output of the agent system. LLM-based evals allow you to generate classification labels in an automated way that resembles human-labeled data—without needing to have users or subject-matter experts label all of your data.
one_liner: Write one binary pass/fail judge prompt per failure mode, then check it against human labels with TPR/TNR.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build an LLM-as-a-Judge eval in Python for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION].

Failure mode to judge: [FAILURE_MODE]
Quality bar / policy (hardcode or load from this source): [POLICY_OR_RUBRIC]
Trace/data format: [TRACE_FORMAT]
Human-labeled dataset (path, with pass/fail labels and critiques): [LABELED_DATASET_PATH]
Judge model: [JUDGE_MODEL]

Do the following:
1. Write a judge prompt template with four parts: role, context, goal (what pass and what fail look like for this one failure mode, including what is NOT a failure), and defined terminology/labels. Add 1-2 few-shot examples (one pass, one fail) drawn from the labeled dataset for edge cases. Include the policy text. The judge must be pointwise (grade a single output) and return only lowercase 'pass' or 'fail' with a brief reason before the verdict, in structured JSON.
2. Implement run_judge(trace) that fills the template, calls the judge model, and parses the verdict robustly (handle malformed output).
3. Split the labeled dataset into train/dev/test (e.g. [SPLIT_RATIOS], default 20/40/40). Use only train for few-shot examples, iterate on dev, and keep test held out.
4. Compute confusion matrix, TPR and TNR vs human labels on dev and on the held-out test set. Print the disagreements with the human critique next to the judge reason so I can refine the prompt.
5. Add a function to run the finished judge over [UNLABELED_TRACES_PATH] and output the pass rate with a confidence interval, flagging that the rate should be corrected for judge TPR/TNR.

Keep the code modular and avoid Likert scales. Output the judge prompt as a separate file I can edit.

sources.excerpt: Human feedback is expensive and slow, so it’s common practice among AI practitioners to use an AI model to evaluate and rate the quality of outputs, either from itself or from other sources. This method leverages the AI’s analytical capabilities to provide a more objective assessment of content quality. [...] However, it’s important to remember that the AI’s judgments are based on its training and may not always align perfectly with human assessments.

name: LLM-Assisted Feedback Mining and Stack-Ranking
definition: A feedback-loop process in which a model analyzes large volumes of qualitative feedback (opt-in user comments, feedback channels, incident reports), groups it into themes, and stack-ranks the most common problems or quality hotspots. The top issues are fixed, by people or by agents that draft fixes for human review, and then re-evaluated recursively.
explanation: The core method is to collect feedback and let a model surface and rank what is going wrong. In the opt-in variant, users who agreed to share more are asked about their experience, for example where the response missed the mark. Their comments form a large library that a model analyzes, including the qualitative feedback, and groups by theme. The issues are then stack-ranked by how common they are. In a backpack shopping example, the AI knew product details but never asked about the user's son and his height. When feedback was stack-ranked, this missing collaborative follow-up was a very common complaint. Fixing it made the product conversational and collaborative, and users voted that it was awesome. The speaker frames this diagnose-and-fix cycle as a loop like an epoch of model training, where each change gets closer to product-market fit. He also mentions following thumbs-up ratings as a signal. The automated-triage variant applies the same idea to team-facing channels. Feedback arrives from internal sources, email, Slack channels, socials and partners. Instead of someone manually reading these channels each morning, a scheduled routine reads them and summarizes themes. It then spawns agents that prepare polish-fix PRs for human review. The same approach is applied across incidents to generate themes and spot hotspots where quality gaps may exist, which used to be a manual process. The member notes that more autonomy might be given to such routines over time. Together the two variants contribute a ranking-and-repeat loop on the user side, and a scheduled, agent-driven triage with human review on the operations side.
when_to_use: When you have users willing to share feedback and want to find root causes of where the AI experience misses
When you want to prioritize which problems to fix by frequency
When iterating toward fit and want a repeatable diagnose-fix-re-measure loop
When feedback volume across channels is too high to stay on top of manually
When you want to find quality hotspots across incidents
When you can keep a human reviewing the proposed fixes
when_not_to_use: When you have no opted-in user base or feedback channel to draw from
When no human can review the proposed fixes or agent-generated PRs
metric_or_method: Collect feedback from opted-in users and from feedback and incident channels, use a model to group the qualitative comments by theme, stack-rank themes by how common each issue is, fix the top issues (optionally via scheduled routines that draft polish-fix PRs for human review), and repeat. Thumbs-up ratings are also tracked.
common_pitfalls: Fixing a feature without first identifying and ranking the root causes of user dissatisfaction
Missing what users need but do not know to ask for, such as the AI not asking clarifying questions like the child's height in a shopping query
Relying on creative solutions without quantifying the weight of the top barrier; the Instagram example used a large survey to quantify weights
Context-switching load grows as more async work is kicked off, so reserve focus time to review it

codex_prompt_template: Build a feedback mining and stack-ranking pipeline in [LANGUAGE, e.g. Python] for my [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Input: [FEEDBACK_SOURCE, e.g. a CSV/JSONL of opt-in user comments, support tickets, Slack exports, or incident reports] with fields [FIELDS, e.g. id, timestamp, comment, thumbs_rating, channel]. Steps: 1) Clean and deduplicate the comments, and strip PII. 2) Use an LLM ([MODEL_NAME]) to assign each comment to a theme. Start by discovering candidate themes from a sample of [SAMPLE_SIZE] comments, merge near-duplicates into a taxonomy of at most [MAX_THEMES] themes, then classify every comment into one theme, or 'other', with a one-sentence rationale and a short verbatim quote. 3) Stack-rank the themes by frequency and by share of negative-rated feedback, and show the trend per week. 4) Output a markdown report with the top [TOP_N] themes, counts, percentages, 3 representative examples each, and a suggested fix hypothesis. 5) For each top theme, draft a proposed fix (prompt change, missing follow-up question, or code change) as a ticket or PR description marked 'needs human review'. Do not auto-merge. 6) Add a re-evaluation step that reruns the same classification on feedback collected after the fix ships ([FIX_SHIP_DATE]) and reports whether the theme's share dropped. Also include a small hand-labeled check of [HUMAN_LABEL_COUNT] comments to measure theme-assignment agreement with the LLM. Make the pipeline runnable on a schedule (e.g. cron) and include unit tests.

name: Minimum Viable Quality Thresholds with Cost Envelope
definition: A launch-readiness framework that defines three explicit quality thresholds (acceptable bar, delight bar, do-not-ship bar) and a cost envelope for an AI feature. The thresholds are set relative to real-world conditions, the human baseline, the usage context and the launch phase. They are checked throughout development, and product design (UI, scaffolding, human handoff) is matched to the measured hit rate.
explanation:
Core method (Minimum Viable Quality): AI performance almost always drops outside the controlled dev environment, and you don't know by how much, so keep the bar high from the start. Define an acceptable bar, a delight bar judged through behavioral signals (fewer retries, fewer 'No, I meant...' corrections), and a do-not-ship bar (failure rates in critical flows that break trust). Add a cost envelope. In the speaker-identification example, 8-9 of 10 attempts working without retry feels magical, while 1 in 5 needing a retry erodes trust. Thresholds depend on strategic context and phase (closed beta vs. broad launch). Test delight with realistic scenarios such as the background chaos test, the 6 p.m. kitchen test and the mid-command correction test.

Cost envelope sub-step: Estimate a ballpark of cost per call x usage frequency per user, and compute the average and heavy-user cases. Test mitigations (caching, smaller models, distillation) and check that the math holds at 10x usage. In the meeting-notes example, about $0.02 per transcript gives about $0.40/month at 20 meetings, about $2.00 at 100 meetings, and about $0.25-$0.30 with mitigations. $0.30/user/month that drives retention is a no-brainer; $5/user/month with unclear impact is a business problem.

Setting the bars from context: Hit rate thresholds vary by context. Background or lean-back recommendations need at least 9 of 10 hits (five duds make users think the playlist is broken). Discovery can accept about 1 of 10 if users expect it, can scan quickly, and a miss costs only a swipe. Compare AI accuracy to the human baseline. Net value is high when the baseline is low (10-20%) and AI reaches 50-80%, with the remainder routed to humans. Closing the last 2% of a ~98% accurate process is not yet a good fit.

Designing to the measured rate: Match the product to the measured task-level success rate. A product for a model that is right 60% of the time differs from one for 95% or 99.5%. Add scaffolding or human review for intolerable errors. Fault-tolerant UI means a one-in-five hit rate calls for at least five candidates shown at once, plus an easy escape hatch. Early Midjourney showed four fast images, implying about a one-in-four hit rate.

Reality gap: POCs often get 60-70% of the way, but each further 'nine' of reliability needs roughly an order of magnitude more effort. Reaching an accuracy everyone is comfortable with, plus legal, policy and regulatory approval and change management, takes 6-12 months. Plan the bars and timeline accordingly.
when_to_use: Before launching an AI feature, to define what is good enough, magical and unshippable
Early in development, alongside quality bars, when a demo looks magical but financial viability is unchecked
When lab accuracy may not reflect real-world conditions
When deciding product shape, UX, number of candidates shown, escape hatches and guardrails for a probabilistic feature
When deciding whether a recommendation belongs in a background experience or an active discovery experience
When choosing which processes to automate and designing human-in-the-loop handoff for the remainder
When setting timelines and investment for moving a pilot to an automated, important process
when_not_to_use: As a fixed universal number; thresholds depend on strategic context and launch phase
When you expect precise cost numbers; a ballpark is sufficient
Before you have any measurement of the model's real hit rate or accuracy
When the system is deterministic or near 100% accurate, so a single-answer UI is safe
Processes already around 98% accurate where AI is expected to deliver the final 2%
metric_or_method: Define acceptable, delight (behavioral signals such as fewer retries and corrections) and do-not-ship bars per context and launch phase, plus a cost envelope (cost per call x usage frequency, average vs. heavy user, mitigations, 10x check). Measure task-level hit rate with use-case-specific evals, compare to the human baseline, and map it to design choices (candidates shown, escape hatch, scaffolding, human review). Validate with realistic scenario tests.
common_pitfalls: Trusting high accuracy from controlled tests (e.g., over 90%) that collapses in real conditions
Applying the same bar for closed beta and broad launch, or one global hit-rate target across background and discovery contexts
Omitting the cost envelope, ignoring worst-case power users, or not checking whether the math survives 10x usage
Designing a single-result UI or product without knowing the model's actual per-use-case reliability
Assuming the last 30-40% after a 60-70% POC is trivial, or judging success from quick demos instead of months of sustained engineering
Skipping legal, policy and regulatory approval, change management, or a mechanism for humans to handle remaining decisions
Judging AI accuracy in isolation rather than against the human baseline
Treating measured accuracy as static when capability changes quickly as new models ship
source_excerpt: But basically what happens is the POCs get to 60 or 70% of the way there, and the human mind goes, oh, the rest is no big deal. But it's like uptime in data centers where every nine is an order of magnitude investment in terms of reliability, backups, et cetera.
one_liner: Set acceptable, delight and do-not-ship bars plus a cost envelope, then shape the UX to your measured hit rate.
codex_prompt_template: You are helping me build a launch-readiness check for an AI feature. Feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Launch phase: [LAUNCH_PHASE e.g. closed beta or broad launch]. Usage context: [USAGE_CONTEXT e.g. background/lean-back or active discovery]. Human baseline accuracy: [HUMAN_BASELINE]. Eval dataset: [EVAL_DATASET_PATH] with columns [INPUT_COL], [OUTPUT_COL], [LABEL_COL], and optional [RETRY_OR_CORRECTION_COL]. Cost inputs: cost per call [COST_PER_CALL], average calls per user per month [AVG_USAGE], heavy-user calls per month [HEAVY_USAGE], mitigation cost multiplier [MITIGATION_FACTOR]. Write a Python script that: 1) computes the task-level hit rate and the retry/correction rate overall and for the realistic-condition slices [STRESS_SLICES e.g. noisy audio, evening peak, mid-command correction]; 2) takes three thresholds from a config file, acceptable bar [ACCEPTABLE_BAR], delight bar [DELIGHT_BAR] (judged on retry/correction rate), and do-not-ship bar [DO_NOT_SHIP_BAR] (failure rate in critical flows [CRITICAL_FLOWS]), and reports PASS/WARN/BLOCK for each slice; 3) compares the hit rate to the human baseline and estimates how many cases would go to human review; 4) computes monthly cost per user for the average and heavy user, with and without mitigations, and at 10x usage, and flags any case above [MAX_COST_PER_USER_PER_MONTH]; 5) recommends design choices from the hit rate, such as the number of candidates to show (about 1/hit_rate), whether an escape hatch is needed, and whether human review is needed; 6) prints a launch-readiness summary table and exits non-zero if any do-not-ship or cost-envelope check fails. Include unit tests with a small synthetic dataset.

name: Multi-Method Model-Swap Evaluation
definition: A repeatable evaluation process for deciding whether a new model should replace the current one. It combines several methods: core-regression evals, A/B tests, captured-trace replay, hands-on hard-problem trials, user feedback signals and informal vibes. It also weighs price-performance (Pareto efficiency) per job function or workflow step.
explanation: The parent method is to avoid depending on any single signal when a new model is released or an RL change ships. Run several complementary methods and check the results against what each job needs and costs. Krieger's contribution is the repeatable process itself: classic A/B testing, internal evaluation, capturing traces and re-running them on the new model, vibes (the field is still early), and trying the model on a really hard problem you ask repeatedly so you can feel the improvement. The Codex team's variant shows how this works for a coding agent whose many integrations and workflows make a complete eval dataset impractical. They keep core-regression evals to protect key behavior, A/B test model or RL changes (for code review, whether it finds the right mistakes and how users react), and watch for signals such as users switching the product off after incorrect reviews. They also track social feedback, and each engineer runs a personal list of hard problems on every new model as a custom eval. Nobody should bet their life on one concrete eval set. The Pareto-efficiency member adds the cost dimension. For each job function, ask whether a model sits on the efficient frontier of performance per unit price, and whether the job's upside justifies frontier pricing. Unbounded or hard-to-calculate upside, such as drug discovery, or possibly customer support where a bug report may be the first breadcrumb to a major change, can justify frontier models. Bounded-upside work such as legal or finance may be better served by good-performance, good-price models, often open-weight and RL-tuned. Frontier models from six months ago may already clear the intelligence threshold for most economically useful problems. The Gamma member extends this to per-step selection in production. Break the workflow into steps (outline, first draft, editing, agent review of the deck, image generation) and continuously test candidate models per step. Gamma uses about 20 models, because different models suit different jobs and putting the most expensive model on everything does not work. Re-test as the leaderboard shifts and consider per-persona choices, such as educators versus consultants. This work is background experimentation and is not easily quantified.
when_to_use: When a new model or RL change is released and you must decide whether to swap it in
When your product is used in many customized ways and you can't enumerate every scenario in an eval set
When your product is a multi-step workflow where steps have different quality and cost needs
When choosing between frontier and cheaper or open-weight models for different job functions
When you need healthy unit economics and want to balance quality against inference cost
When the model landscape changes often and newer or cheaper models may beat incumbents
When you want to track over time how well the product serves its use cases
when_not_to_use: When a single narrow task is clearly served by one model
When you lack the experimentation infrastructure to test models in production
When a job has unbounded or hard-to-calculate upside, where paying for the highest intelligence may be rational regardless of the price-performance curve
When you rely only on vibes or only on a fixed eval set
metric_or_method: Per job function or workflow step, run core-regression evals, A/B tests, captured-trace replay on the candidate model, hard-problem trials and user-reaction signals. Then select the model on or near the price-performance efficient frontier, paying a premium only where upside is large or hard to bound. Re-test as new models appear.
common_pitfalls: Having no repeatable process, so new models are judged ad hoc
Depending on vibes alone, though they remain a part of the process at this early stage
Believing a concrete eval set removes the need for A/B tests, user reaction signals or other feedback
Trying to pre-build evals for every customer scenario
Throwing the most expensive model at every job or assuming one model or architecture fits all functions and personas
Treating verifiability alone as the deciding factor when upside is the real driver
Having no really hard problem to ask repeatedly, so you cannot feel improvement
Being slow to re-test as the leaderboard changes, or wrapping one provider as the whole solution
source_excerpt: repeatable way to evaluate how well your product is serving those use cases and how well if you drop a new model in, is it doing it better or worse? Some of it can be classic A/B testing, that's fine. Some of it may be internal evaluation, some of it may be capturing traces and being able to rerun them on with a new model. Some of it's vibes like we're still pretty early in this process and some of it is actually trying it
one_liner: Mix regression evals, A/B tests, trace replay and vibes, then pick the model on the price-performance frontier.
codex_prompt_template: I'm deciding whether to swap [CURRENT_MODEL] for [CANDIDATE_MODEL] in my product: [PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION]. The workflow steps or job functions are: [WORKFLOW_STEPS]. Build a model-swap evaluation harness in [LANGUAGE] that does the following. 1) Core-regression eval: load [REGRESSION_DATASET_PATH] and run both models on it, scoring with [SCORING_METHOD], and flag any regressions against a threshold of [REGRESSION_THRESHOLD]. 2) Captured-trace replay: read production traces from [TRACE_SOURCE], re-run each input on the candidate model, and compare outputs with the originals using [COMPARISON_METHOD, e.g. LLM judge or exact match]. 3) Hard-problem trials: run my list of [HARD_PROBLEMS] N=[NUM_REPEATS] times on each model and report the pass rate and the variance. 4) A/B test plan: propose a rollout design with a traffic split of [TRAFFIC_SPLIT], the user-reaction signals to log ([USER_SIGNALS], such as thumbs down or feature switch-off), and guardrail metrics. 5) Price-performance: for each workflow step, compute quality score, cost per call from [PRICING_TABLE], and latency, then identify which models sit on the Pareto frontier and recommend the cheapest model that clears [QUALITY_BAR] per step. Output a per-step table with a swap, keep or re-test recommendation, and a short rationale. Make the harness re-runnable so I can re-test whenever a new model ships.
