name: Multi-turn conversation evaluation with single-turn reproduction
definition: Start with a session-level pass/fail on whether the conversation achieved the user's goal, and when it fails, try to reproduce the failure in a single turn to separate knowledge or retrieval problems from conversational memory problems.
explanation: The session-level judgment is the most important measure of success. A common mistake is to assume failures come from the complexities of dialogue. For example, if a shopping bot gives the wrong return policy on the fourth turn, ask it directly. If it still fails, the problem is likely a simple knowledge or retrieval issue. If it succeeds, the failure is conversational, such as losing context.
when_to_use: Evaluating conversational products
Diagnosing the root cause of failed multi-turn sessions
when_not_to_use: Single-turn products such as one-shot classification or summarization, where there is no session to judge and no conversational context to separate out.
Failures that only exist because of earlier turns, such as a user correcting a prior answer or a task built up step by step. A standalone query removes that context and cannot reproduce the failure.
Judging individual turn quality, tone, or safety on its own. A session-level pass/fail on goal completion hides these issues, so use turn-level metrics instead.
Sessions with no clear user goal, such as open-ended chit-chat, where a session pass/fail has nothing to measure against.
metric_or_method: Session-level pass/fail, then single-turn reproduction of the failing query to diagnose the root cause.
common_pitfalls: Assuming the failure is due to dialogue complexity without checking single-turn reproduction
source_excerpt: When evaluating conversations, start at the highest level: Did the entire session achieve the user’s goal? This session-level pass/fail judgment is the most important measure of success.
one_liner: Judge the whole session first, then replay failures as single turns to tell memory bugs from knowledge gaps.
codex_prompt_template:
I am evaluating a multi-turn conversational feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. I have conversation logs in [LOG_FORMAT_OR_PATH], where each session has a list of turns and a user goal. Write a Python eval harness that does the following:
1. Session-level judge: for each session, use an LLM judge with the rubric [SESSION_SUCCESS_CRITERIA] to output pass/fail on whether the user's goal was achieved, plus a one-sentence rationale.
2. For each failed session, identify the failing turn (the first turn where the response was wrong or unhelpful) and extract the user's query from that turn.
3. Single-turn reproduction: send that query alone, with no prior conversation history, to [MODEL_OR_ENDPOINT] using the same system prompt and retrieval setup. Judge the response against [EXPECTED_ANSWER_OR_GROUND_TRUTH].
4. Classify each failure: if the single-turn run also fails, label it 'knowledge_or_retrieval'. If the single-turn run passes, label it 'conversational' (context loss, memory, or instruction drift).
5. Output a CSV with session_id, failing_turn_index, session_verdict, single_turn_verdict, root_cause_label, and a summary table with the percentage of failures in each root-cause bucket.
Include type hints, a small [SAMPLE_SIZE]-session dry run, and unit tests for the classification logic.
source_title: Building eval systems that improve your AI product

name: Off-the-shelf metrics as exploration tools
definition: Calculating off-the-shelf metric scores on traces and sorting by high/low score to review the extremes, which can reveal surprising failure modes or successes and inspire custom evaluators.
explanation: Off-the-shelf metrics are not worth paying attention to directly, because they often don't correlate with real user problems. Reviewing the highest- and lowest-scoring examples is one of the only appropriate uses. It is an advanced technique to try only after mastering the basic error-analysis approach.
when_to_use: After mastering basic error analysis
To find unexpected failure modes or successes to build custom evaluators from
when_not_to_use: As a headline dashboard score
As your starting point instead of error analysis
metric_or_method: Compute generic scores (e.g., hallucination, toxicity) on traces, sort, and manually review the top and bottom examples.
common_pitfalls: Reporting a hallucination or toxicity score on a dashboard
Using this before mastering the basic approach
source_excerpt: Instead of reporting a hallucination or toxicity score on a dashboard, calculate the scores on your traces and sort them by high/low score. Reviewing the highest *and* lowest scoring examples can reveal surprising failure modes or unexpected successes, which in turn helps you build custom evaluators for the patterns you discover.
one_liner: Sort traces by off-the-shelf scores, read the highest and lowest, and mine surprises for custom evaluators.
codex_prompt_template: I have an LLM feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Traces are stored at [TRACES_PATH] in [TRACE_FORMAT] format, with fields for input, output, and any retrieved context. Write a Python script that: (1) loads the traces; (2) computes the off-the-shelf metric [METRIC_NAME] (e.g., hallucination, toxicity, relevance) on each trace using [LIBRARY_OR_LLM_JUDGE]; (3) sorts traces by score and exports the top [N_EXTREMES] and bottom [N_EXTREMES] to a CSV or HTML review sheet with columns: trace_id, score, input, output, reviewer_notes, surprising (y/n), candidate_failure_mode; (4) prints summary stats for the score distribution. Do NOT report the score as a dashboard KPI or set pass/fail thresholds. The score is only used to choose which traces to review by hand. After I fill in the review notes, write a second step that groups the notes by candidate_failure_mode and suggests 2-3 custom binary evaluators (with a clear pass/fail definition for each) for the most frequent or most surprising patterns.

name: Online Outcome and Causal Evaluation of Ranking Models
definition: A method for evaluating ranking, recommendation, matching and other decision-driving models by running experiments that measure business outcomes and the incremental (causal) effect of acting on the model's output, instead of how well the model predicts historical choices or outcomes.
explanation: Core method: a model used to make decisions should be judged by the decisions it leads to. Prediction is inherently about correlation in past data, while decisions require causation. Prediction accuracy should not be the final yardstick for a model that drives actions. Variant 1, online outcome comparison for rankers (from the oDesk example): the real decision is which of two ranking algorithms to deploy. A model that ranks applicants by likelihood of being hired only picks up patterns in past data. Instead, run an online experiment comparing algorithms A and B on bookings, revenue and downstream match-quality signals such as ratings given to the freelancer and whether the freelancer is hired again. Algorithms are compared on making good matches in the future, not recreating the past, and experiments are needed to know the difference. Variant 2, causal decision evaluation (from the LTV example): sending promotions to the highest predicted-LTV customers looks safe, but the real question is how much more a customer spends because they received the promotion. That is a differential, not an absolute. Measure the change in outcome caused by the action using causal inference and experiments. Together, the two members say: identify the decision the model supports, then measure the downstream outcome or incremental effect of that decision, rather than stopping at the prediction task. The shift is from machine learning to causal inference.
when_to_use: Comparing two search, recommendation or ranking algorithms in a marketplace
Evaluating matching or triage models whose predictions are used to make decisions
When business outcomes such as bookings, revenue, ratings or rehire rate can be observed downstream
When a model's output (LTV, hire likelihood, propensity) decides who receives an intervention
When teams are tempted to treat high predicted scores as proof of value
when_not_to_use: When the only goal is pure prediction and no decision depends on the model
When the model's output is the end product and no intervention or decision follows from it
When downstream outcome data or experiment capacity is unavailable (offline prediction metrics become a weaker fallback)
metric_or_method: Run an online experiment comparing algorithms (A vs B) or treated vs untreated groups. Measure core business metrics (bookings, revenue), downstream match-quality signals (ratings given, repeat hiring), and the differential in outcome (e.g., change in spend or LTV) caused by acting on the model's output, rather than offline accuracy or absolute predicted value.
common_pitfalls: Evaluating rankers only by how well they recreate past choices, which just picks up patterns in past data
Assuming good prediction automatically means good decisions
Stopping at the prediction task and not asking what decision the model will be used for
Confusing high predicted value with high incremental value from the action
Treating correlation found by a predictive model as if it were causation
Rewarding sensible-sounding actions (e.g., promoting top-LTV customers) because nobody will criticize them, without testing their incremental effect
Relying on offline accuracy as the final yardstick when the model drives actions
source_excerpt: And when I think about the distinction between two different ranking algorithms, I don't want to be only comparing them in terms of how well they recreate the choices people made in the past. The way I'm really going to evaluate those is in my market, does one of those lead to better matches or more matches than the other one, right? [...] And it's so important to put it that way starkly, because that's so different a question than, does Lenny's ranking algorithm do a better job of predicting over the last two years what bookings people made than Ramesh's ranking algorithm?
one_liner: Judge rankers by A/B-tested outcomes and causal lift, not by how well they predict past choices.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me evaluate a decision-driving model using online and causal methods instead of offline prediction accuracy.

Context:
- Model/feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]
- Decision the model's output drives: [DECISION_SUPPORTED] (e.g., which ranking to show, who gets a promotion)
- Variants to compare: [VARIANT_A] vs [VARIANT_B] (or treated vs holdout)
- Primary business metrics: [PRIMARY_METRICS] (e.g., bookings, revenue)
- Downstream quality signals: [QUALITY_SIGNALS] (e.g., ratings, repeat hire rate)
- Available data: [DATA_SCHEMA] with roughly [SAMPLE_SIZE] units

Write Python (pandas, scipy/statsmodels) that:
1. Designs the experiment: randomization unit, assignment code with a stable hash, a holdout group for causal lift, and a power/sample-size calculation for a minimum detectable effect of [MDE].
2. Runs sanity checks: sample ratio mismatch and covariate balance between arms.
3. Computes per-arm outcomes for the primary metrics and quality signals, reporting the difference, confidence intervals, and p-values (use bootstrap or a t-test, and note multiple-comparison corrections).
4. For the causal case, estimates incremental lift (treated minus control outcome, e.g., extra spend caused by the action) rather than absolute predicted value. Include a uplift-by-predicted-score-decile table to show whether high-score users actually respond more.
5. Contrasts the experimental result with the offline prediction metric (AUC, NDCG, or accuracy on historical choices) to show where the two disagree.
6. Outputs a short ship/no-ship summary with caveats such as novelty effects, interference between units, and time horizon of downstream outcomes.

Return runnable code with clear comments and a small synthetic-data example so I can test it.

name: Outcome Metrics over Engagement Proxies
definition: A method for evaluating and optimizing AI features by writing down the real objective the feature should serve, then choosing metrics that measure that outcome (time saved, issues fixed, high-value downstream engagement) instead of easily measured proxies such as clicks, likes, sessions, or conversation length.
explanation: The core method: state the algorithm's objective explicitly, ideally as a written formula (Cohen's checklist), then choose metrics that track the outcome you actually want rather than what is easy to count. Rich Objective Functions (Chen) contributes the principle: define the dream objective, such as whether AI makes a user's life richer, and train and measure toward it, because optimizing clicks and likes yields sycophancy and time-sucking behavior (e.g., an email assistant that endlessly offers improvements versus one that says to send it). Write Down the Algorithm Objective (Cohen) contributes a PM review checklist: the objective as a mathematical formula, the features or parameters the algorithm learns on (not user-facing features), investment in data collection and fine-tuning, and infrastructure as a lever; AI should not be delegated to engineering as a black box. Feature-Specific Outcome Metrics (Shani) contributes per-feature tailoring: productivity is not the right metric everywhere; for AI in security the goal is more secure code, measured by secrets prevented from leaking and issues detected, found, and fixed before shipping. Outcome-Based Metrics for AI Assistants (Krieger) applies this to conversational AI: a good conversation may be two messages or 200, so track task-completion value such as time saved (e.g., a prototype in 25 minutes instead of about six hours, possibly via survey) and qualitative signals that users feel their creativity is unlocked, plus usage cadence, instead of raw time spent or likability; he admits there is no pithy dashboard metric yet, and thumbs up/down data misses small meaningful moments. Downstream Engagement Metrics for Feeds (LinkedIn) applies it to ranking: because the feed is the landing surface, sessions and click-through include bystanders and bypassers, so targets were set on active, engaged, and high-value engagement and downstream conversations, tracked for both creation and consumption sides of the marketplace. A side effect was that spammers noticed the new objective, so removing bad activity became necessary work.
when_to_use: Defining the north-star behavior or objective of an AI product
When engagement metrics could reward sycophancy, rabbit holes, or artificial conversation length
When AI is embedded in several product areas with different goals, such as security or code quality
Evaluating an AI ranking or feed where the landing surface inflates raw sessions or click counts
Marketplace products where creator and consumer sides both need to stay healthy
Reviewing any product with a ranking, matching, or other learned algorithm at its core
Running AI strategy reviews with PM teams that tend to delegate AI to engineering as a black box
when_not_to_use: As a sole approach for assistants: outcome metrics are harder to quantify and a dashboard version is not yet worked out
For a general-purpose assistant where overall productivity is the main intended benefit, a feature-specific metric may be unnecessary
As a replacement for abuse and quality monitoring; a new objective can attract spammers who must be handled
Products with no algorithm or learned component at their core
metric_or_method: Write the objective down (ideally as a formula), then define feature-specific outcome metrics tied to it, such as time saved via survey, issues fixed before shipping, or active, high-value downstream engagement, instead of raw sessions, clicks, or time spent. Also review the features the algorithm learns on, data collection, and fine-tuning.
common_pitfalls: Optimizing easy proxies like clicks, likes, sessions, or click-through, which let any shift move the number and count bystanders
Over-optimizing on likability or conversation length, leading to sycophancy
Applying one generic productivity metric to every AI feature, or measuring only speed rather than the intended outcome
Relying on thumbs up/down aggregates that miss meaningful small moments
Time-saved surveys can be annoying and hard to quantify, and metrics-obsession can come from trying to convince yourself the product works
Not planning for spammers and bad actors who respond to a new objective
Treating AI as a black box, assuming fine-tuning is only an engineering task, or confusing user-facing features with parameters the algorithm learns on
Ignoring infrastructure as a lever on product outcomes
source_excerpt: I can't just count how many folks engage with the feed because then I'm counting bypassers kind of thing and bystanders that are actually coming into the experience. So we actually started to look at the more, we go a lot into active, engaged and high value engagement. So we go downstream, we kind of put the onus on looking at more downstream engagement there and we build that as the feed engagement.
one_liner: Write the objective as a formula, then measure outcomes like time saved or issues fixed, not clicks or session length.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me replace engagement proxy metrics with outcome metrics for an AI feature.

Feature description: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]
Current metrics (proxies): [CURRENT_PROXY_METRICS]
Real user/business objective: [TRUE_OBJECTIVE]
Available data sources (logs, surveys, downstream events): [DATA_SOURCES]

Do the following:
1. Write the feature's objective as an explicit formula or scoring function (inputs, weights, constraints) and list the assumptions behind it.
2. List the features/signals the algorithm learns on, the data collection and fine-tuning needs, and the infrastructure levers, as a PM review checklist.
3. Identify how each current proxy metric could be gamed or mislead (e.g., sycophancy, rabbit holes, conversation length inflation, bystander/bypasser clicks).
4. Propose 3-5 outcome metrics tied to the objective (e.g., time saved via survey, issues fixed before shipping, active high-value downstream engagement) with exact definitions, numerators/denominators, and the event or survey needed to compute each.
5. Write Python (pandas) code that computes these outcome metrics from an event log with schema [EVENT_LOG_SCHEMA], and compares them against the proxy metrics per user cohort or experiment arm.
6. Add a check that flags divergence, where proxies go up while outcome metrics go flat or down, and output a short report.
7. If the product is a marketplace, split metrics by [SUPPLY_SIDE] and [DEMAND_SIDE] and add a guardrail metric for spam or low-quality activity.

name: Paired safety and progress metrics (stops and strands)
definition: An evaluation framework that tracks AI system behavior along opposing axes: safety/compliance on one side and the ability to make adequate progress on the other, measured through metrics like undue slowdowns, reliance on rescue help, and slowing down other road users, each benchmarked against priors.
explanation: Waymo splits metrics into commercial/operational metrics and system (driver) behavior metrics. Driver performance metrics span safety, compliance with road rules, and the ability to make adequate progress without being unduly stopped or stranded in dense traffic. The speaker explains the progress metrics push in the opposite direction from safety, since a vehicle can be very safe by not moving at all. Progress is measured by how much the vehicle slowed down unduly, how many instances per week required rescue help, and how much it slowed traffic for others, using extensive benchmarking and priors to define adequate performance.
when_to_use: Evaluating autonomous or agentic systems where overly cautious behavior is a failure mode
When a single safety metric could be gamed by inaction
when_not_to_use: Systems where there is no tension between caution and task progress
metric_or_method: Track safety and road-rule compliance alongside progress metrics (undue slowdowns, weekly count of rescue-help instances, slowdown imposed on other traffic), and compare each against benchmarks/priors for adequate performance.
common_pitfalls: Measuring safety only, which rewards a vehicle that does not move
Failing to benchmark progress metrics against priors, leaving 'adequate performance' undefined
source_excerpt: So that's on the safety side and then I would say on the stops and strands, which is trying to, which goes in the different direction. Hey, you can be very safe if you're not moving at all. That's not what we're building. We need to make sure that the riders get to their destination on time. So it has to be appropriately assertive and be making the right progress.
one_liner: Pair safety metrics with progress metrics so your AI can't look safe by just standing still.
codex_prompt_template: Build an eval harness that scores [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] on paired opposing metrics: safety/compliance and progress. Input: a dataset of [TRACE_OR_EPISODE_LOGS] in [FORMAT]. Safety metrics: [SAFETY_METRICS, e.g. policy violations, rule-compliance rate]. Progress metrics: (1) undue slowdown or excess time vs a baseline, (2) weekly count of interventions or rescue-help requests, (3) delay imposed on other users or systems. Steps: 1) Write Python that computes each metric per episode and aggregates weekly. 2) Compare each metric to benchmark priors from [BASELINE_SOURCE, e.g. human performance or a prior release] and flag regressions beyond [THRESHOLD]. 3) Add a gating check that fails a release if safety improves only because progress dropped, or vice versa (a Pareto-style check). 4) Output a summary table and a scatter plot of safety vs progress by release. Include unit tests with synthetic episodes where the system does nothing, which should pass safety but fail progress.
source_title: Product lessons from Waymo | Shweta Shrivastava (Waymo, Amazon, Cisco)

name: Per-Step Pipeline Evaluation
definition: Break a multi-step AI workflow into its component steps (query generation, search, aggregation, summary) and define evaluations for each step so you get coverage, confidence and insight into where the application underperforms.
explanation: Chip uses a deep research application as the example: no single metric can judge the final report. Instead, trace how the result is produced (gather information via search queries, retrieve results, aggregate, notice gaps, search again, summarize) and evaluate each step. For search queries, check whether they are diverse rather than near-duplicates. For results, check overlap across queries, breadth, depth and relevance to the original prompt. The goal is not a number of evals but enough evals for good coverage and high confidence, and to know where the app is not performing well so it can be fixed.
when_to_use: Multi-step applications such as deep research or agentic workflows where a single end-to-end metric is not informative
When you need to localize where in the pipeline performance is poor so you can fix it
when_not_to_use: Low-stakes, non-core features where a vibe check is good enough for now
metric_or_method: Define separate evals per pipeline step (query diversity, result overlap, breadth, depth, relevance to the original prompt) rather than only an end-to-end score.
common_pitfalls: Relying on a single end-to-end metric for a complex output like a research report
Generating near-duplicate search queries that add no diversity
Counting eval number instead of asking whether coverage and confidence are sufficient
Expert-written benchmark prompts reviewed by hand are extremely costly and slow
source_excerpt: So every step of the way, you need evaluations. You don't [inaudible 00:30:21] end-to-end. Maybe it was a search query in my first thing about, okay, now I write five search queries. I might look into how good are the search queries? Do they as they similar to each other because you need five search queries are very similar? [...] So I don't think it's how many eval should I get, but how many eval do I need to get a good coverage, a high confidence in my application's performance and also to help me understand where it is not performing well so that I can fix it.
one_liner: Trace each pipeline step and write evals per step to pinpoint where your multi-step AI app breaks.
codex_prompt_template:
I have a multi-step AI workflow: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. The pipeline steps are: [PIPELINE_STEPS] (e.g., query generation, search, aggregation, gap detection, summary). Here is an example trace of one run: [TRACE].

Write Python eval code that evaluates each step separately instead of only scoring the final output. For each step:
1. Define 2-4 specific eval criteria (e.g., for search queries: diversity/near-duplicate rate via embedding cosine similarity; for retrieved results: overlap across queries, breadth, depth, relevance to the original prompt; for the summary: faithfulness to retrieved sources and coverage of the original request).
2. Implement each as a function that takes the step's input/output from the trace and returns a score from 0-1 plus a short rationale (use an LLM judge where heuristics are not enough, with the judge prompt included).
3. Build a runner that executes all step evals over a dataset of [DATASET_SIZE] traces and outputs a per-step score table with failure counts.
4. Add a summary that identifies the lowest-performing step and lists the 5 worst example traces for it, so I can see where to fix the app.

Known failure modes to prioritize: [FAILURE_MODE].
source_title: Al Engineering 101 with Chip Huyen (Nvidia, Stanford, Netflix)

name: Production Monitoring with Continuous Evals
definition: After launch, log full traces and user interactions, then run validated evaluators (such as LLM judges) automatically and asynchronously on live traffic or a sample of it. Report scores or failure rates over time on dashboards, compare them with human-labeled ground truth and user outcomes, and use proxy signals to find traces worth reviewing. Failure patterns found feed new eval datasets.
explanation: Core method: set up logging up front (what the system sees, what it returns, how people interact with it, including control handoffs), deploy, then run evals designed earlier on live data and track results on a dashboard. Members contributed these pieces. (1) Continuous evals on live traffic: for example, run a friendliness eval on all requests and responses to see whether users are getting more frustrated or whether system changes matter. Compare eval results with human-labeled ground truth and user outcomes to improve the eval framework. Dashboards communicate AI metrics to stakeholders and can be tied to business outcomes as proxy leading metrics. (2) Asynchronous monitoring: log the whole trace (input, intermediate steps and tool calls, final output) and run judges asynchronously on a sample, since judges can be slow or expensive. Production is where unknown unknowns appear, so monitoring is a discovery engine. Use the judges' TPR and TNR to statistically correct raw outputs and estimate the true success rate. (3) Live data and proxy-signal sampling: if cost is a constraint, sample using the system's properties. Proxy signals include a human rerouting a query (a proxy for routing accuracy in customer support v1), conversation turns, thumbs up or down, and control handoff logs. If the data is small, around 2,000 to 3,000 logs, run evals on all of it. (4) Evals plus monitoring: neither alone is enough. Evals encode trusted knowledge about known failures. Monitoring signals point to traces worth examining in high-throughput products. Failure patterns that must not happen become new eval datasets, and monitoring continues after each redeploy because new problems can appear. (5) Online LLM judges: sample around 1,000 production traces daily or weekly, run the judge, and report the failure rate. One practitioner reports cron jobs running weekly after a one-time setup of about three to four days and roughly 30 minutes a week of maintenance, and that teams doing this well gain a sharp sense of their performance.
when_to_use: After launch, to track quality metrics and failure-mode prevalence over time
Once judges or evals are validated against human labels for key failure modes
High-volume products where you cannot read every trace and need signals to pick which to examine
Discovering new, unknown failure modes in production
Communicating AI quality metrics to stakeholders via dashboards
Post-deployment calibration when real user behavior diverges from the reference dataset
When full-dataset evaluation is too costly and a representative subset is needed
when_not_to_use: Before any validated eval or judge exists; validate against human labels first
Before launch when no live data exists; use the reference dataset instead
Blocking bad responses before users see them; use guardrails instead
As the only quality approach; do not rely on monitoring or evals alone
metric_or_method: Log full traces and interactions; sample live traffic (using proxy signals such as reroutes, thumbs up/down, turns, handoff logs, or the full set if about 2,000-3,000 logs); run validated judges asynchronously on a schedule; report failure or pass rates over time on a dashboard, corrected with TPR/TNR and compared to human-labeled ground truth and user outcomes; turn must-not-happen failure patterns into new eval datasets.
common_pitfalls: Running unvalidated judges on production traffic or forgetting to validate eval results against real user feedback
Trusting raw judge outputs without correcting for known TPR/TNR error rates
Running slow or expensive judges synchronously
Not designing logging and control handoffs up front, so no signal is available
Sampling data that is not representative of live user interactions
Treating evals as only a pre-release test, or believing evals or monitoring alone will catch everything
Assuming one eval fix means no other problems will appear after redeploying
Not feeding discovered failure patterns back into new eval datasets
source_excerpt: Set up evals to run automatically on live user interactions. [...] Look for discrepancies between eval results and real-world performance (i.e. human-labeled ground truth). Use these insights to enhance your eval framework and improve accuracy over time.
one_liner: Log full traces, run validated LLM judges on live samples, and turn production failures into new evals.
codex_prompt_template: You are helping me set up continuous production monitoring with evals for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Traces are stored in [TRACE_STORE] with this schema: [TRACE_SCHEMA] (input, intermediate steps/tool calls, final output, user feedback signals such as [PROXY_SIGNALS]). Write [LANGUAGE] code that: (1) samples traces on a schedule, using all traces if the volume is under 3,000 and otherwise about [SAMPLE_SIZE] per [CADENCE], with oversampling of traces that have proxy signals like reroutes, thumbs down, many turns, or control handoffs; (2) runs an asynchronous LLM judge for [FAILURE_MODE] on each sampled trace, returning pass/fail plus a short rationale; (3) corrects the raw failure rate using the judge's TPR [JUDGE_TPR] and TNR [JUDGE_TNR] (Rogan-Gladen style correction) and reports a confidence interval; (4) writes daily or weekly scores to a table that a dashboard can chart; (5) compares judge verdicts with a human-labeled set at [HUMAN_LABELS_PATH] and flags drift in agreement; (6) exports flagged failing traces to a review queue and to a new eval dataset file. Include a cron or scheduler config, basic cost controls, and unit tests with mock traces.

name: Progressive Autonomy Ladder with Human Review Logging
definition: A staged rollout in which an AI system begins with low-risk, easily overridden actions (DMs, drafts, recommendations, routing) backed by hard permissions and human review. Human behavior such as edits, overrides and omitted draft text is logged at each version. Agency is raised one version at a time only when review and calibration show the system has earned trust, and guideline-based checks can gradually replace human review.
explanation:
The core method defines versions by how much agency the system has and how much control you give up, rather than by features (Agency-Control Versioning Ladder). A customer support ladder runs route, then suggest/draft, then auto-resolve with human fallback; marketing and coding assistants follow the same pattern (completions, blocks, PRs). Each step is chosen to be small, testable and observable.

Low-Downside Human Review Gating supplies the first rung. Instead of predicting hallucination rates, cap the downside: DM instead of posting to a channel, draft instead of sending an email, recommendation instead of a decision, appended suggestions instead of edits. Hard platform permissions back this up, so the agent physically cannot take the riskier action.

Progressive Autonomy with Human-Behavior Logging adds the feedback loop. At each stage, log human edits, overrides and how much of a draft was used or omitted. This yields error analysis for free and surfaces data issues such as messy taxonomies (V1 routing, V2 SOP-based copilot drafts, V3 end-to-end resolution). Move up when humans rarely change outputs. Autonomy can also be constrained by number of actions or by topic risk, which matters in high-risk domains like insurance pre-authorization or refunds.

Incremental Trust Calibration Through Review Cycles describes the judgment step. After several cycles, decide how much you trust the agent. If results are good, remove approval steps or add data sources. If not, give candid feedback and iterate on the instructions, either through the tool's feedback mechanism or by editing the original prompt and re-running it. Treat it as building a product for a customer of one.

Minimizing Surprise as a Calibration Readiness Signal gives a heuristic for when to advance. If you calibrate every one or two days and see no new data distribution or behavior patterns, little new information is gained and you can move on. Recalibrate after disturbances such as a model deprecation (GPT-4o to GPT-5) or users attempting more ambitious tasks. In the underwriting example, users asked deeper questions after about three months.

Human-in-the-Loop Review with Gradual Replacement by Guideline Skills covers retiring review. Keep human approval first where brand or quality matters, then substitute a skill encoding brand guidelines with clear dos and don'ts. Human review can shrink as models get better at applying the guidelines. Reversible changes can be unshipped if they turn out bad.
when_to_use: Launching a first version of an agent that takes real-world actions, especially on shared or sensitive systems like Slack, email or documents
When hallucination rates and first-run accuracy cannot be predicted and reliability is unproven
High-risk domains such as insurance pre-authorization or customer refunds
Planning a roadmap for an agentic product and deciding when it has earned more autonomy
Deciding whether to remove approval steps, add data sources, or re-run calibration after model or behavior changes
Early deployment of agents shipping user-facing changes where brand matters and clear dos and don'ts can be written
When changes are reversible so a bad ship can be rolled back
when_not_to_use: When the AI only produces suggestions that a human always reviews and there is no path toward autonomy
Before the agent has produced enough outputs to judge reliability
When actions are high-risk or irreversible and the design cannot limit them
Irreversible or high-stakes actions where an automated brand check alone would not be sufficient
Fully low-risk tasks where autonomy needs no human gate
metric_or_method: Break the end state into versions (v1, v2, v3), each adding agency (e.g., route, suggest, auto-resolve with human fallback). Restrict actions to low-downside outputs with hard permissions. At each version, log human edits, overrides and usage of AI suggestions, review them as error analysis, fix data and context issues, and apply feedback to the instructions. Advance when humans rarely change outputs and calibration cycles (every one or two days) show low surprise; recalibrate after model swaps or user behavior shifts. No formal quantitative metric is specified.
common_pitfalls: Jumping to full or end-to-end agency before observing how the system behaves when it gets things wrong, which loses visibility and user trust
Letting the agent act directly (post, send, edit) before observing it, or relying only on prompt instructions when hard permission constraints are available
Not logging human edits, overrides and omitted draft text, which loses the error-analysis flywheel
Expanding scope too quickly, such as launching with many data sources at once, or expecting the first shot to work without iterating
Not giving candid feedback when the agent is off track
Assuming calibration or staged rollout is permanent; model swaps, new data distributions and evolving user behavior require recalibration
Removing human review before the model reliably applies the guidelines, or writing vague guidelines instead of clear dos and don'ts
Assuming the agent will notice its own silly mistakes, such as overwriting headers
source_excerpt: There's not really a rule book you can follow, but it's all about minimizing surprise, which means let's say you're calibrating every one or two days and you figure out that you're not seeing new data distribution patterns, your users have been pretty consistent with how they're behaving with the system. Then the amount of information you gain is kind of very low and that's when you know you can actually go to the next stage.
one_liner: Climb an autonomy ladder: start with drafts and DMs, log human edits, advance when surprise drops.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build a progressive autonomy rollout with human review logging for an AI agent.

Context:
- Agent description: [AGENT_DESCRIPTION]
- Current autonomy version (e.g., V1 route, V2 draft, V3 auto-resolve with fallback): [CURRENT_VERSION]
- Next proposed version and the added agency: [NEXT_VERSION]
- Review log location/format (CSV, JSONL, DB table): [LOG_SOURCE]
- Fields available (e.g., ai_output, human_final_output, action_taken, overridden, topic, timestamp): [LOG_FIELDS]
- Calibration cadence: [CALIBRATION_CADENCE_DAYS] days
- High-risk topics or action limits: [RISK_TOPICS_AND_CAPS]

Tasks:
1. Write Python that loads the log and computes per calibration window: (a) override rate, (b) edit distance or percent of AI draft text kept vs omitted, (c) acceptance rate without edits, and (d) breakdown of each by topic and risk tier.
2. Add a 'surprise' check: compare the distribution of topics, input types, and edit patterns in the latest window to the previous windows (e.g., Jensen-Shannon divergence or a chi-square test) and flag new clusters of overrides or novel request types.
3. Cluster the human edits and overrides into an error-analysis table (top failure modes with 3 example traces each) and suggest which are data/taxonomy problems versus instruction problems.
4. Output a readiness report with a recommendation of HOLD, ADVANCE to [NEXT_VERSION], or RECALIBRATE. Use configurable thresholds such as [OVERRIDE_RATE_THRESHOLD] and [MIN_STABLE_WINDOWS] consecutive low-surprise windows. Also list the triggers that force recalibration (model swap, new user behavior, more ambitious tasks).
5. Generate a permissions/guardrail checklist confirming the agent physically cannot take actions above [CURRENT_VERSION] (for example DM instead of channel post, draft instead of send).
6. Propose which human review steps could be replaced with a guideline-based check, and write a draft rubric of dos and don'ts for an LLM judge. Include a script to compare that judge against human decisions in the log.

No formal metric is mandated, so make thresholds explicit, configurable, and documented. Include unit tests with a small synthetic log.

name: Qualitative User Testing of AI Products
definition: A qualitative evaluation process in which a team observes real people using an AI product or prototype, rather than relying on theory, internal dogfooding, friends, or LLM-simulated users. It recruits unbiased and varied participants, avoids leading them, stays close over time, and iterates quickly on what the observations reveal.
explanation: The core method is to put a working product or prototype in front of real users and watch what they do, then ask follow-up questions and iterate. Empirical Testing With Users and Fast Iteration contributes the mindset: ship something imperfect and learn from users instead of theorizing, and use direct feedback channels such as a DMable PM, because subtle issues in natural-language agent experiences often surface only on the second or third follow-up question. Unbiased Manual Onboarding and Diverse Early-Access Observation contributes a hands-on early phase. The core team manually onboards a couple hundred users over about two weeks, does not lead the witness, watches which usage patterns emerge unprompted, and recruits unconventional users (such as a coffee-shop owner) to expose blind spots that internal dogfooding misses. When patterns emerge on their own, the team adds a reversible nudge. Rapid Prototype Testing with Zero-Skin-in-the-Game Users contributes a repeatable loop: build a functional prototype, recruit about 20 target-persona participants with no stake in your success via panel platforms such as Voicepanel or UserTesting, have them think aloud through a few tasks with little context, review sessions as a team, and fix what is broken. Features are chunked small so weak ideas die early, and a power-user Slack group gives feedback on later-stage features. Human Usability Testing over AI-Simulated Users contributes the choice among cheap prototypes: run traditional usability tests with real people (e.g. screen-shared), since LLM-simulated users are not expected to be as credible. Exposure Hours contributes a habit: deliberately track and increase time spent watching people use your product and others, including live customer demos to the exec team or company, because builders overrate how well their product works. The AI User Testing Framework (Longitudinal, High-Touch, Attitudinal Segmentation) contributes AI-specific design: test long enough to see engagement after novelty fades (avoiding phantom PMF), stay close to users (e.g. Slack groups) to see attitudes shift, and include and separately analyze AI embracers and AI skeptics to avoid a 'tepid tea' product that satisfies no one. This is qualitative gut-check evidence, not statistically significant, and builds intuition rather than scores.
when_to_use: Early-stage launches of AI or agent products with uncertain usage patterns
Validating an idea before investing heavily in building it, including cheap vibe-coded prototypes
Choosing among several AI-built prototypes of a UI or feature
When internal dogfooding may be biased or the team is too familiar with the product to see usability problems
When novelty-driven engagement may mask long-term retention
When users hold widely differing attitudes toward AI
Before shipping onboarding flows, landing pages, new features, export or sharing flows
To catch unknown pain points and build product intuition through regular observation of real users
when_not_to_use: When you need statistically significant or quantitative scores; this is qualitative observation
When your only participants are friends or colleagues obliged to be nice
At large scale where manual onboarding is infeasible (framed as a roughly two-week early phase)
When bulk, round-the-clock functional testing is needed, where simulated agents serve a different purpose
For non-AI features where attitudes toward the technology are not a factor in segmentation
metric_or_method: Qualitative observation of real users: manual onboarding or think-aloud sessions (about 20 target-persona participants per prototype, recruited via panel platforms), follow-up questions, longitudinal tracking of engagement after novelty fades, separate analysis of AI embracers and skeptics, high-touch channels like Slack groups, and tracked exposure hours, with team review and fast iteration.
common_pitfalls: Leading users toward a pattern so you cannot tell whether it emerges naturally, or making a discovered pattern a one-way door
Relying on friends, family, or dogfooding only, who give biased signal and make everything feel easy
Recruiting participants who have skin in the game or are not true prospective users
Testing too briefly and mistaking novelty-driven engagement for product-market fit (phantom PMF)
Averaging embracers and skeptics into 'tepid tea', or dismissing skeptics who can become superusers with the right messaging and onboarding
Accepting first-pass feedback without follow-up questions, since subtle issues often appear on the second or third
Assuming an LLM simulating user clicks gives results as good as real humans
Over-theorizing, building for months before testing, or avoiding the discomfort of watching people struggle
source_excerpt: Get somebody on Zoom, screen shared using your software, see what happens. You can tell the AI to do it and you can simulate your users with the AI. I don't think that's credible. I don't think you're going to get as good results from ChatGPT pretending to click around on your prototype than you would from an actual human being.
one_liner: Watch ~20 real, unbiased users think aloud on your AI prototype, skip LLM sims and friends, and iterate fast.
codex_prompt_template:
I'm running qualitative user testing for an AI product: [PRODUCT_DESCRIPTION]. Target persona: [TARGET_PERSONA]. Key tasks to test: [TASKS]. Number of participants: [NUM_PARTICIPANTS]. Test duration or follow-up window: [STUDY_DURATION].

Build the following in [LANGUAGE, e.g. Python]:
1. A recruiting screener that includes the target persona plus at least one unconventional user type, and tags each participant as AI embracer, neutral, or AI skeptic. Exclude friends, teammates, and anyone with a stake in the product's success.
2. A neutral, non-leading think-aloud session guide: minimal context, 3-4 tasks, and follow-up probes for the second and third questions where subtle natural-language issues tend to surface. Include a list of leading phrasings to avoid.
3. A structured observation template (CSV or JSON schema) with these fields: participant_id, attitude_segment, task, unprompted_usage_pattern, confusion_or_failure, quote, severity, and timestamp.
4. A synthesis script that reads observation files from [OBSERVATIONS_PATH] and does the following: clusters issues by theme, counts how many participants hit each issue, separates findings by attitude segment, and outputs a ranked list of fixes plus 'weak ideas to kill'.
5. A longitudinal tracker that logs per-participant engagement by week from [USAGE_LOG_PATH], so we can see whether usage holds after novelty fades, and flags drop-off.
6. A short exposure-hours log (date, hours spent observing users, who observed) with a weekly summary.

Treat the output as qualitative gut-check evidence, not statistical significance. Do not simulate users with an LLM. Add a README explaining how to run a session and review it as a team.

name: RAG Retrieval Evaluation (Recall@k)
definition: An evaluation of the retrieval stage of a RAG pipeline that uses queries or tickets paired with known correct documents. It measures recall@k (the percentage of all truly relevant documents captured in the top k results), adds precision@k when a re-ranking stage exists, and checks whether retrieved items are relevant and match what a human agent would have consulted.
explanation: The retriever and generator can fail independently, and an end-to-end correctness score will not say which is broken, so retrieval is evaluated separately and fixed first. The core method is recall@k on a dataset of queries with known correct documents. Recall matters most because if the correct information is not retrieved, the generator cannot invent facts, while modern LLMs can ignore irrelevant noise. Choose k by task: a small k (3 to 5) for single-fact queries and a larger k (10 to 20) for synthesis queries. Precision@k becomes important when a second re-ranking stage is added. The second contribution is a relevance-focused variant for support-style features, where the system moves from routing (v1) to suggesting resolutions (v2) and the eval focus shifts from routing accuracy to retrieval quality. It asks two questions: are the retrieved SOPs, knowledge-base articles or past resolutions actually relevant to the ticket, and are they what a human agent would have looked at? Running this with a human reviewing drafts in v2 also shows where retrieval breaks down and which documents need updates, and it guards against moving to auto-resolution on a wrong SOP.
when_to_use: Evaluating the retrieval stage of a RAG pipeline
Choosing the value of k for your task
Features where the AI retrieves SOPs, knowledge-base articles, or past resolutions
Human-in-the-loop v2 stages before auto-resolution
Pipelines with a re-ranking stage where precision@k matters
when_not_to_use: Features with no retrieval component, such as pure routing
metric_or_method: recall@k on queries with known correct documents; precision@k when a re-ranking stage exists; plus relevance judgments of retrieved items per ticket compared against what a human agent would have consulted.
common_pitfalls: Relying only on an end-to-end correctness score, which cannot show whether the retriever or generator is broken
Improving the generator before the retriever is reliable
Using the same k for simple and complex queries
Moving to auto-resolution without checking retrieval, so a wrong SOP leads to a plausible but incorrect resolution
Not tracing a generation error back to the retrieval or routing step where it started
source_excerpt: The most critical metric for RAG is often **recall@k**. This measures what percentage of all the truly relevant documents are captured within the top *k* results your system retrieves. Recall is paramount because if the correct information is not retrieved, the generator has no chance of producing a correct answer.
one_liner: Score your retriever alone with recall@k on known-correct docs, so you fix retrieval before blaming the LLM.
codex_prompt_template:
Write a Python script that evaluates the retrieval stage of my RAG pipeline in isolation from the generator.

Feature description: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]
Retriever interface: [RETRIEVER_FUNCTION_OR_API]
Labeled dataset: [DATASET_PATH] (each row has a query or ticket plus a list of known-correct document IDs)
Values of k to test: [K_VALUES, e.g. 3,5,10,20]
Re-ranking stage present: [YES_OR_NO]

The script should:
1. Load the dataset and run the retriever for each query to get the top-k document IDs.
2. Compute recall@k per query (relevant docs in top k divided by all relevant docs), then average across queries for each k.
3. If a re-ranking stage exists, also compute precision@k and compare it before and after re-ranking.
4. Break results down by query type, such as single-fact versus synthesis, and recommend a k for each type.
5. Export every query with recall@k of 0 to a CSV with the query, expected docs, and retrieved docs, so I can review misses and find documents that need updating.
6. Optionally add a column where a reviewer marks whether each retrieved item is relevant and whether a human agent would have consulted it, then compute the agreement rate.

Output a summary table and the code, using pandas and plain Python.

name: Repeated Sampling for Stochastic Outputs (Pass@k and Consistency)
definition: Run the identical prompt on the same input multiple times, because model outputs are stochastic. Then either measure success across attempts (pass@1 versus pass@n) or compare the answers side by side for inconsistency, invented content, and repeated omissions, to judge reliability and decide what to fix.
explanation: The core method is to run the same prompt on the same input repeatedly and look at the spread of results rather than a single output. Two variants cover different kinds of features. The Pass@k variant is a metric: the same prompt is attempted multiple times and success is compared between pass@1 (a single attempt succeeds) and pass@n (at least one of n attempts succeeds). Model cards commonly report pass@1 versus pass@n. The variant reflects that a model may solve a task on one try but not another, and it explains why starting over and retrying (e.g., in Claude Code) has a much higher success rate than continuing on one failed attempt. It suits tasks like code generation where a retry is cheap. The Repeated-Run Consistency Comparison variant is a qualitative, hands-on check for chat, summarization, and extraction features. Take a real, messy input such as a meeting transcript, Slack thread, or support log and ask the same question (e.g., 'What were the top 5 decisions?') about 10 times. Compare answers side by side. Did it pick different items each time? Did it invent items not in the text? Did it miss the same important item repeatedly? Mark what changed and why it matters, and ask whether a user who saw the worst of the outputs would still trust the product. Then convert the observed variance into one concrete guardrail, such as a system prompt change. Together, Pass@k quantifies capability across retries, and the consistency comparison exposes worst-case behavior and guides the next fix.
when_to_use: Evaluating stochastic generation tasks such as code where a retry is cheap
Comparing single-attempt reliability with multi-attempt capability
Understanding product value when users can retry
Testing output stability for summarization or extraction features
Choosing the next guardrail to add to the system prompt
when_not_to_use: High-stakes settings where only a single attempt is allowed and reliability must be near-deterministic
When deterministic outputs are already guaranteed by other means
metric_or_method: Run the identical prompt on the same input multiple times (about 10 for manual comparison). Compare pass@1 against pass@n, and compare outputs for different picks, invented items, and repeated misses. Judge trust by the worst outputs, then add one guardrail.
common_pitfalls: Reporting only a single attempt and underestimating capability
Judging only the best output rather than the worst version a user might see
Assuming a retry with the exact same prompt is pointless; starting over and retrying has a much higher success rate than continuing on the failed attempt
Ignoring that users may not be able to verify which attempt succeeded
Not converting the observed variance into a concrete guardrail

codex_prompt_template: Write a Python script that tests the reliability of my AI feature through repeated sampling. Feature description: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Model and API: [MODEL_NAME]. Prompt template: [PROMPT_TEMPLATE]. Test inputs: [INPUT_FILE_OR_DATASET]. For each input, run the identical prompt [N_RUNS] times (default 10) at temperature [TEMPERATURE]. name: RL Environments for Evaluating and Training Agents
definition: An RL environment is a simulation of the real world, like a video game with a fully fleshed-out universe containing tools, data and entities. A model is given tasks there and rewarded when it does well.
explanation: Chen describes building worlds such as a startup with Gmail, Slack, Jira and GitHub where AWS and Slack go down, and the model must figure out what to do. Rewards could be passing unit tests, writing a retro that matches what happened, or checking a spreadsheet cell for the correct profit and loss number. These environments expose weaknesses in end-to-end, long-horizon tasks where step one affects step 50, which single-step academic benchmarks hide. He positions them as the next stage after SFT, RLHF, and rubrics and verifiers, complementing rather than replacing them.
when_to_use: When evaluating or training agents on messy, multi-step, real-world tasks
When models look strong on isolated single-step benchmarks but fail end-to-end
When outcomes can be verified programmatically (unit tests, spreadsheet cell values)
when_not_to_use: When the task is a simple, single-step capability (e.g., classification or short Q&A) where a standard benchmark or rubric-based eval already gives a reliable signal
When you cannot define a verifiable reward (unit tests, ground-truth documents, checkable values) and success would rest on vague or subjective judgment
When the real-world workflow can't be simulated with realistic tools, data, and failure scenarios, so the environment wouldn't reflect actual conditions
When you are treating it as a replacement for SFT, RLHF, or rubrics and verifiers rather than a complement, or lack the budget to build and maintain a full simulated world
metric_or_method: Define a task in a simulated environment with tools and data, and specify rewards (unit tests passing, document matching ground truth, spreadsheet cell correctness).
common_pitfalls: Checking only the final answer ignores how the model got there
Contrived single-step environments don't reflect real-world performance
source_excerpt: So we give them models tasks in these environments, we design interesting challenges for them, and then we run them to see how they perform. And then we teach them, we give them these rewards when they're doing a good job or a bad job.
one_liner: Drop agents into simulated worlds with tools and failures, then reward verifiable outcomes to expose long-horizon…

Build a Python RL-style evaluation environment for testing an agent on [AGENT_TASK_DESCRIPTION]. Requirements:
1. Simulate a mini-world with mock tools ([TOOL_LIST], e.g., email, chat, ticketing, code repo) backed by seeded fake data and entities.
2. Support injected disruptions such as [FAILURE_INJECTIONS] (e.g., service outage, missing data, conflicting instructions) at configurable steps.
3. Expose a reset()/step(action)/get_state() interface and log the full trajectory (actions, tool outputs, state changes).
4. Implement programmatic verifiers for reward: [REWARD_CHECKS] (e.g., unit tests pass, spreadsheet cell equals expected value, report matches ground-truth event log). Return both a final outcome reward and partial-credit sub-rewards.
5. Write a runner that executes [NUM_EPISODES] episodes of my agent at [AGENT_ENTRYPOINT] across different random seeds, and reports success rate, mean reward, steps-to-completion, and the step at which failures first occur.

Include 3 example tasks of increasing difficulty and unit tests for the verifiers.

name: Root-Cause Postmortem of AI Failures
definition: A learning loop in which each AI failure (and optionally each success) is traced to its underlying cause, such as missing context, flawed examples or data, confusing prompts, or knowledge or data gaps. The fix is then written into durable inputs (context systems, rules files, documentation, tooling, instruction files, or data) and verified on the next run so the mistake does not recur.
explanation: The core method: when an AI output is wrong or unexpected, do not just patch or retry it. Ask why it happened, identify the root cause, fix that cause in the system the AI relies on, and re-run to check the behavior improved. Members contribute different sub-steps and variants. (1) Debug inputs first: manually compare the bad output to the examples, context, and source data the agent saw. In the usability-session examples, hallucinated sprint numbers came from stray 'Sprint 5' titles in the examples, and tasks were mislabeled as done because the board had no task status field. Removing the stray term and adding a 'done' checkbox fixed these. (2) Context-engineering root cause: when a good model makes a poor decision, it is almost always missing context. Ask what context was lacking and supply it systematically, for example through an MCP server for a coding agent, rather than waiting for better models. (3) Model introspection: ask the model to reflect on why it made a decision (for example, running tests without using the UI). The answer can reveal a confusing system prompt, a missed requirement, or a subagent that skipped verification, so the harness can be fixed. (4) Post-fix retrospective: once a problem is solved, ask the agent in chat mode how to prompt better so a multi-step fix becomes a one-step fix, then record the lesson in rules.md or project knowledge so the agent applies it every time. (5) Postmortem loop: ask the agent what in its system prompt or tooling caused the mistake, then have it update its documentation, tooling, or /commands. Do this even after successes. The fix is not always a /command. (6) Escalation with trace capture: in production, an agent escalates to a human when stuck, the human coaches it, and the captured traces are used to classify the failure as a knowledge gap or a data gap and supply what the model lacked, so the same case no longer escalates. (7) Meta-feedback loop: users observe real-use results and edit the tool's instruction files or rubric, optionally by asking Claude Code to make the change, supported by persistent state across sessions, so the next session uses the improved version.
when_to_use: An agent hallucinates, mislabels, skips a step, or does something a human wouldn't, especially when it works from examples or data that humans interpret using implicit knowledge
AI coding agents or other agents repeatedly make errors specific to your codebase or product
A bug took several attempts to fix, or revealed that the agent misunderstood part of the codebase
Agents in production get stuck on edge cases and you want to reduce human escalations over time
The AI tool is configured through editable instruction files, prompts, or rules, and real use produces lessons about what it does well or badly
After a successful feature, to review what could have been done better
when_not_to_use: The tool has no editable instructions, rules, or persistent knowledge file in which to store lessons
There are no real-use outcomes or failure cases to learn from yet
Relying on model introspection as the only source of truth, without confirming against data or eval results
For skills whose output is hard to verify, which limits how well feedback loops can work
As a permanent requirement: one member expects it to become less necessary as models improve, so it is partly a stopgap
metric_or_method: For each bad output: (1) check the examples, context, and source data given to the agent; (2) ask the agent or yourself what context, instruction, or knowledge was missing, or what in the system prompt or tooling caused the mistake; (3) classify it as a knowledge gap or data gap; (4) record the fix in the context system, rules file, documentation, tooling, or instruction files; (5) re-run and check the response improves and the same case no longer recurs (ideally solved in one go, or without human escalation).
common_pitfalls: Retrying until it works, then moving on without learning why it failed, or skipping the postmortem when the work succeeded
Assuming errors are model limitations without checking the examples, context, and source data (stray terms in examples, missing status fields, implicit human context left out)
Fixing only the individual bad output or symptom instead of root-causing it and updating the system
Passively waiting for models to improve, or treating the AI tool in isolation rather than as part of a system
Blaming the tool rather than examining your own prompt, references, or context gaps
Assuming the fix always belongs in a /command, when it may belong in other documentation or tooling
Not capturing traces from human coaching, or assuming most work can run autonomously without humans handling exceptions
Letting the rules file bloat without periodically updating project documents, or editing files by hand when describing the change to the agent would be faster

codex_prompt_template: You are helping me run a root-cause postmortem on an AI failure. Feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Failing input: [FAILING_INPUT]. Bad output: [BAD_OUTPUT]. Do not just patch the output. Fix the cause.

name: Routing Accuracy
definition: The fraction of cases in which the system routes a ticket or request to the correct department.
explanation: For a v1 customer support system that only routes tickets, routing accuracy is a simple but strong eval. It shows whether the model is learning the right distinctions and whether the setup is solid. It can be computed against the reference dataset before launch, or on live data using human reroutes as a proxy. Per-department scores show where to dig in, such as Refunds underperforming while Billing looks fine.
when_to_use: Low-agency v1 features where the AI only classifies or routes
Identifying which categories or departments are weakest
when_not_to_use: Evaluating later versions that retrieve documents or generate responses, where retrieval quality and generation quality matter more
metric_or_method: Routing accuracy = correct routes / total routed, computed overall and per department, against the reference dataset and live logs.
common_pitfalls: Relying on routing accuracy alone once the system moves to retrieval or generation
Ignoring per-department breakdowns that reveal where the failures are
source_excerpt: For example, in the routing v1 of the customer support system, a simple but strong eval would be **routing accuracy**—how often the system routes to the correct department. That alone can tell you if the model is learning the right distinctions and whether or not your setup is solid.
one_liner: Score how often tickets land in the right department, then slice by department to find your weakest route.
codex_prompt_template: Write Python code to compute routing accuracy for my ticket-routing feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Input: a CSV at [DATASET_PATH] with columns ticket_id, predicted_department, and correct_department (the reference label). Compute (1) overall routing accuracy = correct routes / total routed, (2) per-department accuracy and support (recall per true department), (3) a confusion matrix of true vs. predicted department, highlighting the top [TOP_N] most common misroutes (e.g., Refunds misrouted to Billing), and (4) 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap so small departments aren't over-interpreted. Also add a function that computes the same metrics on live logs, using human reroutes from [LIVE_LOG_PATH] as a proxy label (a ticket rerouted by a human = incorrect route). Output a summary table and flag any department whose accuracy falls below [ACCURACY_THRESHOLD]. Include pytest tests with a small synthetic dataset.

name: Rubrics and Verifiers as RL Reward Signals
definition: A post-training method in which humans define a measurable success criterion, such as a unit test, a verifier check, or an expert-written rubric. That criterion grades model outputs with detailed feedback and serves as the reward signal. The same criteria can also be run as evals to measure progress.
explanation: The core method follows SFT (input/output data) and RLHF (humans pick the better of several samples). Humans define success criteria and a way to measure them, and the model is rewarded against them. This is RL from AI feedback (RLAIF), which is more scalable and data-efficient. Verifiers check outputs, for example a unit test for code or whether a spreadsheet cell contains the correct number. Rubrics and correct answers written by experts cover domains where criteria are subtler. Rubrics and verifiers are described as learning by being graded and getting detailed feedback on where you went wrong. They became very important over the past year and complement SFT, RLHF and RL environments rather than replacing them. Three contributions fit together. (1) The RLAIF framing: the same artifact, a benchmark/eval or an RL environment verifier, can be used either as the eval or as the post-training reward, so evals and RL environments are essentially the same data type used differently. Defining rewards thoughtfully and mitigating reward hacking is highly impactful. (2) The training-vs-measurement distinction: when evals are used for training, the evaluation produces a reward. When used for measurement, evals run across candidate checkpoints (for example five) to pick the best to release. Be explicit about which role an eval plays. (3) The quality caveat: rubrics should capture real quality, not a checklist. In the poem example, boxes like 'eight lines' and 'contains the word moon' miss the subtle qualities that make a great poem.
when_to_use: When you want to improve model capabilities via RL and need a reward signal
When success can be measured at scale, e.g. unit tests for code or a spreadsheet cell with a known correct answer
When expert criteria in other domains can be captured in a rubric used as a verifier
When you want detailed feedback signals on where a model output went wrong
When clarifying whether an eval feeds a reward/training loop or informs a release decision
When choosing between candidate model checkpoints using the same criteria
when_not_to_use: When no clear success criterion can be defined for the domain
When quality would be reduced to a simple checklist that misses implicit, subtle qualities
metric_or_method: Human- or expert-defined success criteria (unit tests, verifiers, rubrics) score model trajectories and reward desired behavior in post-training. The same criteria are run across candidate checkpoints to choose the best release.
common_pitfalls: Poorly designed rewards invite reward hacking, so define rewards thoughtfully and mitigate hacking
Reducing quality to checkboxes (e.g. 'is it eight lines, does it contain the word moon') and ignoring subtle qualities that define genuinely good output
Conflating training evals (reward signals) with measurement evals (checkpoint selection)
Treating RL environments and evals as fundamentally different things rather than the same data used for different purposes
Assuming newer methods like RL environments make rubrics and verifiers obsolete, when they complement each other
source_excerpt: And then I think over the past year or so, rubrics and verifiers have become very important. And rubrics and verifiers are like learning by being graded and getting detailed feedback on where you went wrong.
one_liner: Turn unit tests and expert rubrics into RL rewards, then reuse them as evals to pick your best checkpoint.
codex_prompt_template: I am building a reward and eval harness for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] in the domain of [DOMAIN]. Success criteria: [SUCCESS_CRITERIA, e.g. unit tests, known correct answers, or an expert rubric]. Write Python code that does the following. (1) Implements a verifier for each criterion that scores a model output or trajectory from 0 to 1 and returns structured feedback on what went wrong. For subjective criteria, implement a rubric-based LLM grader with explicit per-criterion scoring anchors, and avoid shallow checklist items that miss real quality. (2) Aggregates the verifier scores into a single scalar reward function, with a clearly separated interface for the reward role (used in RL post-training) and the eval role (used for measurement). (3) Runs the same verifiers across [NUM_CHECKPOINTS] candidate model checkpoints on a held-out set of [HELDOUT_SET_SIZE] prompts and reports mean score, per-criterion breakdown, and confidence intervals so I can choose the best checkpoint to release. (4) Adds reward-hacking checks: flag outputs that score high on the verifiers but fail a small human-reviewed sample of [REVIEW_SAMPLE_SIZE] examples, and list the most suspicious patterns. Output the code, a sample rubric file, and a short README explaining which role each eval plays.

name: Sample-Then-Scale Prompt Validation
definition: A prompt validation process in which a prompt (and model choice) is first refined on a small sample set until outputs are consistent, then run across a large test set to measure the rate of deviations from expected behavior, and adjusted until that failure rate is minimized before the prompt is frozen and used at scale.
explanation: The method has two stages. Stage 1 is sample-set refinement (from the pixel-art avatar workflow): validate the workflow on a few test outputs, then use a playground to repeatedly test and refine the prompt and compare which models work best. Keep adjusting until all samples follow the same target style. Once the prompt is stable, freeze it and automate the full batch run (there, Claude Code wrote a CLI tool to generate every avatar in one go). Stage 2 is scale testing (from Schulhoff's product-focused approach): run the prompt over a battery of thousands of inputs and measure how often outputs deviate from expected behavior. In his GPT-4 example, the model wrote out its reasoning 99 of 100 times but gave only a final answer 1 in 100 times. Adding a thought-inducing phrase made the reasoning happen reliably and improved performance across the whole test set. The first member contributes the cheap, qualitative, early iteration loop and model comparison; the second contributes the quantitative failure-rate check needed when millions of users hit a prompt and you cannot watch every output. Together: iterate cheaply on a small sample for consistency, then verify robustness on a large input set, and only then lock the prompt in. Classical techniques remain useful for robustness at scale, and vendor claims that a newer model no longer needs a technique should be verified at scale.
when_to_use: Before bulk-generating many assets that must share a consistent style
When choosing between models for a generation task
When you need a stable, reusable prompt before automating
Product-focused prompts that process thousands or millions of inputs
When a new model is claimed to make a technique unnecessary and you need to verify it at scale
Before locking in a prompt that will not be monitored output by output
when_not_to_use: One-off generations where cross-output consistency does not matter
Conversational, one-off prompting where you see each output directly
metric_or_method: Stage 1: qualitative visual comparison of sample outputs across prompt and model variants in a playground until all samples match the target. Stage 2: run the prompt over a large test set, measure the rate of outputs deviating from expected behavior (e.g. missing reasoning), and iterate to reduce that rate. Then freeze the prompt and batch-run.
common_pitfalls: Scaling to the full batch before the prompt is stable
Not testing multiple models for the task
Trusting vendor claims that a new model no longer needs a technique without testing at scale
Checking only a handful of outputs and missing rare failure modes
Making small, unvalidated prompt changes that can have large unpredictable effects on performance
Relying only on qualitative sample checks when the prompt will serve a large user base
source_excerpt: And I was running, I guess, GPT-4 on a battery of thousands of inputs and I was finding 99 out of a hundred times it would write out its reasoning, great, and then give a final answer. [...] But one in a hundred times it would just give a final answer, no reason. Why? I don't know, it's just one of those random LLM things. But I had to add in that thought-inducing phrase like, make sure to write out all your reasoning in order to make sure that happens. Because I wanted to make sure to maximize my performance over my whole test set.
one_liner: Perfect the prompt on a few samples, then stress-test it on thousands to hunt failure rates before you freeze it.
codex_prompt_template: Build a two-stage prompt validation harness in [LANGUAGE, e.g. Python] for my feature: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Stage 1 (sample refinement): load [SAMPLE_SIZE, e.g. 10] sample inputs from [SAMPLE_INPUT_PATH]. Run each one against every combination of prompt variant in [PROMPT_VARIANTS_FILE] and model in [MODEL_LIST]. Write the outputs to a side-by-side comparison table (CSV or HTML) so I can review them manually. Add a consistency check that flags variants where outputs do not all match this target format or style: [TARGET_BEHAVIOR_SPEC]. Stage 2 (scale testing): take the selected prompt and model and run them over [DATASET_SIZE, e.g. 5000] inputs from [LARGE_INPUT_PATH], with concurrency and retries. For each output, run a programmatic or LLM-judge check for this deviation: [FAILURE_MODE, e.g. missing reasoning, wrong format, off-style]. Report the deviation rate with a 95% confidence interval, list the top 20 example failures, and cluster the failures by pattern. Then suggest 3 prompt edits (e.g. adding an explicit instruction such as [CANDIDATE_PROMPT_FIX]) and re-run to compare failure rates before and after. Finish by writing a freeze step that saves the final prompt, model and version hash to [OUTPUT_CONFIG_PATH] only if the failure rate is at or below [MAX_FAILURE_RATE, e.g. 1%], and generates a CLI command to batch-run the full workload.
