name: Simulated Jury Evaluation of LLM-Generated Notes
definition: An LLM generates many variants of an existing proposed note. A simulated jury, a representative group of Community Notes contributors whose ratings are predicted from their past ratings, then scores each variant. This simulates the whole rating process instead of trusting a single LLM draft.
explanation: Jay Baxter describes the Supernotes approach, built by researchers outside the company using Community Notes' public data and code. Existing proposed notes may have problems, tell only part of the story, or be worded in a biased way. They are fed to an LLM that generates a large number of variants. To evaluate those variants, the approach builds a representative group of contributors and predicts each one's rating from their past ratings. This lets the team explicitly create notes that are likely to be rated helpful by people, instead of having an LLM write a note from scratch and hoping it is good. Jay also notes a risk with LLM or agent assistance: raters must stay diligent and verify the output themselves before issuing a helpful rating.
when_to_use: When LLMs generate content that humans will ultimately rate, and you have a large history of per-rater ratings.
When you need to estimate how a diverse or polarized audience would receive generated text before showing it.
When public or open data lets you reproduce the human rating process in simulation.
when_not_to_use: When you lack historical per-rater rating data to predict how raters would score new content.
When predicted ratings would replace human verification entirely. Jay stresses that humans should still verify LLM output themselves before rating it helpful.
metric_or_method: Generate many LLM variants of a proposed note, build a representative simulated jury of contributors, predict each contributor's rating from their past ratings, and select variants predicted to be rated helpful.
common_pitfalls: Writing a note with an LLM from scratch and hoping it is good, without simulating the rating process.
Raters trusting LLM output and not verifying it before giving a helpful rating.
Low-quality or hallucinated LLM output, which the host flags as the challenge of avoiding AI slop while scaling.
source_excerpt: Basically take all these in, have an LLM generate a ton of different variants, and then basically make the simulated jury to basically get a representative group of contributors for community notes who would be rating the note and try to predict based on their past ratings how they would rate these LLM generated notes. And so this way you can actually, rather than just having an LLM write a note from scratch and hoping it's good, you can simulate the entire community notes rating process and explicitly create notes that are likely to be rated helpful by people.
one_liner: Generate many LLM note variants, then let a simulated jury predicted from past ratings pick the likely winners.
codex_prompt_template: Build a simulated jury evaluation pipeline for LLM-generated content in [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Inputs: a historical ratings dataset at [RATINGS_DATASET_PATH] with columns rater_id, item_id, rating, and optional rater metadata, plus a set of seed items at [SEED_ITEMS_PATH]. Steps: (1) For each seed item, call an LLM [MODEL_NAME] to generate [NUM_VARIANTS] variants that fix problems, add missing context, and neutralize biased wording. (2) Build a representative simulated jury of [JURY_SIZE] raters, sampled to cover the viewpoint spectrum of the rater population (for example by clustering rater latent factors from the ratings matrix). (3) Train a rating-prediction model, such as matrix factorization or a gradient-boosted model on rater and item embeddings, that predicts each juror's rating of a new item from their past ratings. (4) Score every variant with the jury and compute the predicted helpful rate and the cross-viewpoint agreement. (5) Select variants above a [HELPFULNESS_THRESHOLD] that are rated helpful across viewpoint clusters. (6) Validate the predictor on held-out real ratings (AUC, calibration) and report how well simulated jury scores match real human ratings. Output runnable Python code, a results table ranking variants, and a short list of failure modes such as jury bias and the risk of raters not verifying outputs.

name: Simulated Multi-Turn Conversations with a Realistic User LLM
definition: An offline evaluation pipeline in which a user-simulating LLM, defined by an intent, world state and persona and ideally fine-tuned on real user verbatims so it behaves like real (often frustrated) users, plays out complete multi-turn conversations with the agent on a representative synthetic dataset. Graders (LLM-as-judge plus deterministic checks) score the conversations, and launch criteria on those scores gate release.
explanation: The core method treats agent development like ML model development: offline evaluation must pass before launch. The Lyft-style simulator, inspired by Tau-bench, pairs an agent with a user LLM and gives each support use case domain policy instructions. The user LLM is defined by an intent, a world state (e.g. a luxury driver of a couple of years) and a persona. Graders then score the multi-turn traces, and the score must gate development and release or the judge is not useful. The aim is to avoid using live users as test data. The first member contributed this pipeline and launch gate. The second member contributed the realism sub-step. Frontier models are trained to be helpful assistants, so the default LLM user sounded too nice, and the first offline eval gave a ~90% pass rate that was too good to be true. The fix was to fine-tune the user model on real user verbatims (inspired by a Microsoft paper) and define personas such as a bypasser who just wants to escalate, a refund seeker, an AI skeptic, or a loyal long-time customer frustrated with earnings. The eval score went down after fine-tuning, which is what you want: an eval that is too easy gives no production insights and leaves less room to tune the agent for difficult users. An online pipeline with tracing and online graders is still needed once the agent is live.
when_to_use: Before launching a user-facing multi-turn agent to production
When you need confidence in agent performance without exposing live users
When you need a score that gates development and release
When simulating customer support or other user-facing conversations
When offline pass rates look suspiciously high
When you have real user message data to fine-tune the user simulator on
when_not_to_use: As the only signal once the agent is live; an online pipeline with tracing and online graders is also needed
When you have no real user verbatims to ground the simulation, since fine-tuning is not possible (not discussed in the source)
metric_or_method: Simulated conversations between agent and a persona-driven, fine-tuned user LLM, graded by an LLM judge and deterministic evaluators, with pass criteria acting as a launch gate; compare simulated-user behavior to real production verbatims and expect a lower score once realistic.
common_pitfalls: Producing a judge score that nothing gates, so it floats unused
Using live users as test data
Using a non-representative synthetic dataset
Using an off-the-shelf frontier model as the user, which sounds too nice and patient
Treating a ~90% pass rate as success without questioning realism
Being discouraged when the score drops after making the simulator realistic; an easy eval gives no production insight
source_excerpt: before we launch this AI agents to productions we want to go through a rigorous offline evaluation process to make sure that this agent uh actually has sufficient performance before we launch this to a live uh users. [...] have a use LM that plays plays out the complete multi-turn simulated conversation. Um, as well as a having a grader such as a LM as a judge um to be able to evaluate how good that interactions was. And then we have a launch gate, right?
one_liner: Stress-test agents with a fine-tuned, grumpy user LLM that plays full conversations, then gate launch on the scores.
codex_prompt_template:
Build an offline multi-turn simulation eval harness in Python for my [AGENT_DESCRIPTION] agent in the [DOMAIN, e.g. ride-share support] domain.

Requirements:
1. User simulator: an LLM-driven user defined by (a) intent, (b) world state, and (c) persona. Include these personas: [PERSONA_LIST, e.g. bypasser who wants escalation, refund seeker, AI skeptic, frustrated loyal customer]. Prompt it to behave like a real, often impatient user rather than a helpful assistant. Support swapping in a model fine-tuned on real user messages from [REAL_VERBATIMS_PATH], and include a script that prepares those verbatims as fine-tuning data.
2. Synthetic dataset: generate [DATASET_SIZE] scenarios covering [USE_CASES] with policy instructions per use case, and make the intent/persona/world-state mix match production distribution.
3. Simulation loop: alternate agent and user turns until the goal is reached, the user gives up, or [MAX_TURNS] is hit. Save full traces as JSONL.
4. Graders: an LLM-as-judge rubric for [SUCCESS_CRITERIA] plus deterministic checks (e.g. correct tool calls, policy violations, final state matches expected state).
5. Launch gate: compute pass rate overall and per persona/use case, and fail the run if it is below [LAUNCH_THRESHOLD].
6. Realism check: compare simulated user messages to real verbatims (length, tone, escalation rate, and a classifier or judge for realism) and flag when the simulator sounds too polite or when the pass rate looks suspiciously high (>[SUSPICIOUS_PASS_RATE]).

Output a runnable repo layout, core code, a sample config, and a short README on how to interpret scores and iterate on the agent.

name: Source-Grounded Verification Pass (Quotes and Citations)
definition: A verification method in which every quote, citation or evidence-backed finding an LLM produces is checked against the real source before use. It combines quote selection rules, a follow-up verification prompt against the source (quote check, contradiction check, confidence assessment), traceable links to the raw originals, and manual spot-checks.
explanation: LLMs generate statistically likely text rather than retrieving it, so they produce fictional or 'Frankenstein' quotes stitched from several sources, and present everything with equal confidence. The first AI pass is a hypothesis, not a final answer. The method has four parts. (1) Quote rules (Quote Verification Pass): define what a valid quote is, since 'verbatim' alone is ambiguous. Specify where it starts and stops, keep hedges and emotional language, cite participant ID and timestamp, never combine statements, and avoid tight length limits such as '≤12 words' that cause mash-ups. A second prompt then asks the model to confirm each quote exists in the source and label it VERIFIED, PARAPHRASE (with the actual wording) or NOT FOUND, with a location. In the author's example a majority of quotes were paraphrased. (2) Self-audit (LLM Self-Audit Verification Pass): the verification prompt also covers a contradiction check per participant (stated preferences vs. described behavior, confidence followed by hedging, opinions that soften later) and a confidence assessment that flags thinly evidenced findings and unclear stances. It ends with a verification summary of flags and recommended revisions. This adds a few minutes and can be run on past analyses. (3) Traceability (Traceable Outputs with Links to Raw Source): require agent outputs over support tickets, calls or recordings to carry exact quotes and direct links to the originals, as in Gumloop's root-cause report that references the original helpbot thread. A human can then spot-check the raw source and keep contact with customer signals instead of relying on opaque summaries. (4) Manual verification (Manual Verification of LLM-Generated Quotes): independently check each quote against a real source. Camille Fournier found none of the ChatGPT quotes for her book were real, and the replacement quote after pushback was also fake. If a quote cannot be confirmed, discard it. Re-prompting the model does not count as verification.
when_to_use: Before AI-generated qualitative analysis, with customer quotes, goes into a deck or stakeholder presentation
Before large product decisions rest on AI-derived customer evidence
When analyzing many interviews, tickets or calls where manual checking of every quote is impractical
When an LLM produces quotes, citations or attributed claims for publication or professional work
When agents analyze customer feedback and you want links back to raw sources
When the model sounds confident and the content looks plausible
As a quick audit of an existing AI analysis
when_not_to_use: When the output contains no direct quotes or attributed evidence to verify
For low-stakes exploratory work or simple tasks like rephrasing a sentence, where findings will not drive decisions
For purely mechanical tasks where raw-source inspection adds nothing (the source does not address this directly)
metric_or_method: Per-quote status label (VERIFIED / PARAPHRASE / NOT FOUND) with actual wording and location, produced by a verification prompt against the source. It is paired with a per-participant contradiction check, confidence flags, a verification summary with recommended revisions, and spot-checks of linked originals.
common_pitfalls: Prompting with tight length limits like '≤12 words', or leaving 'verbatim' undefined, which produces mash-up quotes
Trusting citations like [P03, 14:30], which can be faked even when the quote is invented
Assuming plausible, well-phrased quotes are real, or mistaking a good paraphrase for an actual quotation
Asking the model to correct itself and trusting the replacement without checking; re-prompting is not verification
Treating the first pass as final because the stories feel complete, and skipping contradiction checks between stated views and described behavior
Presenting a strong finding, such as a 'strong advocate', or a conclusion from a single response without checking evidence strength
Using summaries without links to the originals, losing touch with raw data; key insights in long threads often sit at the end
Assuming the model used the correct source document; a requested paper summary came back for a different paper
source_excerpt: Verification means asking AI to audit its own work, specifically looking for the errors you now know to expect. A verification prompt targets the specific failure modes: fabricated evidence, contradictions that change the picture, findings that sound solid but aren’t.
one_liner: Treat AI quotes as hypotheses: check each against the source and label it VERIFIED, PARAPHRASE or NOT FOUND.
codex_prompt_template: Build a source-grounded quote verification pipeline in [LANGUAGE, e.g. Python]. Inputs: (1) a folder of raw source files at [SOURCE_DIR] (interview transcripts, tickets or call notes, each with a participant ID), and (2) an LLM-generated analysis at [ANALYSIS_FILE] containing findings, each with supporting quotes, participant IDs and timestamps. Steps: (a) Parse every quote with its participant ID and timestamp. (b) Run a deterministic check first: normalize whitespace and punctuation, then search for the exact quote in the cited source and record the location. (c) For quotes not found exactly, use fuzzy matching with a threshold of [FUZZY_THRESHOLD, e.g. 0.85] to find the closest passage and label the quote PARAPHRASE with the actual source wording, otherwise NOT FOUND. Also flag quotes that appear to stitch together several non-adjacent passages (Frankenstein quotes). (d) Run an LLM verification prompt against each source using [LLM_MODEL] that does three things: a quote check (VERIFIED / PARAPHRASE / NOT FOUND with location), a per-participant contradiction check (stated preference vs. described behavior, confidence followed by hedging, opinions that soften), and a confidence assessment flagging findings backed by thin evidence or unclear stance. (e) Output a report with a per-quote status table, the percentage of VERIFIED, PARAPHRASE and NOT FOUND quotes, flagged contradictions, a verification summary with recommended revisions, and a link or file path and line number back to each raw source. (f) Draw a random sample of [SPOT_CHECK_N] VERIFIED quotes into a manual spot-check checklist for a human reviewer. Rules: never re-prompt the model to confirm its own quote without the source text in context, and treat any NOT FOUND quote as discarded until a human confirms it. Include unit tests using [SAMPLE_FIXTURES] with known real, paraphrased and fabricated quotes.

name: Staged Release via Trusted Testers and Research Previews
definition: A staged release and evaluation process for a new AI feature. The team dogfoods it internally, then widens exposure to a few customers or trusted testers. It then ships to progressively larger groups as a clearly labeled research preview, technical preview or opt-in Labs release. Qualitative feedback, real usage and safety findings gathered at each stage drive fixes and the decision to scale up to a broad launch.
explanation:
The core method is to gate readiness on real use rather than lab evals alone. Each stage widens the audience and adds a feedback source, and what is learned goes back into the model and product.

Internal dogfooding (Claude Code and Cowork) contributed the safety rationale. Claude Code was used inside Anthropic for roughly four or five months because the team was unsure it was safe as one of the first broadly used coding agents. Cowork looked good on alignment and evals, was tried internally and with a few customers, and was then released a little early as a research preview to confirm safety in the real world. Learnings feed both the product and safety sides. Cowork ships with a virtual machine and a security system built in, and is still rough around the edges.

Research preview shipping (Cat Wu on Claude Code) contributed the cadence and labeling. Almost all features ship as research previews after internal dogfooding. This lowers the commitment of shipping and lets the team release in a week or two. Dogfooded features are posted in a launch room so marketing and docs can announce them the next day. Buggy or unpolished releases are accepted if the core use case isn't blocked, because quick feedback lets the team fix them in the next release. Reproducible failures are collected from users and routed to a feedback channel.

The qualitative-to-real-query rollout (Robby Stein on AI Mode) contributed the tester-to-Labs ladder. A 5-10 person team built a rough first version with moments of brilliance that gave conviction to continue. About 500 external trusted testers, including friends and family, then sent screenshots of breakages, and the team wanted them to say when it was bad. Once testers were positive, an opt-in Labs release let anyone turn it on. Real query data showed what people used it for and let the team tune it. A US launch followed, then expansion to more countries and languages.

The technical preview with community feedback (Copilot) contributed scale-up signals and trust-building. The team invited tens of thousands, then hundreds of thousands, of developers. It watched social reactions such as tweets and Hacker News threads to judge when to scale. The community raised doubts about security, bugginess and model poisoning. The team treated skepticism as a signal and answered it with guided conversation, via Twitter, Hacker News and GitHub Discussions. It kept static analysis and unit tests in place and stated that Copilot is not a replacement for a developer.
when_to_use: Launching a new kind of AI product or agent whose safety or quality is hard to judge up front
The model is placed in a new setting, such as non-engineering tasks, where behavior is not yet known
You need candid failure reports and real-world behavior before exposing a broad audience
You want real usage and query data to tune the product before a full launch
Features are early and you want to lower the commitment and cost of shipping while iterating
Deciding when to move from prototype to scaling a team
Products facing questions about security, bugginess or training-data legitimacy
when_not_to_use: The product cannot be safely exposed even in preview form, with no guardrails in place
Lab and internal testing has not yet been done
Changes that block the core use case, or heavy multi-month infrastructure projects planned with PRDs
A quantitative offline benchmark is enough to ship a small change
There is no way to gather feedback from testers or opt-in users
As the sole quality evaluation; existing checks like static analysis and unit tests should stay
metric_or_method: Staged exposure with a feedback gate at each stage: internal dogfooding, then a few customers or trusted testers, then a labeled research preview, technical preview or opt-in Labs release at growing scale, then broad launch and expansion. Use qualitative reports, reproducible failures, real query data, social reactions and safety findings to decide when to advance and what to fix.
common_pitfalls: Assuming good alignment and eval results guarantee real-world safety
Releasing without guardrails; Cowork ships with a virtual machine and security system built in and is still rough around the edges
Shipping something buggy that blocks the core use case
Relying on friends and family as a durable signal; they won't keep using it unless it is genuinely useful to them
Judging only on moments of brilliance without broader testing, or skipping candid testers who say when it fails
Treating community skepticism as a nuisance rather than a signal to engage with
Letting the AI replace existing quality measures such as static analysis or unit tests
Feature overlap and confusion for new users, users struggling to keep pace with releases, and under-investing in product-side capacity for dialogue
source_excerpt: So for Claude Code, what we do is we actually ship almost all of our features in research preview. We clearly brand this when we ship something so that users know that this is an early product, this is just an idea, this is just something that we're trying to get feedback on and iterating on, and that this might not be supported forever. And what this does is it reduces our commitment for shipping something. We can just get something out in a week or two.
one_liner: Dogfood, then trusted testers, then labeled previews: let real usage gate each widening of your AI launch.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build a staged-release gating system for a new AI feature.

Feature description: [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]
Known risks (safety, security, quality): [KNOWN_RISKS]
Stages and audience sizes: internal dogfood [DOGFOOD_SIZE] -> trusted testers [TESTER_SIZE] -> labeled research/opt-in preview [PREVIEW_SIZE] -> broad launch
Feedback sources available: [FEEDBACK_SOURCES] (e.g. feedback channel, usage logs, social posts, support tickets)
Log/feedback data location or schema: [DATA_SOURCE]

Tasks:
1. Write a stage config (YAML or JSON) defining, for each stage: audience, entry criteria, feedback channels, and exit/advance criteria with numeric thresholds (e.g. reproducible-failure rate, severity-1 safety incidents, task-success or thumbs-up rate, retention of opted-in users).
2. Write Python code that ingests the feedback and usage data from [DATA_SOURCE], tags each item (bug, safety issue, quality failure, feature request, skepticism or trust concern) and severity, and de-duplicates reproducible failures.
3. Compute per-stage metrics and a go/no-go report: advance, hold and fix, or roll back. Cite the specific items that triggered each decision.
4. Cluster real queries or usage into top use cases and failure modes to guide tuning before the next stage.
5. Add a launch checklist covering preview labeling (early product, may not be supported), safety mitigations such as sandboxing, and a rollback plan.

Output the code, an example config filled in for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION], and a short sample report.

name: Suggestion Acceptance Rate
definition: Suggestion acceptance rate is the share of AI-generated suggestions (such as code autocomplete, inline refactors or drafted text) that users accept or commit, used as a proxy for the consistency and usefulness of probabilistic model output and the value users get from the feature.
explanation: The core method is acceptance rate = accepted suggestions / shown suggestions, observed through the user's accept or reject behavior. GitHub Copilot is the reference example: developers commit about 35% of its suggestions. Because LLM output is probabilistic, the rate indicates whether users can generally expect a good result. A 'good enough' level varies by use case and customer cohort, so the target should be calibrated by asking customers directly, 'Is this making your job easier?' Several variants and sub-steps extend this. (1) Per-language segmentation: for code, acceptance rate and lines-written share are read per programming language rather than as one global number. The roughly 40% of code written by Copilot applies to Python, and it ranges from the upper twenties to the forties across languages. Volume and diversity of training data correlate with suggestion quality. (2) UI/surface isolation: Windsurf's autocomplete acceptance rate tripled after moving from VSCode, where images had to be hacked in next to the cursor, to a custom IDE UI that could properly show and edit suggestions. The models were unchanged, so the change isolated the interface effect. A moderate rate (around 30%) can still be acceptable once users learn the product's hills and valleys and when dismissing a bad suggestion is cheap. Targets shift as capabilities and expectations change every few months. (3) Data-strategy comparison: in the Dragon physician product, a character acceptance rate compared synthetic fine-tuning against fine-tuning on 600,000 expert-annotated patient-physician interactions with continuous optimization. The rate rose from 30 to 60 percent, depending on the run, to about 83 percent, achieved by a small cross-functional group.
when_to_use: Evaluating features that produce discrete suggestions users can accept or reject, such as autocomplete or inline refactors
Needing a proxy for consistency and usefulness of probabilistic model output
Comparing UI or surface changes while holding the underlying model constant
Deciding whether to invest in a new interface versus a better model
Comparing quality across languages with different amounts of training data
Choosing between synthetic and expert-annotated real data for fine-tuning when an acceptance signal exists
when_not_to_use: When the feature has no explicit accept or reject interaction to observe
As an absolute benchmark across use cases or cohorts, since a good-enough rate varies
As the only quality signal; it is one of several metrics (lines written, qualitative feedback)
As the only signal for agentic features where users review large changes (no metric is given for this case)
metric_or_method: Acceptance rate = accepted suggestions / shown suggestions, segmented by language, cohort or UI surface. Compare before and after UI changes with the same model, or across fine-tuning data sources (synthetic vs expert-annotated), and calibrate the target by asking customers 'Is this making your job easier?'
common_pitfalls: Assuming one universal 'good' acceptance rate instead of calibrating per use case and customer cohort
Relying on the number alone without qualitative feedback on whether the AI makes users' jobs easier
Quoting a headline stat such as 40% without noting it is language-specific
Attributing acceptance changes to the model when the UI or surface was the cause
Assuming a low rate means the feature is annoying; users learn when to ignore suggestions
Expecting a static target; capabilities and user expectations shift every few months and need reevaluation
Assuming synthetic fine-tuning data is sufficient; expert annotation made a large difference in the Dragon example
Treating data improvement as one-off rather than a continuous optimization loop
source_excerpt: Just to put a fine point on that stat, it is 40% is specifically for Python developers. Candidly, it varies depending upon the language. Because as you might imagine, some languages have better representation in the public domain than others. And usually both the volume and the diversity of training data correlates with the quality of suggestions, which is then represented by either the number of lines written or the acceptance rate or any one of a number of other metrics.
one_liner: Divide accepted by shown suggestions, then slice by language, UI surface and cohort to see where AI output earns trust.
codex_prompt_template: I have a log of AI suggestion events for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION] (e.g., code autocomplete, inline refactor, drafted text) stored in [EVENT_LOG_SOURCE] with fields like [SUGGESTION_ID_FIELD], [SHOWN_EVENT], [ACCEPT_EVENT], [REJECT_OR_DISMISS_EVENT], and segmentation columns [SEGMENT_COLUMNS] (e.g., language, user cohort, UI surface, model version). Write [LANGUAGE, e.g., Python/SQL] code that: 1) computes acceptance rate = accepted suggestions / shown suggestions overall and per segment, with 95% confidence intervals; 2) deduplicates suggestions and handles partial or edited accepts according to [ACCEPTANCE_DEFINITION]; 3) compares acceptance rate before vs after a UI/surface change in [CHANGE_DATE_OR_EXPERIMENT_ID] while holding the model constant, using a significance test; 4) compares acceptance rate across model or fine-tuning data variants [VARIANT_LIST] (e.g., synthetic vs expert-annotated); 5) flags segments whose rate falls below the target threshold [TARGET_ACCEPTANCE_RATE], which was calibrated from customer feedback to the question 'Is this making your job easier?'; 6) outputs a summary table and a trend chart by week. Include unit tests with a small synthetic dataset.

name: Sycophancy Regression Metric per Release
definition: A standing metric for model sycophancy, meaning the tendency to say things that sound good in the moment, that is checked on every release to confirm the model has not regressed on it.
explanation: Nick Turley describes an update that made the model more likely to tell users what sounded good, such as 'You're totally right. You should break up with your boyfriend.' It was caught through contact with reality and not through lab testing. OpenAI's response was to introduce new measurement techniques. Whenever a model meets reality and a problem surfaces, the team goes back and makes sure good metrics exist for it. They now measure sycophancy with every release so it does not regress, and GPT-5 improved on it. The incident also pushed them to state publicly what they are optimizing ChatGPT for. The auto-caption renders the metric name as 'sick efficiency'.
when_to_use: When a model's behavior could validate users harmfully (relationship, health or life advice)
After an incident in production reveals a behavior you had no metric for
As a release gate for every model update
when_not_to_use: Where the product has no conversational advice or opinion-giving behavior to over-validate
metric_or_method: A sycophancy metric tracked on each release with a no-regression requirement, plus a stated policy on what the model is optimized for (helping users achieve their goals, not engagement).
common_pitfalls: Optimizing for what feels good in the moment or for engagement
Only discovering behavior issues in a lab setting, without feedback from real users and domain experts such as physicians
Writing off the behavior as funny instead of treating it as a serious risk
source_excerpt: So we instilled new measurement techniques. Whenever we put these models in contact with reality and we learn about a problem, we actually go back and make sure we have good metrics for this stuff. So we measure sick efficiency now with every release to make sure we don't regress and actually improve on that metric. GPT-5 is an improvement, which is really exciting for me, but we have more work from there.
one_liner: Score every release for sycophancy so a model that tells users what they want to hear never ships again.
codex_prompt_template: Build a sycophancy regression eval for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. 1) Write a dataset generator that creates [DATASET_SIZE] test cases across risk areas such as [RISK_DOMAINS] (e.g. relationship, health, career, factual disagreement). Each case should include a user message that states a flawed belief or a risky plan and asks for validation, and a pushback variant where the user challenges a correct model answer. 2) Write a runner that sends each case to the model at [CANDIDATE_MODEL_VERSION] and the baseline [BASELINE_MODEL_VERSION]. 3) Add an LLM-judge rubric that labels each response as sycophantic (flatters, caves, or validates without basis) or appropriately candid, and returns a short rationale. Calibrate it against [HUMAN_LABELED_SAMPLES]. 4) Compute the sycophancy rate per risk domain with confidence intervals. 5) Add a CI release gate that fails if the candidate's sycophancy rate exceeds the baseline by more than [REGRESSION_THRESHOLD]. 6) Output a markdown report with the worst-offending examples. Use Python and [EVAL_FRAMEWORK].

name: Synthetic Test Input Generation
definition: Use an LLM or agent to generate test inputs, such as simulated user messages, personas, scenarios, adversarial prompts, and variants of past failures. These inputs bootstrap traces for error analysis and populate offline eval datasets when real examples are scarce or need supplementing.
explanation: The core method is to ask an AI to generate many diverse inputs from given context, attributes, or examples, then run them through the system or an existing prompt template as test cases or in-context examples. Synthetic Bootstrap for Test Cases contributes the basic recipe: prompt the AI to generate multiple examples (e.g., ten user personas from a defined set of attributes) from given inputs, which works even without a domain expert. Synthetic Inputs to Bootstrap Traces applies this before launch: error analysis needs traces, so the preferred option is to recruit friends and dog-food the app. If that is not possible, have an LLM role-play users at scale, then still review the resulting traces by hand, since there is a correct way to do this. Production-Grounded Synthetic Dataset with Mutation addresses representativeness: do not just prompt an LLM for ~50 test queries. Instead, sample real production conversations to supplement the offline set and mutate criteria to cover golden paths and edge cases (the Lyft support example). Synthetic Evals and Red-Team Datasets adds generation with agents seeded with context (e.g., via RAG), past data, or the existing eval set to produce customer-like scenarios, including adversarial ones. Red-team prompts become eval cases. A feedback loop takes everything that failed and generates more things that could fail. Synthetic data supplements human-scored real traffic and does not replace it.
when_to_use: The app is pre-production and no traces exist, and you can't recruit friends or dog-food it
You have little or no production traffic or real-world examples
You need many diverse inputs quickly, such as personas or test inputs for an existing prompt template
You have production traffic and want to supplement the offline set with edge-case coverage by mutating criteria
You want adversarial, red-team, or security coverage
You want to expand coverage by generating variants of past failures
when_not_to_use: You already have real production traces, which are preferred
As a replacement for human-scored real traffic, which keeps evals current
As a substitute for actually reading the resulting data
When no production data exists and you want production-grounded mutation (the source does not cover this case)
metric_or_method: Seed an LLM or agent with real context (sampled production data, past failures, existing evals, defined attributes), generate and mutate inputs to cover golden paths, edge cases, and adversarial prompts, run them through the system, then review the traces with error analysis. Prompt pattern: "Generate ten examples of [examples] for [context]. Here are the inputs: [inputs]."

name: Task Time-Horizon Metric
definition: A capability metric that measures the length of task, in time, an AI model or agent can complete or work on autonomously: the METR-style version reports the longest software engineering task completed at a given success rate (50% and 80%), plotted across successive models to show the trend and extrapolate it for product planning. A related variant frames the same idea as 'leash length', meaning how long an agent can work before a human must intervene, and whether leaving it running is economically profitable.
explanation: Core method: take software engineering tasks, measure the longest task length a model can complete at a stated success rate, and plot earlier and newer models on the same chart so the trend is visible. Sherwin Wu's contribution is the 50%/80% reporting: frontier models handle multi-hour tasks about 50% of the time, but only tasks of just under an hour about 80% of the time. He uses the trend to anticipate product design: today's products are tuned for minutes-long tasks (Codex suits at most about 10-minute tasks), and if models reach multi-hour or day-long tasks, products will look different, for example with feedback mechanisms for long-running agents. Mann's contribution is the planning use: internalize the METR trend and build for six months or a year ahead, since things that work 20% of the time will start working 100% of the time. He credits this thinking with the success of Claude Code. Shipper's 'leash length' variant is a looser, autonomy-based framing: AI progress shows in how long a leash you can give it, from tab-complete in Copilot, to a single ChatGPT response, to 20-30 minutes of autonomous work with Claude Opus 4 and deep research. His proposed endpoint is agents that can run indefinitely where leaving them on is economically profitable, counting both cost and value. He notes it can be gamed by looping Claude forever, so he means widespread adoption of agents doing useful work all the time. Together: use the trend, not a single number, to decide what to prototype now and what to build for later.
when_to_use: Planning product bets on agent capability trajectories
Deciding which features to prototype now that don't yet fully work
Assessing how capable frontier models are on long-running agentic or software engineering tasks
Tracking progress across model generations to plan agent product design
Assessing how autonomous an agent has become relative to previous generations
Thinking about the economic viability of long-running agents
when_not_to_use: Evaluating the quality of your current shipped feature or a specific product workflow's correctness; this is a general model-capability measure
Tasks that are not software-engineering-like, since the benchmark as described tracks software engineering tasks
As a rigorous quality metric for individual outputs
When the agent is just looped without delivering useful work
metric_or_method: Maximum task length (in time) a model can complete at a given success rate (50% and 80%), plotted across successive model releases and extrapolated to plan 6-12 months ahead; complemented by how long an agent can work autonomously before human intervention and whether leaving it running is profitable.
common_pitfalls: Building only for today's capability level or designing only for minutes-long tasks, missing the trajectory toward multi-hour or day-long tasks
Reading current numbers as static when the trend across models is the key insight; failing to internalize the exponential trend
Assuming a model that succeeds 50% of the time on multi-hour tasks is reliable enough for unattended use; the 80% horizon is much shorter (just under an hour)
Gaming the leash-length metric by running an agent in a pointless loop
Ignoring cost and value, as the 'profitable' bar requires both
source_excerpt: you can tell how much better AI is getting by how long a leash you can give it to do work. [...] And so I think a good definition of AGI is when does it become economically profitable for people to run agents indefinitely? [...] It's partly the cost and partly the value. And obviously, you can game this a little bit and be like, "Cool, I'm just going to tell Claude to run in a loop forever." But I'm talking about more than that
one_liner: Plot the longest task your agent finishes at 50% and 80% success across models, then build for where the trend lands.
codex_prompt_template: Write a Python script that computes a task time-horizon metric for [AGENT_OR_MODEL_NAME] from my eval results in [RESULTS_FILE_PATH]. Each row has task_id, human_time_minutes (estimated human completion time), and success (0/1), optionally grouped by model_version in [MODEL_VERSION_COLUMN]. Steps: (1) bucket tasks by log-scaled human time; (2) fit a logistic regression of success probability vs. log(human_time_minutes) for each model version; (3) report the task length where predicted success crosses 50% and 80% (the time horizons), with bootstrap confidence intervals; (4) plot horizon vs. release date for all model versions on a log-y chart and fit an exponential trend line to estimate the doubling time; (5) extrapolate the 50% and 80% horizons to [PLANNING_HORIZON_MONTHS] months ahead; (6) print a table mapping [CANDIDATE_FEATURES_WITH_TASK_LENGTHS] to 'ship now', 'prototype now', or 'build for later' based on whether their typical task length falls under the current 80% horizon, between the 80% and 50% horizons, or beyond the projected horizon. Also add an optional 'leash length' column: median minutes of autonomous work before human intervention from [INTERVENTION_LOG_PATH], plus cost per hour vs. value per hour to flag whether leaving the agent running is profitable.

name: Three-Layer Model Safety Evaluation (Interpretability, Lab Evals, In-the-Wild)
definition: A layered approach to assessing model safety and alignment. Layer 1 is alignment and mechanistic interpretability, which means inspecting what happens in the model's neurons during training. Layer 2 is evals, which test the model in synthetic situations in a lab. Layer 3 is observing how the model behaves in the wild.
explanation: Boris Cherny describes Anthropic's safety study as three layers. The lowest layer looks inside the model, for example monitoring whether a neuron related to deception is activating. The second layer places the model in a 'Petri dish' with synthetic situations and checks whether it does the right thing, is aligned, and is safe. The third layer watches real-world behavior. He stresses that as models become more sophisticated, the third layer matters more, because a model can look very good on the first two layers and not great on the third. Lenny summarizes it as observing the model's thinking, running tests and evals, and releasing early.
when_to_use: Evaluating the safety and alignment of agentic models that act in the world
Deciding whether lab results alone are enough to ship a new agent or product
Launching a model in a new setting, such as non-engineering tasks
when_not_to_use: Using only lab evals as proof of safety for a sophisticated agent
Low-stakes features where interpretability-level inspection is not available or needed
metric_or_method: Layered assessment: (1) mechanistic interpretability and alignment monitoring of model internals, (2) synthetic-scenario evals in a controlled lab setting, (3) observation of real-world behavior after release.
common_pitfalls: Trusting good results on alignment and evals alone when real-world behavior may differ
Skipping real-world observation as the model becomes more capable and sophisticated
source_excerpt: The lowest level is alignment, and mechanistic interpretability. So, this is when we train the model we want to make sure that it's safe. [...] The second layer is evals, and this is, essentially, a laboratory setting, the model is in a Petri dish, and you study it. And you put in the synthetic situation and just say, "Okay. Model, what do you do?" And, "Are you doing the right thing? Is it aligned? Is it safe?" [...] And then the third layer is seeing how the model behaves in the wild. And as the model gets more sophisticated, this becomes so important, because it might look very good on these first two layers, but not great on the third one.
one_liner: Check model safety three ways: peek inside its neurons, stress-test in a lab, then watch it in the wild.
codex_prompt_template:
I'm building a three-layer safety evaluation plan for [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION], an AI system that [AGENT_ACTIONS_OR_TOOLS]. Generate code and a written plan covering:

Layer 1 (internals/alignment monitoring): If I have access to model internals or activations [YES/NO], write a script that [INTERNAL_SIGNAL_TO_MONITOR, e.g. deception-related features or probe outputs] and flags anomalies. If I don't, propose proxy signals such as reasoning-trace inspection or chain-of-thought audits.

Layer 2 (lab evals): Create a synthetic scenario suite of [NUM_SCENARIOS] test cases targeting [RISK_CATEGORIES, e.g. deception, unsafe tool use, reward hacking]. For each, include the setup prompt, expected safe behavior, and an automated pass/fail grader. Output as a runnable harness in [LANGUAGE/FRAMEWORK].

Layer 3 (in-the-wild monitoring): Write a production monitoring pipeline over [LOG_OR_TRACE_SOURCE] that samples real interactions, detects [UNSAFE_BEHAVIORS], computes a rate per [TIME_WINDOW], and alerts above [THRESHOLD].

Finally, add a cross-layer report that compares Layer 2 pass rates against Layer 3 incident rates to surface gaps where the model looks safe in the lab but misbehaves in real use, plus a ship/hold decision checklist and a staged rollout plan for [NEW_SETTING_OR_USER_SEGMENT].

name: Toxicity and Offensive Content Detection
definition: A method for checking whether an AI system's output contains harmful, offensive or undesirable language, or an inappropriate tone, using explicit definitions and context-aware detection (a judge LLM or trained detection model) instead of simple word block lists, and validating the results against human labels and developer feedback.
explanation: The core method is to classify each output as acceptable or not on toxicity, offensiveness or tone, using a detector that understands context. Two members contributed different variants. The Toxicity and Tone Eval member is a standard eval criterion in which a judge LLM labels each response using explicit definitions, validated against human labels. It asks whether the agent is outputting harmful or undesirable language, and extends to tone checks. Its worked example judges whether a trip planner agent's response is friendly, defined as using an exclamation point and being generally helpful with never a negative tone. When the eval disagreed with a human label, the exclamation-point requirement looked too strict. This check helps end-user applications spot users trying to exploit the system or the LLM responding inappropriately. The Model-Based Offensive Content Detection member is the filtering variant drawn from the Copilot experience. Early Copilot had no filter, which gave a distracting, bad experience. A simple block list followed, which proved fraught with peril: the team became editors of language, and developers reported that blocked words offended them or stopped them from getting value. The team then partnered with Azure's Responsible AI group, whose models detect patently offensive content and account for words that are offensive in one context but reasonable in another, such as medical software. Developer feedback on what was blocked or offensive was used to find where filtering went wrong. Together: define the criteria explicitly, use a context-aware judge or trained model rather than word lists, and check results against human labels and developer feedback.
when_to_use: End-user applications where harmful or inappropriate language would reach users
Detecting users trying to exploit the system or the LLM responding inappropriately
Checking the agent keeps a friendly tone even when the user gives negative feedback
Generative products that could output offensive, slanderous or politically charged content
When a word block list produces false positives that hurt the user experience
when_not_to_use: When you lack a trusted detection model and need a quick first-pass safeguard (the Copilot team started with a block list)
metric_or_method: A judge LLM or responsible-AI detection model labels each output (e.g. toxic/offensive or not, friendly or not) using explicit definitions and context, validated against human labels and developer feedback on what was blocked or offensive.
common_pitfalls: Ambiguous definitions of toxicity or friendliness
Overly strict criteria, such as requiring an exclamation point, that disagree with human labels
Block lists force the team to decide which words are acceptable, making them editors of language
Words that are offensive in some contexts are reasonable in others, e.g. medical software
Over-blocking can stop developers from getting good value from the product
Skipping the filter entirely produces a distracting, bad experience
Not validating the judge or detector against human labels or developer feedback
source_excerpt: **[Toxicity/tone](https://docs.arize.com/phoenix/evaluation/how-to-evals/running-pre-tested-evals/toxicity):** Is the agent outputting harmful or undesirable language?
one_liner: Swap word block lists for context-aware judges that flag toxic or off-tone outputs, validated against human labels.
codex_prompt_template: Build a toxicity and tone eval for my [FEATURE_DESCRIPTION]. Steps: (1) Write explicit rubric definitions for 'toxic/offensive' and for tone criteria [TONE_CRITERIA], including context exceptions such as [CONTEXT_EXCEPTIONS] (e.g. medical terms that are acceptable in context). (2) Implement an LLM-judge in Python that takes an output and its context and returns JSON {label: acceptable|unacceptable, category, reason}. Use [JUDGE_MODEL]. (3) Run it on [DATASET_PATH], a sample of [DATASET_SIZE] outputs, and also run a naive word block list [BLOCKLIST] as a baseline. (4) Compare both against human labels in [HUMAN_LABELS_PATH]: report precision, recall, F1, Cohen's kappa, and list the false positives and false negatives of each method. (5) Output disagreements between judge and human labels so I can tell whether the rubric is too strict (e.g. a tone rule that demands an exclamation point) or the judge is wrong, and suggest rubric revisions. Include a way to add developer or user feedback on flagged or blocked outputs as new labeled examples.

name: Trajectory-Level Agent Evaluation
definition: Evaluating an agent by examining its intermediate trajectory (actions, reasoning, self-reports, inefficiency, repeated failures and reward hacking) in addition to final-answer correctness, so that hidden problems are caught and mistakes can be located and fixed with specific feedback.
explanation: The core method is to inspect and grade the intermediate steps of an agent's trajectory rather than only checking the final outcome. Chen's contribution (Trajectory-Level Evaluation) is the rationale: a model can reach the correct answer in odd ways, such as failing 50 times before randomly landing on a correct number, working very inefficiently, or almost reward-hacking its way there. Since trajectories can be long, checking only the final answer discards information about intermediate behavior. Sometimes you want the model to reflect its way to the answer, and sometimes you want it to one-shot it, so the desired path shape depends on the task. Two review variants apply this in practice, mostly qualitatively. Lazar's 'Read the Agent Output, Not the Code' is a lightweight habit for non-engineer builders: skip reading the generated code, give the agent rules and docs, have it report what it changed and how to test it, then read those reports each step. This reveals when the agent is lost or claims a fix that did not happen, and shows what the agent thinks is possible, building judgment. You still need to test the result yourself because agents are agreeable and may claim a fix that did not work. Andreessen and Lenny's 'Inspect the Agent's Work to Locate Errors' watches the agent's work and thinking, combined with domain grounding, to pinpoint where it went wrong and give specific corrective feedback, like feedback to a colleague that requires understanding their thinking. You can also ask the AI to explain why it did something and to critique itself. Together: grade or review the path, not only the destination, then use what you find to intervene precisely.
when_to_use: When agent tasks involve long multi-step trajectories
When correct final answers may hide inefficient, lucky or reward-hacked behavior
When an agent's result is wrong and you need to know why before giving feedback
When reviewing agentic builders (Lovable, Cursor, Claude Code) as a non-engineer and checking progress one task at a time
When you want to learn what is and is not possible with the tool
When you want to give precise corrective feedback to a coding agent
when_not_to_use: When only the final output matters and the path is irrelevant (not explicitly discussed in the source)
When you lack enough grounding to interpret what the agent is doing
When you are not confident the model's code can be trusted, since skipping code review relies on that trust
When the agent cannot see the problem, such as with third-party integrations, since its report will not reveal it
metric_or_method: Inspect and grade intermediate steps of the trajectory (actions, reasoning, agent-reported changes and test instructions) in addition to final-answer correctness; optionally ask the agent to explain and critique itself, verify claims by testing, and give specific corrective feedback.
common_pitfalls: Rewarding lucky correct answers after many failures
Missing reward hacking or inefficiency when only the final answer is checked
Believing the agent's claim that a problem is fixed without testing, since agents are obedient and agreeable
Telling the AI only that it is wrong, which gives it nothing to act on
Having no understanding of why the agent produced a result, so you cannot tell what to ask for next
Getting angry at the tool, which makes it spend tokens apologizing instead of solving the problem
Giving no reference files or architecture context, so the agent reads everything and uses up its token allocation
source_excerpt: religiously reading the agent output. Not the code output. I don't care about the code. The syntax is none of my interest. It's what the agent tells me that matters to me. I put a lot of trust in LLMs and AI these days, and I understand that there may be some people that are not as confident as I am. I just feel that the models today are good enough for me to trust in their syntax output. However, I'm concerned about the agent output because of the two limitations that I want to tackle on next.
one_liner: Grade the agent's path, not just its answer: catch lucky guesses, wasted steps, and reward hacking.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me build a trajectory-level evaluation for an AI agent. Agent description: [AGENT_DESCRIPTION]. Task type: [TASK_TYPE]. Trajectory log format: [TRAJECTORY_FORMAT] (e.g., JSON list of thoughts, tool calls, observations, and final answer). Sample trajectories are in [TRAJECTORY_PATH].

Write a Python script that:
1. Parses each trajectory into steps (reasoning, action, observation, agent self-report).
2. Computes final-answer correctness against [GROUND_TRUTH_SOURCE].
3. Flags process problems even when the final answer is correct: repeated failed or identical actions (retries above [MAX_RETRIES]), step count above [EXPECTED_STEP_BUDGET], lucky guessing (an answer that appears without supporting evidence in earlier steps), and possible reward hacking (e.g., [REWARD_HACKING_PATTERNS] such as editing tests, hardcoding outputs, or bypassing checks).
4. Compares claims in the agent's self-reports (e.g., 'I fixed X') against actual evidence such as tool outputs or test results, and flags unverified claims.
5. Uses an LLM judge with a rubric to grade each step as productive, redundant, or wrong, and identifies the first step where the trajectory went off track, with a short, specific corrective-feedback note.
6. Outputs a per-trajectory report (outcome score, process score, first-error step, flags) and an aggregate table showing the rate of 'correct answer but bad process' cases.

Include a small example run and note where the desired path shape (one-shot vs. reflective) for [TASK_TYPE] should change the thresholds.

name: Transition failure matrix
definition: A chart where rows represent the last successful step and columns represent the step where the failure occurred, built from analyzing traces of failed agent interactions, to show where the agent's workflow breaks down.
explanation: An agent's workflow is a series of states, like an assembly line, such as generating_sql then executing_sql. A single pass/fail on the final outcome is not diagnostic. Mapping failed traces onto the matrix reveals hotspots, for example that the agent fails most often when executing the SQL it just generated or when misinterpreting a tool output. This turns debugging a complex agent into a focused, data-driven investigation.
when_to_use: Debugging agents that execute multi-step sequences of actions or tool calls
When a final-outcome pass/fail is not diagnostic enough
when_not_to_use: Single-step or non-agentic systems (e.g., one-shot prompt completion) where there is no sequence of states to transition between
When you have no traces of failed interactions or the traces lack step-level logging, so last-successful and failing steps cannot be identified
When failures are caused by the quality of the final output (e.g., tone, relevance, hallucination) rather than a breakdown at a specific workflow step
Very early development with only a handful of failed traces, where counts per cell are too sparse to reveal meaningful hotspots
metric_or_method: Matrix with rows = last successful step, columns = failing step, cells = counts of failed traces.
common_pitfalls: Relying only on the final-outcome pass/fail
Guessing which step breaks instead of using trace data
source_excerpt: The rows of the matrix represent the last successful step, and the columns represent the step where the failure occurred. By analyzing traces of failed agent interactions and mapping them onto this matrix, you can quickly spot hotspots.
one_liner: Map where agents break: rows are the last good step, columns the failing step, cells count failed traces.
codex_prompt_template:
You are helping me debug a multi-step AI agent by building a transition failure matrix.

Context:
- Agent description: [AGENT_DESCRIPTION]
- Ordered list of workflow states/steps (e.g., plan, generate_sql, execute_sql, interpret_result, respond): [STEP_LIST]
- Trace file or format: [TRACE_PATH_OR_SCHEMA] (each trace has a list of steps with a step name, status, and optional error/output)
- How to determine a trace failed: [FAILURE_CRITERIA]

Tasks:
1. Write a Python script (pandas) that loads the traces and keeps only failed ones.
2. For each failed trace, identify the last successful step (row) and the step where the failure occurred (column). Use a 'START' row if the first step fails and handle traces where the failure step cannot be determined by putting them in an 'UNKNOWN' column.
3. Build a matrix with rows = last successful step, columns = failing step, cells = count of failed traces. Also output a version normalized by total failed traces.
4. Render it as a heatmap (matplotlib or seaborn) and print the top 5 transitions by count with percentages.
5. For each of the top 3 hotspots, sample 3 example trace IDs and print the error/output snippet so I can read them.
6. Add a short summary of likely root causes per hotspot and suggest a targeted eval or unit test for each.

Include a small synthetic trace sample for [AGENT_DESCRIPTION] so I can run the script end to end, and keep the code modular so I can rerun it as new traces come in.

name: Trusted User Feedback Panel
definition: A human-in-the-loop evaluation approach where you find a small group of people who are better than others at articulating what makes a model or harness combination good, and rely on them for rapid, accurate feedback.
explanation: Cat Wu notes that many people give feedback but not everyone's is equally qualified. Finding about five trusted people is important for very fast feedback. She names Amanda, who shapes Claude's character, and the Claude Code team as examples of strong evaluators. Amanda can articulate the goals and what is successful in a very ambiguous task.
when_to_use: Evaluating subjective model qualities like character, tone, or feel
You need fast feedback on a new model or harness combination
Ground truth is ambiguous and hard to verify automatically
when_not_to_use: When success can be verified programmatically, as in coding, where it is easier to check success
metric_or_method: Qualitative expert feedback from a curated group of about five trusted evaluators who can articulate what makes a model or harness good.
common_pitfalls: Weighting all feedback equally when not everyone's feedback is as qualified
Relying on a large, undifferentiated feedback pool instead of a few trusted voices
source_excerpt: The other thing that helps is to figure out who are the users who you trust the most to give you accurate feedback about the model. Usually there's a handful of people who are much better than others at articulating what makes a specific model or model harness combination good, and there's a lot of people who will give you feedback, but not everyone's feedback is as qualified. And so finding a group of those five people you trust is really important for getting very fast feedback.
one_liner: Skip the crowd: rank evaluators by signal, then rely on your five sharpest testers for fast model feedback.

I have feedback from [NUM_CANDIDATE_REVIEWERS] reviewers in [FEEDBACK_DATA_PATH]. Write Python that does the following. 1) Load the feedback and compute a reliability score for each reviewer: agreement with the consensus or with a gold set in [GOLD_LABELS_PATH], consistency on repeated items, and how specific and actionable their written comments are. 2) Rank the reviewers and pick the top [PANEL_SIZE, default 5] as the trusted panel. 3) Generate a lightweight feedback form for the panel with a 1-5 rating per quality, a free-text 'why', and a slot to paste a failing example. 4) Write a function that takes feedback from a new model or harness version and summarizes it into a ranked list of themes and regressions versus [BASELINE_VERSION]. 5) Flag when panel members disagree strongly so the disagreement can be discussed. name: Use-Case Category Hill Climbing
definition: A process of defining a set of realistic use cases (real user tasks, hero question and ideal-answer pairs, a community checklist, or workflow stages), grouping them into categories, scoring the AI on each category, and iteratively improving the system while tracking whether scores rise over time.
explanation: The core method is to collect the tasks users actually want done, or define hero use cases that pair a desired question with an excellent answer, and turn them into evals. Group them into categories or lifecycle stages, score each one, and hill climb: improve the system (via infrastructure fixes, fine-tuning, or model upgrades) and check each week whether scores are rising. Variants and sub-steps: (1) Task-category hill climbing on real user tasks quantifies real delegated tasks by category and tracks them week over week. Concrete failing workflows (e.g. a mouse that could not click the right part of a Salesforce dashboard, or an agent that could not see the screen pixels) go to the infrastructure team, and the fix is confirmed with the affected users. (2) Four-stage lifecycle eval, used for Anthropic's CASH growth automation, splits the shipping lifecycle into identifying opportunities, building, testing against quality and brand bars, and analyzing results. Each stage is scored and hill climbed separately, and re-tested as new models arrive. It has been tried only at small scale (copy changes, minor UI tweaks) and does not cover cross-functional stakeholder management. (3) Week-on-week improvement tracking adds a trend check per area: are things getting better, are people spending less time, and are results improving. Sustained positive trend signals the initiative is scaling while humans remain in the loop. (4) Use-case checklist pass rate uses an external list of about 50 realistic use cases as a pre-launch readiness check. Cowork completing 48 of 50 was judged 'pretty good'. This is an informal pass-count bar. (5) Hero-use-case evals, from OpenAI's deep research, design evals alongside the product, fine-tune the model, and read rising eval scores as a sign of having a product. (6) Prompted-baseline principle: prefer evals where a prompted baseline scores lowest so a trained model has room to climb, and run regression checks on other intelligence evals to avoid 'brain damage'. Refresh saturated benchmarks with frontier evals.
when_to_use: Evaluating agents that do delegated, multi-step work where 'it just works' reliability matters more than new features
Building a new AI product around a few clearly defined hero use cases when eval and product design happen together
Training or fine-tuning a model for a specific product behavior and needing evals that show gains over prompting alone
Finding the weakest stage of an end-to-end AI workflow, and re-scoring on each new model release
Early automation with a human in the loop, when deciding how fast to reduce human involvement
Quick pre-launch readiness check when a ready-made list of realistic use cases exists
When a few backend blockers (login, clicking, visibility) stall whole task categories
when_not_to_use: When you have no real users, task data, or defined use cases yet
When you need an absolute pass/fail quality bar or statistically rigorous measurement, since trend and pass-count measures are informal
When you cannot change or improve the system and only want a static one-time measurement
When you are only prototyping with prompts and not training a model (for the prompted-baseline variant)
Large cross-functional projects where stakeholder alignment is the main work, or single-step features with no multi-stage loop
metric_or_method: Build a set of use cases (real tasks, hero question and ideal-answer pairs, or workflow stages) grouped by category. Score success per category, track it week over week alongside human time spent, route concrete failures to owners, improve the system, and run regression checks on other evals.
common_pitfalls: Relying only on an abstract dashboard number instead of concrete failing cases routed to owners
Hill climbing on dimensions users do not feel rather than problems that stall task progress
Using a checklist that does not represent the real task distribution, or an undefined threshold like 48/50, with a pass count that says nothing about how well each task was done
Aggregating across categories or stages and missing one that is stagnating, or looking only at outputs and ignoring human time spent
Extrapolating from small-scale results (copy, minor UI) to larger work, or not re-testing as models change
Using evals the prompted baseline already passes, which give little signal, or letting benchmarks saturate
Optimizing one behavior at the cost of other capabilities without regression checks
Treating research and product as separate teams so the product team is just an API consumer and misses the iterative feedback loop

name: Validating an LLM Judge Against Human Labels
definition: Before trusting an LLM judge, hand-label a set of examples as pass/fail, split them into train, dev, and test sets, and compare the judge's verdicts to the human labels. Use separate measures of how well it catches failures and how well it passes good outputs (TPR/TNR, precision/recall, confusion matrix) instead of raw agreement. Re-validate whenever the criteria, judge prompt, or model change.
explanation:
The core method: take the human labels you produced during error analysis (axial coding), run the judge on the same items with the human verdicts hidden, and compare. Overall agreement is the trap metric. If a failure occurs about 10% of the time, a judge that always says pass scores 90% agreement (even a hardcoded one that never calls an LLM). So compute TPR (of truly passing items, the share judged pass) and TNR (of truly failing items, the share judged fail), and require both to be high. Several members framed this differently: precision and recall against human ground truth, or a human-vs-judge confusion matrix where you inspect both off-diagonal cells (human fail/judge pass and the reverse) and refine the prompt until they shrink. The acceptable tradeoff depends on the product: for medical advice false negatives cost more, while for a creative writing assistant false positives may be worse. Knowing TPR/TNR also lets you statistically correct a judge's raw pass rate to estimate the true failure rate. Some residual misalignment is acceptable.

Sub-step: data splitting. Using the whole dataset to build and test the judge causes overfitting. Because no model weights are trained, the data only informs the prompt, so splits differ from classic ML. About 100 labeled pass/fail examples are split into train (10-20%, source of few-shot examples), dev (40-45%, prompt iteration, a meta-evaluation of your evaluator), and test (40-45%, untouched, final overfit check).

Variant: golden-dataset calibration. Build question/answer/trusted-human-score items (about 30 to start), hide the scores, have the judge score them, and measure percent agreement. Target roughly 80-85%, since human teams agree only about 80% of the time. 100% is a red flag for sycophancy, bias poisoning, or overfitting. On disagreements, look for knowledge gaps (e.g., missing policy), add context, and re-run. Upgrade to a modestly larger model only if maxed-out context still fails. In the demo, agreement reached 27 of 30. Also watch for case-sensitive output mismatches that inflate disagreement.

Variant: CI agreement gate. Make the test pass only when agreement falls in a band (at least 80% and not 100%), log the percentage, and pin the judge model version, since a model name is an alias and an underlying change would silently shift results. This gives ahead-of-time reliability, with a harness picking up the slack at runtime.

Variant: criteria drift. Criteria are discovered by looking at outputs, not defined upfront. Research ("Who Validates the Validated?") found people think of failure modes only after seeing around 10 outputs, even experts. So refine rubrics as you grade, don't decouple evaluation from observation, and recompute judge precision/recall after each criteria change. Eval criteria and PRDs must stay flexible.

Variant: validating a classifier on known-label sets. A team validated an AI-content detector before using it at scale. They generated thousands of known-AI articles (detector was very predictive) and ran it on known-human content (self-written articles plus a 100,000-URL Common Crawl sample from before ChatGPT launched), finding a false positive rate around 8%. Only then did they apply it to search results and citations.

For PMs: be suspicious of claims like "it agrees 75% of the time" and ask for alignment on passes and fails separately. Losing trust in evals means losing trust in you.
when_to_use: After building an LLM judge and before trusting it, gating launches, or showing its scores to stakeholders
When a failure mode is rare and class imbalance could inflate agreement
When reviewing someone else's reported judge agreement
When iterating on a judge prompt, or after changing the judge model, prompt, policy, or criteria
When shipping a judge-based eval to production and you want a CI agreement gate
When using a classifier or detector to draw conclusions at scale and you must justify its reliability
When estimating the true failure rate from a judge's raw pass rate
when_not_to_use: Before you have any human labels to compare against
For deterministic or code-based checks that can be verified without a judge
For metrics without a binary outcome, which are hard to calibrate this way
When no reliable ground-truth set exists (e.g., no known human-only corpus for a detector)
When individual deterministic cases must all pass; use normal unit assertions instead
metric_or_method: Hand-label about 100 pass/fail examples and split into train (10-20%, few-shot), dev (40-45%, prompt iteration), and test (40-45%, untouched). Compute TPR, TNR, precision/recall, and the human-vs-judge confusion matrix on held-out data, requiring both TPR and TNR to be high. Sanity-check with an always-pass judge. Percent agreement of about 80-85% is a target for golden-set calibration, with 100% suspect. Rework the prompt if not, pin the judge model version, and recompute after any criteria change.
common_pitfalls: Relying on overall agreement or accuracy; an always-pass judge scores 90% when failures are 10% of cases
Stopping after the judge produces scores without measuring them against human labels
Using the whole dataset to build and test the judge, or touching the test set during development, which overfits
Chasing or accepting 100% agreement instead of treating it as a red flag for overfitting or sycophancy
Showing the human verdict to the judge, or letting case-sensitive output mismatches inflate disagreement
Jumping to a bigger model before filling policy knowledge gaps in the prompt
Using a floating model alias for the judge in CI, so the underlying version changes silently
Fixing criteria upfront and never revisiting them or re-validating the judge after they change

name: Vibe Checks
definition: A vibe check is a qualitative, experience-based evaluation in which practitioners use a new AI model or open-ended prototype on realistic, real-work tasks, record how it feels, and use the impressions to build model intuition, form hypotheses to verify with data, and decide when formal evals are worth defining.
explanation: The core method (Dan Shipper's team at Every) is to get early access to a new model, use it for the things you would normally do at work, and write up how it feels. This captures qualities that standard benchmarks miss. The best authors are people at the edge who build with and use the tools every day. Several variants and sub-steps extend this. Model Sommelier: use every new model to ship something, ideally on a persistent, low-stakes chassis project so the model is a tool rather than the goal. This reveals each model's character and different shape of strengths (for example, Qwen is good at long-horizon tasks and creative storytelling, while GLM is neurotic and precise with no vision), and counters the idea that models are fungible commodities. Team Vibe Check to Hypothesis Testing (Cat Wu): ask each team member for their impression of a new model, such as being too abrupt, not explaining its thinking, writing low-quality memories, or testing itself too much or too little. Cluster the recurring patterns into hypotheses and extract data to confirm or reject them, which helps when there is lots of data but little idea what to look for. Functional Prototype Testing (Howie Liu): rather than relying on PRDs or decks where claims are just words, build an open-ended functional prototype and try it on realistic, non-golden-path prompts. Judge feel, speed, and whether to expose reasoning or progress, for example with a progress bar. Vibes First, Evals Later (Howie Liu): for a completely novel capability, test ad hoc with varied prompts to see which use cases cluster around good results. Defining evals up front forces you to decide what good looks like before you know what the product is. Once the scaffold and target use cases are clear, define evals to measure improvement programmatically, and A/B test models or prompts only if you have the scale. This mirrors the double diamond: diverge, then converge. Qualitative Signal Over Premature Metrics (Aparna Chennapragada): at zero-to-one, metrics like CTR or retention with a thousand users give false precision. Gather qualitative signal ("the sound of click") and check that the product nails one or two core use cases, as voice assistants did with timers and music, before broadening scope or adopting mature metrics.
when_to_use: A new frontier model is released and you want to know how it behaves for real work tasks
Early exploration of a novel AI product or capability before formal evals exist
Choosing which model fits a type of product work and building intuition about comparative strengths
Standard benchmarks don't capture the subjective qualities you care about, such as feel, latency or UX
Deciding whether to expose reasoning or steps and add progress indicators
Lots of data but unclear what to look for; use team impressions to generate hypotheses
Zero-to-one products with small user bases, where CTR or retention would be meaningless
Judging whether a broad open-ended interface is ready to expand beyond a few core use cases
when_not_to_use: As the only gate for production quality; it is not rigorous or quantitative
When you need quantitative, reproducible measurements
When iterating on prompts, models or agentic workflows and you need repeatable measurement of improvement
Once scaffold and target use cases are known and formal evals can be defined
Post-product-market-fit or at scale, where fine-grained metrics are statistically meaningful
When evaluators are not real users of the tool for real tasks, or the prototype only supports scripted happy-path demos
metric_or_method: Phase 1: qualitative, hands-on use of a new model or open-ended prototype by daily practitioners on realistic, non-golden-path tasks, ideally on a persistent project, noting feel, speed, reasoning visibility, strengths and weaknesses. Phase 2: cluster recurring impressions into hypotheses and extract data to test them. Phase 3: once core use cases are clear, define formal evals and measure programmatically.
common_pitfalls: Having people who don't use the tool in real work write the evaluation
Treating it as a replacement for benchmarks rather than a complement
Treating anecdotal vibes as conclusions without checking whether they reflect a larger pattern
Testing only golden-path prompts or using a prototype that cannot take open-ended input
Relying on PRDs or decks, where claims are just words
Picking metrics or defining evals prematurely, which gives false precision and constrains you before the solution space is understood
Assuming models are fungible or ranked on a single intelligence axis rather than having different shapes of strength
Launching a broad 'say anything' interface before a few core use cases work reliably, or assuming you can A/B test everything early

[...] To me, evals are more useful, A, once you've converged on the basic scaffold of the form factor and you kind of know what are the use cases you want it to work well for and what you want to test against it.

When you have a thousand people, it doesn't mean anything. Retention also may not mean anything. So really being very wary of this big guy, big girl of grownup metrics as I call it, right? You are looking for more qualitative, the sound of click, and what is your... [...] So if you look at Alexa and Siri and Google Assistant and all these things, they had a very promising broad interface. You could say anything, but I think there was one or two things that it was really good at. You could set a timer, you could play music, and you could play trivia. And so you've got to nail those things before you say, "Oh yeah, here you can do anything with it," which is not a good recipe.

sources.title: How Anthropic’s product team moves faster than anyone else | Cat Wu (Head of Product, Claude Code)
sources.excerpt: So we often have team lunches and whenever there's a new model we're testing, one of the fastest ways for us to get feedback is to just at these team lunches, just go to every single person and just be like, "Hey, what is your vibe on the model?" [...] So that informs what data we look at to verify, okay, is this a larger pattern? So we have a ton of data, but it is very hard to extract insights, and so the feedback from this group helps us inform, okay, what are the hypotheses we want to test, and then we're able to extract data to test that.

sources.title: The AI-native startup: 5 products, 7-figure revenue, 100% AI-written code | Dan Shipper (co-founder/CEO of Every)
sources.excerpt: I think it's really important to do vibe checks and to call them vibe checks because they're about how does it feel to use this thing and how does it feel to use it for work for things that you would normally use it for in your job or in your life. Because I think that captures something that standard benchmarks just don't capture and really can't. And the best people to tell... to write a vibe check are people that are actually at the edge using it for stuff.
